en: The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Assembly. Chapter One: The Assembly.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery in the Jeta Grove near Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, one thousand upāsakas, and five hundred beggars.
At that time, there was a son of a householder in the assembly named Sujāta, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The six heretical teachers constantly expound the Dharma, instructing sentient beings, saying:..."
"If one can pay respectful homage to the six directions at dawn, one will obtain an increase in both life-span and wealth.
Why is this? The eastern quarter belongs to Śakra; if there is one who makes offerings, Śakra-devānām-indra will provide protection and assistance."
The southern region belongs to King Yama; those who make offerings there, King Yama shall protect and assist them.
The western region belongs to the deva Varuṇa; those who make offerings there, Varuṇa shall protect and assist them.
The northern region belongs to the deity Kubera; those who make offerings there will receive his protection and assistance.
The lower region belongs to the deity Agni; those who make offerings there will receive his protection and assistance.
"The land above belongs to the realm of Vāyu; those who make offerings there shall also be protected.
"World-Honored One!
Within the Buddha-dharma, do such six directions exist?"
“Good son! Within my Buddha-dharma there are also six directions, namely the six pāramitās.
The eastern direction is the dāna-pāramitā.”
Why is this? It is because that which first emerges does so for the sake of the causal conditions for the emergence of the light of wisdom.
That eastern direction belongs to the minds of sentient beings; if there are sentient beings who can make offerings to that *dānapāramitā*, their lifespan and wealth will thereby increase.
The south is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Why is this?
The perfection of ethical discipline is called "the right"; if one makes offerings there, one will likewise increase in lifespan and wealth.
The western direction is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Why is this?
That which is called the west is designated as "the rear"; because all unwholesome dharmas are cast behind, if one makes offerings there, one will obtain an increase in lifespan and wealth.
The north is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Why is this?
The name "North" signifies victory over all unwholesome dharmas; if one makes offerings there, one will obtain an increase in lifespan and wealth.
The lower part represents the dhyāna-pāramitā. Why is this?
Because it enables one to correctly observe the three evil realms; furthermore, if one makes offerings to it, one will also increase both lifespan and wealth.
The zenith is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Because the zenith is the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed; if one makes offerings there, one will obtain an increase in both life-span and wealth.
"Good son! These six directions belong to the minds of sentient beings; they are not as described by the six heterodox teachers.
Who is able to make offerings to these six directions?"
“Good son! Only a bodhisattva is able to make such offerings.
“World-Honored One!”
"For what reason is one called a Bodhisattva?
The Buddha said,
"Because they attain Bodhi, they are called Bodhisattvas."
“Because of the nature of bodhi, one is called a bodhisattva.
[The interlocutor asked: “World-Honored One!
If it is said that one is called a bodhisattva only after having attained bodhi, then before one has made offerings to those six directions, how can one be named a bodhisattva?”
If one is called a bodhisattva by virtue of having a nature, who possesses this nature?
One who possesses this nature is able to make offerings; if one lacks this nature, then one cannot make offerings!
Therefore, the Tathāgata should not say:
"Those six directions belong to the minds of sentient beings. "Good son!
One is not called a bodhisattva because of having attained awakening. Why is this?
One who has attained awakening is called a Buddha; one who has not yet attained awakening is called a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, it is because they do not possess such a nature that they are called Bodhisattvas. "Good son!
All sentient beings lack the nature of bodhi, just as all sentient beings lack the nature of a human or a celestial being, nor the nature of a lion, tiger, wolf, dog, or other such creatures."

In the present world, by reason of the harmonious causes and conditions of various wholesome karmas, one obtains the body of a human or a deva; by reason of the harmonious causes and conditions of unwholesome karma, one obtains the body of an animal such as a lion.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: because of the causal conditions of the harmonious integration of various wholesome karmas, one gives rise to the bodhicitta; therefore, one is called a "Bodhisattva.
If anyone were to say that all sentient beings possess the nature of a Bodhisattva, this meaning would not be correct.
Why is this? If there were an inherent nature, one would not need to cultivate the causes and conditions of wholesome deeds by making offerings to the six directions. Good son!
If there were such a thing as a fixed nature, then there would be neither the initial resolve nor the mind of regression;
rather, it is because of the causes and conditions of immeasurable wholesome karma that the arousal of the bodhicitta is called the "nature of a bodhisattva."

“Good son! There are sentient beings who practice the teachings of non-Buddhists; because they do not delight in the inverted doctrines of those external scriptures, they resolve their minds on Bodhi.
Or there are sentient beings who dwell in places of tranquility; through internal, virtuous causes and conditions, they resolve their minds on Bodhi.”
There are some sentient beings who, contemplating the faults of birth and death, give rise to the bodhicitta;
there are some sentient beings who, seeing evil or hearing of evil, give rise to the bodhicitta;
and there are some sentient beings who, deeply understanding their own greed, anger, ignorance, stinginess, and envy, give rise to the bodhicitta for the sake of self-reproach.
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing the five-fold supernatural powers of non-Buddhist seers and immortals, resolve their minds on Bodhi;
there may be sentient beings who, desiring to know whether the world is finite or infinite, resolve their minds on Bodhi;
and there may be sentient beings who, having seen or heard of the inconceivable nature of the Tathāgata, resolve their minds on Bodhi.
"Or there are sentient beings who, out of compassion, give rise to the bodhicitta;
or there are sentient beings who, out of love for sentient beings, give rise to the bodhicitta.
Good son!..."
The bodhicitta is of three kinds: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
If it were said that sentient beings definitely possess a fixed nature, why would one speak of these three kinds?
Sentient beings can transform a lower state of mind into a middling one, a middling mind into a superior one, a superior mind into a middling one, and a middling mind into a lower one.
Because sentient beings diligently cultivate immeasurable wholesome dharmas, they are able to progress upward;
because they do not diligently cultivate them, they regress and fall to a lower state.
If one skillfully cultivates progress, it is called non-retrogression; if one does not cultivate progress, it is called retrogression.
Because one constantly cultivates and accumulates goodness for the sake of all infinite sentient beings at all times, it is called non-retrogression;
if it is not thus, it is called retrogression, and such a bodhisattva would possess a mind of retreat and a mind of fear.

If, at all times, you cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings and attain non-retrogression, I therefore grant you this prediction: you shall soon realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment on this Ground of Great Joy.
“Good son! The three kinds of bodhi have no fixed nature;
if they possessed a fixed nature, those who have already resolved upon the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha would be unable to resolve upon the mind of bodhi.”
Good son! Just as the Sangha has no fixed nature, these three natures are likewise.
If anyone says that there is a fixed nature, they are called a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
Why is this? Because various non-Buddhists lack the principle of cause and effect; for example, Īśvara is neither cause nor effect. "Good son!

Some may say that the nature of a bodhisattva is like the certain presence of gold-nature within a stone; because it is brought forth through skillful means and conditions, it becomes functional as gold.
To claim that the nature of a bodhisattva is likewise is the teaching of the Brahmins.

Why is this? The Brahmins and others constantly claim that there is a nyagrodha tree within a nyagrodha seed, and that fire and stone exist within the eye; therefore, for these Brahmins, there is neither cause nor effect—the cause is itself the effect, and the effect is itself the cause.
That a *nyagrodha* tree exists because it is fully possessed of *nyagrodha* seeds should be understood as the cause-and-effect relationship of a brahmin;
however, this interpretation is not correct. Why is that?
Because the cause is subtle while the effect is coarse.
If one were to say that fire definitely exists within the eye, then the eye would be burned;
if the eye were burned, how could it see?
If there is a stone in the eye, the stone will obstruct the eye;
if the eye is thus obstructed, how can it see? Good son!
As the brahmins say:
"What exists is indeed existent; what does not exist is indeed non-existent.
That which is non-existent does not arise, and that which exists should not perish."
If one says that there is the nature of gold within stone, the gold does not speak of the nature, nor does the nature speak of the gold.

Good son! It is through causes and conditions that there is conjunction; because of the conjunction of conditions, that which was originally non-existent subsequently comes to be. It is not as the Brahmin claims—that what is non-existent is eternally non-existent.
What is the meaning of this?
When gold is combined with mercury, the gold is destroyed; if one were to say that it exists, it should not be destroyed.
What is the meaning of this?
If one says that sentient beings possess the nature of a bodhisattva, this is called the way of externalists and not the Buddha-way. Good son!
For example, it is because of the conditions of combining stones that gold becomes functional; the nature of a bodhisattva is also like this.

Sentient beings possess volition, which is called the mind of desire; by means of such desire, through the causal conditions of wholesome karma, they give rise to the bodhicitta—this is what is termed the nature of a bodhisattva.

Good son! For example, just as sentient beings have no bodhi beforehand and only possess it later, so too is the nature [of phenomena]: it does not exist beforehand and exists afterward; therefore, one cannot say that it definitely exists.
“Good son! One is called a bodhisattva because they seek great wisdom;

because they desire to know the reality of all dharmas, because of their great adornment, because their mind is firm and steadfast, because they deliver many sentient beings, and because they do not begrudge their own body or life—this is called a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna.”
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who regress; second, those who do not regress.”
One who has already cultivated the karma for the thirty-two marks is called "non-retrogressive";
if one has not yet been able to cultivate them, this is called "retrogression.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
The first is the renunciant, and the second is the householder.
A renunciant bodhisattva who upholds the eight grave precepts with complete purity is called "non-retrogressive";
a householder bodhisattva who upholds the six grave precepts with complete purity is likewise called "non-retrogressive."
“Good son! The merit obtained by non-Buddhists who have severed desire surpasses all the merit possessed by sentient beings in the desire realm;
a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) surpasses all non-Buddhists with divergent views.”
The Sakṛdāgāmin surpasses all those who have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna;
the Anāgāmin surpasses all those who have attained the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin;
and the Arhat surpasses all those who have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
A person who is a pratyekabuddha surpasses all those who have attained the fruit of arhatship;
a layperson who gives rise to the bodhicitta surpasses all those who have attained the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.

For those who have left the household life to generate the bodhicitta, this is not difficult; however, for those who remain in the household life to generate the bodhicitta, this is truly called inconceivable.
Why is this? Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
When a person living at home resolves upon the Bodhicitta, all the devas from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven are filled with great wonder and joy, and speak these words:
"I have now obtained the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Chapter Two: Generating the Bodhicitta. In the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Two, "Generating the Bodhicitta," Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
"How do sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta? "Good son,
they give rise to the bodhicitta for two reasons:"
First, increasing the lifespan; second, increasing wealth and resources.
"Furthermore, there are two matters:
first, to ensure that the lineage of the Bodhisattvas is not severed; second, to sever the afflictions of sin and suffering for sentient beings."
"Furthermore, there are two matters:
first, that one observes for oneself how throughout immeasurable lifetimes one has undergone great suffering and affliction without obtaining any benefit;
second, that although there are immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, none of them can deliver my person, and thus I must deliver myself."
“Furthermore, there are two things:
first, performing various wholesome deeds; second, not losing them once they have been performed.
Furthermore, there are two things:”
First, it is to surpass the karmic rewards of all humans and devas; second, it is to surpass the karmic rewards of all followers of the two vehicles.
"Furthermore, there are two matters:
first, to undergo great suffering for the sake of seeking the path to bodhi; second, to attain immeasurable and great benefits."
"Furthermore, there are two matters:

first, that all Buddhas of the past and future, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were all like my own body; second, that one deeply contemplates that Bodhi is a dharma that can be attained; for these reasons, one resolves the mind [for enlightenment]."
“Furthermore, there are two matters:
first, observing that although those at the sixth stage may have regressive thoughts, they still surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
second, because they diligently seek the unsurpassed fruit.”
"Furthermore, there are two matters:

first, the desire to cause all sentient beings to attain complete liberation; second, the desire to cause sentient beings' liberation to surpass the fruits and rewards obtained by those of external paths."
"Furthermore, there are two things:
first, not abandoning any sentient beings; second, relinquishing all afflictions.
Furthermore, there are two things:"
First, to sever the present suffering and affliction of sentient beings; second, to prevent the future suffering and affliction of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two matters:
first, to sever the obstacles to wisdom; second, to sever the physical obstacles of sentient beings.
“Good son! There are five matters for generating the bodhicitta: first, associating with virtuous friends;
second, severing the mind of anger; third, following the teacher’s instructions; fourth, giving rise to a heart of compassion; and fifth, practicing diligence with vigor.”
"Furthermore, there are five matters: first, not seeing the faults of others;

second, although seeing the faults of others, the mind feels no regret [regarding one's own conduct]; third, having attained wholesome dharmas, not giving rise to arrogance; fourth, seeing the virtuous deeds of others, not giving rise to envy; fifth, regarding all sentient beings with the thought of them being as one's only son."
“Good son! Once a person of wisdom has resolved upon bodhicitta, they are able to destroy the fruits of evil karma, even if they are as vast as Mount Sumeru.
A person of wisdom resolves upon bodhicitta for three reasons:”

First, seeing the sentient beings of the five turbidities in this degenerate age; second, seeing that the Tathāgata possesses inconceivable supernatural powers and the strength of the Way; third, hearing the eight kinds of wondrous voices of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, there are two matters:

first, clearly knowing for oneself that one's own body possesses suffering; second, knowing the suffering of sentient beings as if it were one's own suffering, and acting to sever that suffering just as one would for oneself, without distinction."

“Good son! If there is anyone who can resolve their mind toward bodhicitta, you should know that such a person is able to pay homage to the six directions and increase their life-span and wealth; this is not as the non-Buddhists proclaim.”
Chapter 3: On Compassion. In the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Three, "On Compassion," Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!
Those six teachers and their like do not speak of cause and effect, yet the Tathāgata now speaks of two kinds of causes: [text continues]"
The first is the productive cause (*janakahetu*), and the second is the revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*).
As the Buddha first taught regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta, is this a productive cause or a revealing cause?
“Good son! For the sake of sentient beings, I may speak of one cause, or two causes, or three causes, or four causes, or five causes, or six, seven, up to twelve causes.”
To speak of "one cause" refers to the productive cause (*janakahetu*).
To speak of "two causes" refers to the productive cause and the revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*).
To speak of "three causes" refers to afflictions, karma, and the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*).
Regarding the "four causes," these refer to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the "five causes," these refer to the five future factors (*pañca-anga*).
Regarding the "six causes," these are as described in the sūtras as the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*).
Regarding the "seven causes," they are as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the "eight causes," they are the eight factors of the present.
Regarding the "nine causes," they are as explained in the *Mahānagara-sūtra*.
Regarding the ten causes, they are as explained to the upāsaka Mahānāman.
Regarding the eleven causes, they are as explained in the *Jñānamudrā*.
Regarding the twelve causes, they are as in the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

“Good son! All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) have immeasurable and boundless causes, and all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) have immeasurable and boundless causes. Because a wise person desires to know them all completely, they resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*);
for this reason, the Tathāgata is named ‘Omniscient One’ (*sarvajña*).”
“Good son! When all sentient beings resolve upon bodhicitta, there may be a productive cause, or a revealing cause, or both a productive cause and a revealing cause.”
You should now know this:
that which is the cause of birth is none other than great compassion;
because of this compassion, one is able to resolve upon the mind [of enlightenment]. Therefore, the compassionate mind serves as the cause of birth.
“World-Honored One!
How does one cultivate the mind of compassion? “Good son!
The wise one deeply perceives that all sentient beings are submerged in the great ocean of the suffering of birth and death; wishing to rescue and deliver them, he therefore gives rise to compassion.

Furthermore, seeing that sentient beings do not yet possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, or the three types of mindfulness, he thinks: "How may I cause them to be fully endowed with these?"
Therefore, compassion arises.
Furthermore, seeing that sentient beings harbor much resentment and malice, yet one regards them as kin, compassion arises.
Moreover, seeing that sentient beings are迷失 (lost) on the right path and have no one to guide them, compassion arises.
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings lying in the mire of the five desires and unable to emerge from it, yet remaining heedless as before, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings constantly bound by wealth, property, wives, and children, and unable to abandon them, he gives rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings give rise to arrogance because of their physical form and life-span, he therefore gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings harbor thoughts of intimacy toward evil associates who deceive and delude them—such as the six heretical teachers—he therefore gives rise to compassion."

"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings fallen into the realm of birth and existence (*bhavāgra*), undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, yet still delighting in and attached to them, he gives rise to compassion.

Furthermore, seeing sentient beings who create unwholesome and evil karma of body, speech, and mind, and who undergo much suffering as its fruit, yet still delight in and are attached to it, he gives rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings thirsting for the five desires like one who drinks salt water when parched, he gives rise to compassion.
Moreover, seeing that although sentient beings seek happiness, they do not create the causes of happiness;
and although they do not delight in suffering, they joyfully create the causes of suffering."
Seeing that they do not possess the precepts while desiring to experience celestial bliss, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings give rise to notions of "I" and "mine" regarding that which is non-self and devoid of "mine," he gives rise to compassion.
"Furthermore, seeing that sentient beings lack a fixed nature and transmigrate through the five realms of existence, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing that sentient beings fear birth, aging, and death, yet continue to create the karma for birth, aging, and death, he gives rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings undergo physical and mental suffering while continuing to create karma, one gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings suffer from the pain of separation from those they love yet fail to sever that attachment, one gives rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings dwelling in the darkness of ignorance, unaware of the blazing lamp of wisdom, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings being scorched by the fire of afflictions, yet unable to seek the water of samādhi-concentration, he gives rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings commit immeasurable evils for the sake of the pleasures of the five desires, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings who know the suffering of the five desires yet seek them without ceasing—like a hungry person eating poisoned rice—he gives rise to compassion."

Furthermore, seeing sentient beings dwelling in an evil age, encountering tyrannical kings and undergoing much suffering and affliction, yet still remaining heedless, he therefore gives rise to compassion.
“Furthermore, seeing sentient beings transmigrating through the eight sufferings and not knowing how to sever such causes of suffering, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings afflicted by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, lacking self-mastery, he gives rise to compassion.”
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings who violate the prohibitive precepts and are destined to undergo rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals, one gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings who lack mastery over their physical form, strength, lifespan, well-being, and eloquence, one gives rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings with incomplete faculties, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings born in borderlands who do not cultivate wholesome dharmas, he gives rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings dwelling in an age of famine, their bodies emaciated and weak, plundering one another, he gives rise to compassion.

Furthermore, seeing sentient beings dwelling in an age of war, harming one another, their malevolent minds flourishing, and destined to receive the fruit of immeasurable suffering as retribution, he gives rise to compassion."

"Furthermore, seeing sentient beings encounter a Buddha appearing in the world and hear the preaching of the pure Dharma of ambrosia, yet being unable to receive and uphold it, I give rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings place their faith in evil friends and never follow the teachings of spiritual benefactors, I give rise to compassion."
"Furthermore, seeing that sentient beings possess great wealth and treasures yet are unable to practice renunciation and giving, he gives rise to compassion.
Furthermore, seeing that sentient beings engage in plowing fields, sowing seeds, and the buying and selling of merchants—all of which are suffering—he gives rise to compassion."

Furthermore, seeing sentient beings who do not love or cherish one another—such as parents and children, brothers and sisters, wives and children, slaves, retinues, and kinsmen—he gives rise to compassion.

“Good son! A wise person should contemplate the meditative bliss of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as being like the suffering of hell; since all sentient beings share it equally, one should therefore give rise to compassion.”
“Good son! When one has not yet attained the Way, practicing such contemplation is called compassion;
once the Way has been attained, it is called great compassion.”
Why is this? Before one has attained the Way, although one performs such contemplations, both the contemplation and sentient beings are finite;
once the Way has been attained, both the contemplation and sentient beings are entirely infinite. For this reason, it is called "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā).
Before attaining the Way, the mind of compassion wavers and shifts; therefore, it is called "compassion" (karuṇā).
Once the Way has been attained, there is no longer any wavering or shifting; therefore, it is called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā).
Before one has attained the Way, because one is as yet unable to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, it is called "compassion" (karuṇā);
once the Way has been attained, because one is able to provide great rescue and deliverance, it is called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā).
When one has not yet attained the Way, one practices without being conjoined with wisdom; therefore, it is called "compassion" (karuṇā).
Once the Way has been attained, one practices in conjunction with wisdom; therefore, it is called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā).

“Good son! When a wise person cultivates compassion, although they may not yet be able to sever the suffering and affliction of sentient beings, there are already immeasurable matters of great benefit.
Good son!”
The six pāramitās all take compassion as their generative cause.
"Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
The first is the renunciant, and the second is the householder.
For a renunciant to cultivate compassion is not difficult;
for a householder to cultivate compassion is indeed difficult.
Why is this? Because those who live at home have many adverse causes and conditions. Good son!
If a layperson does not cultivate compassion, they cannot obtain the upāsaka precepts; however, once they have cultivated compassion, they will immediately obtain them.
Good son!

Those who have left the household life can only fulfill five of the perfections (pāramitās), but cannot fulfill the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā); those who remain at home, however, are able to fulfill it.
Why is this? Because they practice all forms of giving at all times.

Therefore, a householder should first cultivate compassion; once compassion has been cultivated, it should be known that such a person is able to fully possess ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

If one cultivates a heart of compassion, one can give what is difficult to give, endure what is difficult to endure, and perform what is difficult to perform; for this reason, compassion is the root of all wholesome dharmas.

“Good son! If a person can cultivate such a mind of compassion, you should know that this person can destroy evil karma as vast as Mount Sumeru; before long, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Whatever small amount of wholesome karma this person performs, the fruit and retribution they obtain will be like Mount Sumeru.”
Chapter Four: On Liberation The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Chapter Four: On Liberation “Good son!
If a good man or a good woman practices compassion, you should know that such a person attains the factors of liberation, which constitute the essence of all dharmas.”
Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what you have called ‘essence,’ what constitutes that essence?”
“Good son! These are body, speech, and mind.
This body, speech, and mind are obtained through skillful means.”
There are two kinds of skillful means:
first, hearing with the ears; second, contemplation.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
"First is generosity, second is ethical discipline, and third is extensive learning. Sujāta said,
"World-Honored One!"
"As the Buddha has taught that one attains the factors conducive to liberation through three skillful means, do these three skillful means have a fixed number?
"No, son of good family."
Why is this? There are those who, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, have bestowed immeasurable wealth upon immeasurable people, yet are still unable to attain the factors conducive to liberation;
whereas there are those who, in a single moment, give a handful of flour to a single beggar and are able to attain such factors conducive to liberation.
There are those who, having upheld the prohibitive precepts under immeasurable Buddhas, are still unable to attain the factors conducive to liberation;
yet there are others who, by upholding the eight precepts for a single day and night, are able to obtain the factors conducive to liberation.

There may be someone who, throughout immeasurable lifetimes and in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, has received, upheld, read, and recited the twelve divisions of the scriptures, yet still cannot attain the dharmas conducive to liberation;
whereas another person, by reading only a single four-line verse, is able to obtain the dharmas conducive to liberation.
Why is this? Because the minds of all sentient beings are not the same. "Good son!

If a person cannot single-mindedly contemplate the faults of birth and death and the peace and bliss of nirvana, such a person, though they may practice generosity, maintain precepts, and possess extensive learning, will ultimately be unable to attain the factors conducive to liberation.

If one can feel weary of the faults of birth and death and deeply perceive the merit, peace, and bliss of nirvana, such a person, even with little giving, little morality, and little learning, will immediately be able to attain the factors conducive to liberation.
“Good son! One who attains this Dharma, during the three periods—the time when a Buddha appears in the world; the time when a Pratyekabuddha appears;
[and the time when a Śrāvaka appears]—”
If these two did not exist, then when the Akaniṣṭha devas speak of liberation, such a person, having heard it, will attain the stage of liberation. Good son!

In the past, when I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I saw neither Buddhas nor pratyekabuddhas; I heard the devas of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) speak of the Dharma of liberation, and upon hearing them, I immediately resolved my mind [upon awakening].
“Good son! Such a Dharma as this cannot be attained by the devas of the desire realm. Why is that?
Because of negligence,
it is also not something that can be attained by the gods of the Form Realm. Why is this?
Because it lacks the three skillful means,
it is also not something that can be attained by the gods of the formless realm. Why is this?
Because there is no body or speech.
This essence of the Dharma consists of body, speech, and mind;
it is likewise unattainable by the people of Uttarakuru.
Why is this? Because they lack the three skillful means.
This stage of liberation can be attained by three types of persons: namely, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

If sentient beings encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they may transform the liberation of a śrāvaka into the liberation of a pratyekabuddha, and transform the liberation of a pratyekabuddha into the liberation of a bodhisattva;
the portion of the dharma of liberation attained by a bodhisattva cannot be regressed from, nor can it be destroyed.
Sujāta said: "World-Honored One!
By what further principle can a person who expounds the Dharma skillfully distinguish that such individuals possess the portion of liberation?"
"Do such people as these lack the portion of liberation?
"Good son, such a Dharma is attained by two kinds of persons: namely, the layperson and the renunciant."

These two kinds of people listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart; having heard it, they receive and uphold it. Upon hearing of the sufferings of the three evil realms, fear arises in their hearts, the hairs on their bodies stand on end, and tears flow profusely. They steadfastly maintain the precepts and fasts, not daring to violate them even in the case of minor offenses. It should be known that such persons have attained the dharma of the stage of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

“Good son! Although various non-Buddhists may attain the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and live for immeasurable kalpas, if they cannot obtain the dharmas conducive to liberation, you should regard such persons as beings of the hells.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who has endured great suffering in the Avīci Hell for immeasurable kalpas, yet is able to attain such a dharma conducive to liberation, one should regard that person as one destined for nirvāṇa.
"Good son! For this reason, I give rise to a heart of compassion for Udraka Rāmaputra, but I do not give rise to a heart of pity for Devadatta. Good son!"

For instance, although Śāriputra and others sought the path to bodhi for sixty thousand kalpas and subsequently regressed, it was because they had not yet attained the dharmas conducive to liberation;
nevertheless, they still surpassed those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle in terms of their sharp faculties.
“Good son! This Dharma has three levels, namely: inferior, middling, and superior. The inferior refers to the śrāvakas;
the middling refers to the pratyekabuddhas; and the superior refers to the Buddha.”
"Good son!

There are those who diligently seek the upāsaka precepts and practice according to what they have heard for immeasurable lifetimes, yet still do not obtain the precepts. Likewise, there are renunciants who seek the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī precepts and practice according to what they have heard for immeasurable lifetimes, yet are likewise unable to obtain them."
Why is this? Because they are unable to attain the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-dharma*).
Therefore, this may be called the cultivation of morality (*śīlabhāvanā*), but it is not called the upholding of morality (*śīladhāraṇa*).

“Good son! If bodhisattvas attain the dharmas conducive to liberation, they will never create karma with the intent to seek birth in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they always vow to be born in places where they can benefit sentient beings.
If they know for certain that they possess karma for rebirth in the heavens, they immediately dedicate this karma toward seeking birth among human beings.”
"Karma refers to what are called giving, precepts, and the cultivation of meditative concentration. 'Good son!
If a śrāvaka attains the stage of liberation, they will not exceed three lifetimes before attaining full liberation."
The Pratyekabuddhas are likewise so;

the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the stage conducive to liberation, though they pass through immeasurable bodies, never regress in the interim, and with this non-regressive mind, they surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"Good son!
If one attains such dharmas conducive to liberation, even though one's giving may be slight, one obtains immeasurable fruit;
the same is true for slight observance of precepts and slight learning."
Even if such a person were to dwell in the three evil realms, they would ultimately not suffer the pains experienced by those in the three evil realms.
If bodhisattvas attain such factors conducive to liberation, it is called the Stage of Flexibility.
For what reason is it called the Stage of Taming and Softening?
Because all afflictions gradually become weak and feeble, it is called "flowing against the current.
"If, O son of good family!"
There are four kinds of persons:

first, those who follow the current of birth and death; second, those who go against the current of birth and death; third, those who neither follow nor go against it; and fourth, those who have reached the other shore.
Good son! Such a dharma is called the Stage of Softness for śrāvakas; for bodhisattvas, it is also called Softness, and is further named the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
For what reason is it called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi)?
Because one does not regress upon hearing [the Dharma], it is called the Stage of Joy.
For what reason is one called a Bodhisattva?
Because they are able to constantly awaken the minds of sentient beings.
Although such bodhisattvas know external treatises, they do not personally uphold them, nor do they teach them to others.
Such bodhisattvas are not called humans or devas; they are not subsumed within the five destinies. This is called practicing the path of non-obstruction.
“Good son! Enlightenment has four seeds: first, not coveting wealth and goods;
second, not begrudging one’s body or life; third, practicing patience; and fourth, having compassion for sentient beings.”
Good son! There are five further matters that cause such seeds of bodhi to increase:
first, one does not give rise to thoughts of self-contempt within oneself, saying, "I am unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Second, though one's own person undergoes suffering, the mind feels no weariness or regret;
third, one practices with diligent vigor, neither ceasing nor resting;
fourth, one rescues and relieves sentient beings from their immeasurable sufferings and afflictions.
Fifth, they constantly praise the subtle and wondrous merits of the Triple Gem.
When a person of wisdom cultivates bodhi, they should always practice and accumulate these five matters.
"There are six further matters for increasing and inflaming the seeds of bodhi, namely: the *dānapāramitā* through to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
These six kinds of matters increase by means of a single factor, which is heedfulness (*apramāda*).
If a bodhisattva is heedless, they cannot increase these six matters; if they are heedful, they can increase them."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva seeks awakening, there are further four matters: first, to draw near to virtuous friends;
second, to have a mind that is firm and difficult to destroy; third, to be able to perform what is difficult to perform; and fourth, to have compassion for sentient beings.”
Furthermore, there are four matters:

first, to feel joy in one's heart upon seeing others obtain benefit; second, to always delight in praising the merits of others; third, to always delight in cultivating and accumulating the dharmas of the six foundations of mindfulness; and fourth, to diligently speak of all the faults inherent in birth and death.
"Good son!
If anyone were to say that one can attain bodhi apart from these eight dharmas, there is no such possibility. Good son!"

If there is a bodhisattva who, at the very moment they first resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, is then named an unsurpassed field of merit; such a bodhisattva excels all worldly affairs and all sentient beings.
“Good son! Although people may say that there are immeasurable Buddhas in immeasurable worlds, this path of the Buddha is extremely difficult to attain. Why is this?
The worlds are boundless, and sentient beings are likewise;
sentient beings are boundless, and the Buddhas are also thus.
If the path of Buddhahood were easily attained, then a single Buddha, a World-Honored One, would have already transformed and delivered all sentient beings!
If that were so, then the sentient beings in the world would be finite. Good son!

When a Buddha appears in the world, he can deliver ninety-nine thousand nayutas of people, and his śrāvaka disciples deliver one nayuta; yet all sentient beings still cannot be exhausted, and for this reason they are called infinite.
Therefore, in the Śrāvaka sūtras, I have stated that there are no Buddhas of the ten directions. Why is this?

It is because I feared that sentient beings might disparage the Buddha-way—since the holy path of the Buddhas is not encompassed by the mundane world—and thus the Tathāgata’s teaching is not false. The World-Honored Tathāgatas possess no envy; it is because they are difficult to encounter that I have said there are no Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in the ten directions.
"Good son!
Immeasurable sentient beings resolve to attain bodhicitta, yet they are unable to practice the bodhisattva path to its ultimate conclusion.
If someone were to raise an objection, saying:"

If there are immeasurable Buddhas existing in the present, why does the sutra speak only of immeasurable Buddhas in the two periods of the past and the future, and not mention immeasurable Buddhas in the present?
"Good son!
In one land, I say that there have been Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past and future, while in the present world, there is but a single Buddha. Good son!"

The meaning of ultimate reality enables one to attain the Buddha-way; yet among the immeasurable sentient beings who practice this Buddha-way, many fall back, and only occasionally does a single person succeed in crossing over, like the *āmra* flower or the spawn of fish.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For an ordained bodhisattva to attain the factors conducive to liberation is not difficult;
for one who is a householder to attain them is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are entangled by many evil causes and conditions.
Chapter Five: The Three Kinds of Bodhi In the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Five: The Three Kinds of Bodhi, Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.
There are three kinds of bodhi:
First is the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, second is the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas, and third is the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
If one who attains enlightenment is called a Buddha, for what reason are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas not called Buddhas?

If awakening to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) constitutes being a Buddha, then since śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also awaken to the nature of phenomena, for what reason are they not called Buddhas?
If possessing all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) constitutes being a Buddha, then since śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also possess all-knowledge, for what further reason are they not called Buddhas?
"What is called 'all' refers precisely to the Four Noble Truths.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
There are three kinds of bodhi:
first, that which is attained through hearing; second, that which is attained through reflection; and third, that which is attained through cultivation.
Because Śrāvakas attain [realization] through hearing, they are not called Buddhas;
because Pratyekabuddhas awaken to a small portion [of truth] after reflection, they are called Pratyekabuddhas;
the Tathāgata has no teacher and does not rely on hearing or reflection, but attains awakening to all things through cultivation—therefore, he is called a Buddha.
“Good son! Because one thoroughly understands the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one is called a Buddha.
There are two kinds of the nature of phenomena:”
First is the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), and second is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Because śrāvakas know only the general characteristic, they are not called Buddhas.
Pratyekabuddhas likewise know the general characteristic, but because they do not attain it through hearing [the teachings of others], they are called pratyekabuddhas and are not called Buddhas.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has fully awakened to all general and specific characteristics; not relying on hearing or reflection, he attained realization alone without a teacher through cultivation, and is therefore named Buddha.
"Good son!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with the wisdom of conditions (*pratyaya-jñāna*). Although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas know the Four Truths, they are not fully endowed with the wisdom of conditions; for this reason, they cannot be called Buddhas.
Because the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with the wisdom of conditions, he is named Buddha."
“Good son! It is like the river Ganges, which three kinds of animals cross together: the rabbit, the horse, and the fragrant elephant.
The rabbit does not reach the bottom, but passes by floating on the water;”
The horse may reach the bottom or not reach the bottom;
the elephant, however, reaches the very bottom.
The River Ganges is, in fact, the river of the twelve links of dependent origination.
When the Śrāvakas cross over, they are like that rabbit;
when the Pratyekabuddhas cross over, they are like that horse;
when the Tathāgata crosses over, he is like the fragrant elephant. For this reason, the Tathāgata is named Buddha.

Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have severed their afflictions, they have not severed their habitual tendencies; the Tathāgata, however, is able to uproot the very source of all afflictions and habitual tendencies, and is therefore called a Buddha.
“Good son! There are two kinds of doubt:
first, the doubt of affliction; second, the indeterminate doubt.”
Those of the Two Vehicles sever the doubt of afflictions but do not sever the indeterminate;
the Tathāgata severs both such doubts entirely, and for this reason he is called a Buddha. "Good son!

The śrāvaka grows weary of extensive learning, and the pratyekabuddha grows weary of contemplation; the Buddha, however, never tires of these two mental activities, and for this reason he is called a Buddha.
“Good son! It is like a pure object placed in a pure vessel; both the interior and exterior are pure.
Although the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is pure, their vessels are not. The Tathāgata is not so; his wisdom and his vessel are both pure. For this reason, he is called a Buddha.”
Good son! Purity is of two kinds:
first, purity of wisdom; second, purity of practice.
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess pure wisdom, their conduct is not pure;
the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has both wisdom and conduct that are pure, and for this reason he is called a Buddha.
“Good son! The practices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are limited, whereas the practices of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, are limitless; for this reason, he is called a Buddha.
Good son!...”

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is able to destroy the two obstacles in a single thought-moment—the first being the obstacle to knowledge (jñeyāvaraṇa) and the second being the obstacle to liberation (vimokṣāvaraṇa)—and for this reason he is called a Buddha.
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the causes of wisdom and the fruits of wisdom; for this reason, he is called a Buddha. "Good son!

The words spoken by the Tathāgata are non-dual and without error, nor are they false. His wisdom is unimpeded, and his eloquence is likewise so. He is fully possessed of the knowledge of causes, the knowledge of time, and the knowledge of signs. He has nothing to conceal and requires no protection; none can find fault in him. He thoroughly knows the causes and conditions for the arising of afflictions and the knots of all sentient beings, as well as the causes and conditions for their cessation. He cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas. Possessing great compassion, he rescues others from suffering and distress. He is fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three mindful establishments. Both the power of his body and the power of his mind are completely perfected."
“What is meant by being fully endowed with physical strength? Good son!

In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is a great city named Sudarśana. That city is ten thousand li in both length and breadth, contains one million palaces and chambers, and is inhabited by one million six hundred and sixty-six thousand six hundred and sixty-six devas.”

During the three months of summer, Śakra Devānām Indra desired to go to the Pārijāta grove to enjoy himself and take pleasure. On Mount Gandhamādana there was a fragrant elephant named Airāvata, endowed with seven heads. When Śakra formed this thought, the elephant, knowing his intention, immediately came forth. All the gods residing within the city of Sudarśana mounted upon its heads, and it traveled by circling toward that grove, which lay fifty yojanas from the city.

The physical strength of this elephant surpasses the physical strength of all other fragrant elephants; even if eighteen thousand such fragrant elephants were joined together, their combined strength would only equal that of a single joint of the Buddha’s body. Therefore, his physical strength excels the strength of all sentient beings.
The world is boundless, and sentient beings are likewise;
the power of the Tathāgata’s mind is also boundless.
For this reason, only the Tathāgata is uniquely entitled to be called a Buddha; those of the two vehicles are not called Buddhas.

For these reasons, he is called the Unsurpassed Teacher; he is called the Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa), the Fragrant Elephant among Men, the Lion, the Dragon King, and the Tamer and Guide; he is called the Great Captain, the Great Physician, the King of Great Bulls, and the Bull-King among Men; he is called the Pure Lotus, the Self-Awakened One without a Teacher, and the Eye for all sentient beings!
He is a great donor, a great śramaṇa, and a great brāhmaṇa; he maintains tranquility and the precepts, practices with diligent vigor, has reached the other shore, and has attained liberation.
"Good son!
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess bodhi, they entirely lack these qualities; for this reason, they are called 'Buddha. Good son!"
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.
For a bodhisattva who has left the home life, it is not difficult to distinguish these three kinds of bodhi.
To engage in conceptual discrimination while living at home is indeed difficult.
Why is this? Because those who live at home are entangled and surrounded by many unwholesome causes and conditions.
Chapter Six: Cultivating the Karma for the Thirty-two Marks. Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Chapter Six: Cultivating the Karma for the Thirty-two Marks.
Sujāta said: “World-Honored One!”
“As the Buddha has spoken of the physical strength of a bodhisattva,
when will it be accomplished? The Buddha said, “Good son!
When first cultivating the karma for the thirty-two marks,
O son of good family!
When a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates such karma, they receive the name "Bodhisattva" and simultaneously attain two concentrations:
First, the concentration of bodhi; second, the concentration of existence.
Furthermore, there are two concentrations:
first, the concentration of knowing past lives; second, the concentration of producing the causes for the True Dharma.
"Good son!
From the time a bodhisattva cultivates the karma for the thirty-two marks until he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, throughout that interval, he remains insatiable in his extensive learning."

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates each individual mark, it is surrounded by a hundred merits; cultivating fifty aspects of the mind and perfecting fifty aspects of the mind constitutes what is called the "hundredfold merits."
“Good son! All the merit possessed by all the worlds is not equal to the merit of a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata;
the merit of all the pores of the Tathāgata is not equal to the merit of a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana).”
The merit of the eighty secondary marks, when combined, does not equal the merit of a single primary mark;
the merit of all the primary marks is not equal to the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft) mark;
and the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark, in turn, cannot equal that of the *uṣṇīṣa* (invisible crown) mark.

“Good son! Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Bodhisattva has constantly performed great benefit for all sentient beings and diligently cultivated all wholesome deeds with a sincere heart. For this reason, the Tathāgata has fully accomplished immeasurable merits;
these thirty-two marks are the fruition of his great compassion.”
Although a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses these marks, they are not clearly manifest nor fully perfected.
The essential substance of the karma for these marks consists of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
When practicing this karma, it is not among the devas nor in Uttarakuru; it occurs only in the three continents, in a male body and not in a female body.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have cultivated these practices, they are said to have fulfilled three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and will successively attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! In the past, under the Buddha Ratnashikhin, I fulfilled the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa;
under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I fulfilled the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.”
Under the Buddha Kāśyapa, I completed the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa. Good son!

In the past, under the Buddha Śākyamuni, I first gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Having given rise to this mind, I made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, planted various roots of goodness, cultivated the path, maintained the precepts, and applied myself with diligence and extensive learning.
"Good son!

Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated these karmas for the thirty-two marks, he knows with absolute clarity that he will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, as clearly as one observes an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand."
Although these karmas are fixed, the sequence of their cultivation is not necessarily fixed!
"Some people say:
'The Tathāgata first attained the mark of the bull-king’s eyes.'"

Why is this? While practicing as a bodhisattva over immeasurable lifetimes, he delighted in gazing upon sentient beings with a benevolent eye and a harmonious look; for this reason, he first attained the mark of the bull-king eyes, and subsequently attained the remaining marks.
"Or there are those who say:
'The Tathāgata first attained the mark of the eightfold Brahma-voice, and the others were attained in succession. Why is this?'"

When he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly used gentle speech, prefacing his words with truthfulness to teach and transform sentient beings; for this reason, he first attained the mark of the eight qualities of Brahma-sound.
"Some may say: 'The Tathāgata first attains the mark of the invisible crown of the head, and the others are attained in succession. Why is this?'"

When he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he made offerings to his teachers, elders, Buddhas, and bodhisattvas; because he prostrated with his head at their feet to overcome pride, he first attained the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
"Or there are those who say:
'The Tathāgata first attained the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, and the others were attained in succession. Why is this?'"
When he was a bodhisattva, because he did not deceive any sentient beings throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he first attained the mark of the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows,
O son of good family!
Except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, no one else is able to explain such characteristics of karma.
"Good son! Or again, there may be someone who explains them in succession, saying:
The Tathāgata first attained the mark of level soles, and the others were attained in succession. Why is this?

While he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes he practiced giving and maintained the precepts; when he cultivated and accumulated the Path, his mind remained unshakable. For this reason, he first attained the mark of level soles.
"Having attained this mark, he successively attains the mark of wheels on the soles of his feet.

Why is this? While he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he made offerings to his parents, teachers, elders, and virtuous friends; he protected all sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma. For these reasons, he next attains the mark of wheels on his hands and feet."
"Having attained this mark, he successively attains the mark of long, slender fingers. Why is this?
Because when he was a bodhisattva, he wholeheartedly upheld the first and fourth lay precepts; therefore, he next attains the mark of long, slender fingers and the mark of long heels."
"Having attained this mark, he subsequently attains the mark of the body being well-rounded and full. Why is this?

Because when he was a bodhisattva, he properly received the instructions and admonitions of his teachers, elders, parents, and virtuous friends; therefore, he next attains the mark of the body being well-rounded and full."
"Having attained these marks, he next attains the mark of webbed hands and feet. Why is this?
Because when he was a bodhisattva, he gathered sentient beings through the four means of attraction; therefore, he next attains the mark of webbed hands and feet."
"Having attained this mark, he subsequently attains the mark of hands and feet that are more supple than those of other bodies. Why is this?

Because during his time as a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he rubbed and washed the bodies of his teachers and parents with his own hands, removing their filth and anointing them with fragrant oils; therefore, he next attains the mark of soft hands and feet."
"Having attained this mark, he next attains the mark of body hairs curling upward. Why is this?

While acting as a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly transformed sentient beings, causing them to cultivate all wholesome dharmas such as generosity and ethical discipline; for this reason, he next attains the mark of body hairs curling upward."
"Having attained this mark, he successively attains the mark of calves like those of a deer-king. Why is this?

When he was a bodhisattva, he listened to the Dharma with a sincere heart and expounded the Dharma with a sincere heart, in order to destroy all the faults of birth and death; therefore, he next attains the mark of calves like those of a deer-king."
"Having attained this mark, he subsequently attains the mark of the body being well-proportioned and symmetrical, like the king of trees, the nyagrodha. Why is this?

Because while he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly bestowed upon all sentient beings medicine for their illnesses; therefore, he next attains the mark of the body being well-proportioned and symmetrical."
“Having attained this mark, he subsequently attains the mark of hands reaching below the knees. Why is this?

While practicing as a bodhisattva, he never deceived any sages, parents, teachers, elders, virtuous friends, or spiritual mentors; for this reason, he next attains the mark of hands reaching below the knees.”
“Having attained this mark, he next attains the mark of the male elephant and horse’s sheathed organ.

Why is this? While he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he was able to provide protection to those who were terrified; his heart was filled with a sense of shame and remorse, he did not speak of the faults of others, and he skillfully concealed the transgressions of others. For these reasons, he next attains the mark of the sheathed organ of the elephant and horse.”
"Having attained these marks, he next attains the mark of a supple body and a single hair growing from each pore. Why is this?

Because during his time as a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he drew near to the wise, delighted in hearing and discussing the Dharma, and having heard it, delighted in its cultivation; he delighted in repairing roads and removing thorns. For this reason, he next attains the mark of soft skin and a single hair growing from each pore."
"Having attained this mark, he successively attains the mark of a golden-colored body. Why is this?

While he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly gave sentient beings dwellings, bedding, food and drink, and lamps; therefore, he next attains the mark of a golden-colored body."
“Having attained this mark, he subsequently attains the mark of the seven parts of the body being full. Why is this?

While practicing as a bodhisattva over immeasurable lifetimes, he did not give rise to anger toward objects that might provoke it; instead, he delighted in giving sentient beings whatever they required according to their wishes. For this reason, he next attains the mark of the seven parts of the body being full.”
"Having attained these marks, he next attains the mark of the full collarbones. Why is this?

While practicing as a bodhisattva over immeasurable lifetimes, he was well able to distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome signs; his speech was free from error, and he did not speak what was meaningless. He constantly proclaimed with his mouth those teachings that were worthy of acceptance, and did not falsely propagate those that were not. For this reason, he next attains the mark of the full collarbones."
"Having attained these marks, he next attains two further marks: first, his upper body, and second, his jaw, both of which are like those of a lion."

Why is this? Because while practicing as a bodhisattva throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he himself refrained from divisive speech and taught others not to engage in it; therefore, he next attains these two marks.
"Having attained this mark, he next attains three marks:
first, forty teeth; second, the mark of pure whiteness; third, the mark of even and closely set teeth. Why is this?"

When he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he taught and transformed sentient beings by means of the ten wholesome dharmas; once the beings had received them, his heart gave rise to joy, and he always delighted in praising the merits of others. For this reason, he next attained these three marks.
"Having attained this mark, he successively attains the mark of four white canine teeth. Why is this?

While practicing as a bodhisattva, for immeasurable eons he cultivated loving-kindness toward the desire realm and delighted in contemplating wholesome dharmas; therefore, he next attains the mark of four white canine teeth."
"Having attained this mark, he next attains the mark of the most excellent flavor among all flavors. Why is this?

Because when he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he did not wait for others to solicit him before giving; therefore, he next attains the mark of the supreme flavor among flavors."
"Having attained these marks, one next attains two further marks:
first, the uṣṇīṣa (the cranial protuberance), and second, the broad and long tongue. Why is this?"

When he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he wholeheartedly upheld the teachings of the ten wholesome paths of action while simultaneously transforming sentient beings; for this reason, he next attained these two marks.
"Having attained this mark, one next attains the mark of the Brahma-voice.

Why is this? Because while practicing as a bodhisattva over immeasurable lifetimes, one did not engage in harsh speech oneself and taught others not to do so; for this reason, one next attains the mark of the Brahma-voice."
"Having attained this mark, he next attains the mark of eyes like those of a bull-king, deep blue in color. Why is this?

Because while he was a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he looked upon both enemies and kin with equal kindness and compassion; therefore, he next attains the mark of eyes like those of a bull-king."
"Having attained this mark, he next attains the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows. Why is this?

While acting as a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he proclaimed the True Dharma; his speech was truthful and not false. For this reason, he next attains the mark of the white tuft radiance."
"Having attained this mark, he next attains the mark of the invisible crown of the head.

Why is this? While practicing as a bodhisattva, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he prostrated with his head at the feet of all sages, worthies, teachers, and parents; he honored, praised, and reverently made offerings to them. For this reason, he obtained the mark of the invisible crown of the head."
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For an ordained bodhisattva to cultivate such karma is not difficult;
for a person living at home, however, it is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
*Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Fascicle One;
*Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Making Vows.
Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
Who is able to perform the karma for these thirty-two marks?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! The wise are able to do so.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'one who is wise'?
"Good son! One who is able to skillfully give rise to the unsurpassed great vow is called one who is wise."

“Once a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), whatever wholesome karma they perform through body, speech, and mind, they vow that it shall be for the sake of all sentient beings;
when the fruit is attained in the future, they wish to share it entirely with them.”

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly draw near to Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), making offerings and showing them respect; they inquire about the profound Dharma and receive and uphold it without loss, making this vow:

"Now that I draw near to the Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and virtuous friends, I would rather undergo great suffering and affliction for immeasurable eons than give rise to a mind of regression regarding bodhi!"
If sentient beings should strike, revile, or humiliate my body with evil intent, may I, because of this, further increase my heart of loving-kindness and not give rise to an evil thought!
May I, in all future births, in every place, never receive a female body, nor a body lacking sexual organs, nor a body with dual organs, nor the body of a slave!
Furthermore, may my own body possess sovereign power so that I may serve others, and may no other person possess sovereign power to drive me into service!

May my body be endowed with all its faculties, may I remain far removed from evil friends, and may I not be born in evil lands or remote border regions; may I always be born into noble lineages, possessing extraordinary physical strength and beauty, and mastery over wealth and treasures!
One will attain a mind of right mindfulness and a mind of mastery; the mind will become courageous and robust!
Whatever one speaks will be joyfully received by listeners, and all obstacles will be left behind!
Be free from negligence; abandon all unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, and always act for the great benefit of sentient beings!
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, do not cling to body or life, and do not commit unwholesome karma for the sake of body or life!
When benefiting sentient beings, do not seek gratitude or recompense!
Always delight in receiving and upholding the twelve divisions of the scriptures; having received and upheld them, teach them to others!
You will be able to destroy the evil views and evil karma of sentient beings, such that no worldly affairs can overcome you.
Having attained victory, he further teaches others!

He skillfully heals the grave illnesses of body and mind of sentient beings; seeing those who are estranged or broken, he is able to bring them into harmony; seeing those who are terrified, he provides them with protection. Having protected them, he expounds various teachings for them, so that upon hearing them, their minds attain subduing and transformation.

Seeing those who are hungry, I give my body so that they may be fully satisfied; I vow that they shall not give rise to thoughts of greed or malice, but when they devour me, treat me as if eating grass or wood!

May I always delight in making offerings to teachers, elders, parents, virtuous friends, and those of long-standing merit; and toward both enemies and kin, may my mind remain equanimous and one-pointed!
Constantly cultivate the six recollections, the notion of non-self, and the twelve links of dependent origination!
Where the Three Jewels are absent, delight in solitude and cultivate and accumulate loving-kindness and compassion!
May all sentient beings who see my body, hear it, or touch it be freed from afflictions!
"Although the Bodhisattva knows that apart from Bodhi he seeks no other fruit, for the sake of sentient beings, he seeks it in order to bring about vast benefit.

'Good son! If a Bodhisattva can establish his vow in this way, you should know that such a person is a great elder of the unsurpassed Dharma-wealth; he is one who seeks the Dharma King but has not yet attained the status of a Dharma King.'"
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with three things, he is called a ‘Dharma-wealth Elder’:

first, his mind finds no pleasure in the scriptures of external paths; second, his mind does not crave the pleasures of birth and death; third, he always delights in making offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.”
"Furthermore, there are three matters:

first, when undergoing suffering for the sake of others, one does not give rise to regret; second, one is fully endowed with subtle and unsurpassed wisdom; third, when possessing wholesome dharmas, one does not give rise to arrogance."
"Furthermore, there are three matters:

first, to undergo the sufferings of hell for the sake of all sentient beings as if they were the bliss of the third dhyāna; second, to feel no jealousy when seeing others obtain benefit; and third, to perform virtuous deeds not for the sake of saṃsāra."
"Furthermore, there are three matters:

first, seeing others suffer as if it were no different from oneself; second, dedicating all cultivated wholesome deeds to sentient beings; and third, skillfully employing expedient means to cause them to leave suffering behind."
"Furthermore, there are three matters:

first, viewing the pleasures of birth and death as being like a great venomous snake; second, delighting in remaining within birth and death for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; and third, observing that the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) possesses manifold merits."
"Furthermore, there are three things:
first, the relinquishing of the body; second, the relinquishing of life; and third, the relinquishing of wealth.
One relinquishes these three things entirely for the sake of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, there are three things:
first, insatiability in hearing the Dharma; second, the ability to endure all evils; third, teaching others to cultivate patience."
Furthermore, there are three matters:
first, to examine one's own faults; second, to skillfully conceal the transgressions of others; and third, to delight in cultivating a mind of loving-kindness.
"Furthermore, there are three matters:
first, to wholeheartedly uphold the prohibitive precepts; second, to gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction; and third, for one's speech to be gentle and not coarse."
"Furthermore, there are three things:

first, the ability to perform the great gift of Dharma; second, the ability to perform the great gift of material wealth; and third, the exhortation of sentient beings to practice these two kinds of giving."
“Furthermore, there are three matters:

first, to constantly teach and transform sentient beings by means of the Mahāyāna; second, to constantly cultivate superior practices that advance further and further; third, not to give rise to thoughts of contempt toward any sentient being.”
"Furthermore, there are three matters:

first, although possessing afflictions, one is able to endure them; second, knowing the faults of afflictions, one delights in them rather than loathing them; third, while possessing afflictions oneself, one is able to destroy the fetters of others."
"Furthermore, there are three matters:

first, to rejoice as if for oneself when seeing others obtain benefit; second, not to delight in receiving peace and happiness alone when one obtains them oneself; third, not to give rise to a sense of sufficiency within the Lesser Vehicle."
"Furthermore, there are three things:
first, hearing of the ascetic practices of various bodhisattvas without fear; second, never saying 'no' when seeing a petitioner; third, never giving rise to the thought, 'I am superior to all.'"

“Good son! If a bodhisattva can contemplate the cause and contemplate the fruit, can contemplate cause and effect, and can contemplate the fruit and its cause, such a bodhisattva is able to sever cause and effect and is able to attain cause and effect.”
If a bodhisattva can sever and attain the cause and fruit, this is called the fruit of the Dharma; such a one is the King of all dharmas and possesses mastery over the Dharma. "Good son!
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.
For a bodhisattva who has left the home life to establish such a vow is not difficult.
For a householder bodhisattva to establish such a vow is indeed difficult.
Why is this? Because a householder bodhisattva is entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Eight: The Bodhisattva in Name Only. In the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Eight, "The Bodhisattva in Name and Meaning," Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas."
"First, there is the nominal bodhisattva; second, there is the bodhisattva in the true sense.
What is meant by a 'nominal bodhisattva'? Good son!"

If sentient beings, having already resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), take pleasure in external arts and their scriptures, upholding, reciting, and reading them, and then use these very teachings to instruct others while killing the lives of other beings for the sake of their own livelihood;
if they do not delight in cultivating compassion but instead delight in birth and death, constantly creating various karmas to experience the pleasures of saṃsāra;
and if they lack faith, giving rise to a mind entangled in doubt toward the Triple Gem;
They cherish their own bodies and lives and are unable to practice forbearance; their speech is coarse and violent, and they harbor regret and negligence.

They conceive a sense of self-deprecation regarding themselves, thinking, "I shall not attain unsurpassed bodhi. They give rise to thoughts of terror toward the afflictions (*kleśa*) and do not diligently cultivate the means to destroy the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
They constantly give rise to stinginess, greed, jealousy, and anger; they associate with evil friends and are indolent and distracted in mind, delighting in dwelling within ignorance.

One who does not believe in the six perfections, does not delight in cultivating merit, does not contemplate birth and death, and constantly delights in receiving and upholding the malicious words of others—this is called a "nominal bodhisattva."

“Good son! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who resolve their minds on bodhi and desire to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet, upon hearing that one must practice the path through austerities for immeasurable kalpas before finally attaining it, they give rise to regret.
Although they cultivate the path, their minds lack sincerity, and they possess neither shame nor remorse.”
They lack compassion and delight in serving non-Buddhist paths, slaughtering sheep to sacrifice to the gods;

though they may possess slight faith, their minds are not firm, and for the sake of the pleasures of the five desires, they commit various evils. Clinging to form, life, and wealth, they give rise to great arrogance; their actions are inverted, and they are unable to bring benefit.

To practice giving for the sake of the pleasures of birth and death, to observe the precepts for the sake of the pleasures of rebirth in heaven, and to cultivate meditative concentration for the sake of prolonging life—these are called nominal bodhisattvas.

"A Bodhisattva of True Meaning is one who can hear profound teachings, delights in associating with virtuous friends, and rejoices in making offerings to teachers, parents, and virtuous friends; they delight in hearing the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, receiving, upholding, reciting, copying, and contemplating their meaning;
for the sake of the Dharma, they do not begrudge their own body, life, wife, children, or wealth, and their resolve is firm;
they have compassion for all beings, their speech is gentle, they always speak first with truthful words, and they are free from harsh speech and divisive talk."
They do not give rise to thoughts of self-depreciation;
