they extend their hands in generosity without restriction;

they constantly delight in whetting and sharpening the sword of wisdom; and although they study external treatises, it is for the purpose of destroying false views and emerging victorious over false views, skillfully knowing the expedient means to discipline and transform sentient beings.
They do not give rise to fear in the midst of great assemblies; they constantly teach sentient beings that bodhi is easily attained, enabling those who hear them to feel no dread;
they diligently cultivate vigor and treat afflictions with contempt, ensuring that those afflictions cannot gain mastery over them;
their minds are never negligent as they constantly practice patience, observing the precepts and exerting vigor for the sake of the fruit of nirvāṇa.
May I serve as a messenger and attendant for all sentient beings, causing them to dwell in peace, joy, and happiness;
may I undergo suffering for the sake of others without a single thought of regret; may I give rise to compassion upon seeing those who retreat from Bodhi;

may I be able to rescue all from their various afflictions and distresses; may I be able to contemplate all the faults and transgressions inherent in birth and death; and may I be able to fulfill the unsurpassed six pāramitās.
In all worldly affairs he excels all sentient beings;
his faith is firm and steadfast, and he cultivates and accumulates loving-kindness and compassion, yet does not seek the karmic rewards of such compassion.

Toward both enemies and kin his mind is without duality; he is impartial when giving, and likewise when sacrificing his own body. Knowing the mark of impermanence, he does not begrudge his own life or body.
They gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction; because they understand conventional truth, they conform to the speech of sentient beings.

When undergoing suffering for the sake of all beings, their minds remain as unshakable as Mount Sumeru. Even though they see that sentient beings mostly commit various evils while possessing little goodness, they never forget them in their hearts.

They harbor no doubts regarding the Triple Gem and delight in making offerings to it; when resources are scarce, they first give to the poor and destitute, and only later bestow upon the fields of merit; they first attend to those who are impoverished and suffering, and only afterwards to the wealthy.
One who delights in praising the virtues of others so as to open the way to Nirvana;
one who wishes for others to learn all arts and crafts, and gives rise to a heart of joy upon seeing those whose learning surpasses their own;

one who does not think of self-benefit but constantly thinks of benefiting others, such that all the various good deeds performed through the actions of body, speech, and mind are never for oneself but always for others—this is called a Bodhisattva in the true sense.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a bodhisattva who has left the household life to be a bodhisattva of true meaning is not difficult;
for a bodhisattva who remains at home to be so is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Nine: The Firm Resolve of the Bodhisattva-Mind, from the Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra. Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
“Regarding the Bodhisattva of Meaning (Arthabodhisattva), how does he know himself to be a Bodhisattva of Meaning? “Good son!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices asceticism, he first admonishes his own mind.”
"Good son!
I remember that in the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I first followed the ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists, observing them with a sincere heart and without any retreat."
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he smeared his body with ash and consumed only a single grain each day of sesame, mung beans, non-glutinous rice,
millet, and wild grasses; he used thorns, prickly brambles, wooden stumps, and stones as his bedding,
and employed cow dung and cow urine as medicine for his ailments.
In the month of midsummer, one’s body is scorched by the five heats;
at the onset of early winter, one’s body is pressed against freezing ice.
Whether one undergoes the practice of eating grass, roots, stalks, leaves, fruits, earth, or wind—when performing such ascetic penances as these, there is no benefit for either oneself or others.
Nevertheless, my mind remained without retreat, and I excelled all the ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists. "Good son!
In the past, for four reasons, I relinquished my body and life:

First, for the sake of destroying the various afflictions of sentient beings; second, for the sake of causing sentient beings to receive peace and happiness; third, for the sake of personally eliminating attachment to the body; and fourth, for the sake of repaying the kindness of one's parents who gave birth to and raised one.
If a bodhisattva is able to disregard their own body and life, they may know with certainty that they are a true bodhisattva. "Good son!
In the past, for the sake of the True Dharma, I carved out my own body to serve as three thousand six hundred lamps."

At that time, I was fully possessed of afflictions and my body truly felt the pain; yet, for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain liberation, I admonished my mind to remain firm and did not give rise to any thought of retreat.

At that time, one immediately attains the fulfillment of three matters: first, being ultimately without regression; second, becoming a bodhisattva of true meaning; and third, being named "inconceivable. This is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, in the past, for the sake of the True Dharma, throughout the course of one kalpa, my entire body was afflicted with the suffering of a thousand sores on every side.

At that time, though I was fully possessed of all afflictions and my body truly felt the pain, for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain liberation, I admonished my mind to remain firm and did not give rise to any retreat; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, in the past, for the sake of a single pigeon, I abandoned this body.

At that time, although I was fully possessed of all afflictions and my body truly experienced suffering, for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain liberation, I exhorted my mind to remain firm and did not give rise to any retreat; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva."
“Good son! All evil friends, afflictions, and karmic actions are themselves the companions that adorn the path of a bodhisattva. Why is this?

All ordinary beings lack wisdom and a mind of right mindfulness; therefore, they regard afflictions as enemies. Bodhisattvas, being fully endowed with wisdom and right mindfulness, regard afflictions as companions on the path;
the same applies to evil friends and karma.
"Good son!
Having abandoned and left behind the afflictions, one will ultimately never receive a body within an evil existence.
Therefore, although a bodhisattva manifests what appear to be evil deeds, these are in fact not produced by evil actions of body, speech, or mind; they are the power of his vow."
By the power of this vow, he assumes the body of a fierce beast for the purpose of subduing those animals.

Once the Bodhisattva has manifested in the body of an animal, he is well-versed in human speech, Dharma-speech, truthful speech, speech that is not coarse or evil, and speech that is not meaningless; his mind is always compassionate, he cultivates and accumulates loving-kindness and compassion, and he is never indolent—this is called the inconceivability of a Bodhisattva.
“Good son! In the past, when I took the body of a bear, although I possessed afflictions, the afflictions had no power over me. Why is this?
Because I possess right mindfulness, at those times I felt compassion for sentient beings, protected the True Dharma, and practiced the conduct of the Dharma.

I took on the bodies of a goat, a *kapinjala* partridge, a rabbit, a snake, a dragon, an elephant, a *garuḍa*, a pigeon, a deer, a monkey, a ram, a rooster, a pheasant, a peacock, a parrot, and a frog. When I took such forms as birds and beasts, although I possessed afflictions (*kleśa*), the afflictions had no power over me.
Why is this? Because they possess right mindfulness, they have compassion for sentient beings, protect the true Dharma, and practice the conduct of the Dharma. "Good son!

In an age of famine, I established a great vow; by the power of that vow, I assumed the body of a great fish so that all sentient beings might be freed from hunger and thirst. Those who ate my flesh cultivated the Way, remained mindful of the Way, and were free from evil transgressions.

In an age of pestilence, I again established a great vow; by the power of that vow, my body became a medicinal tree. All those with illnesses—whether they saw, heard of, or touched me, or ate my skin, blood, flesh, and marrow—had their diseases completely healed.
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva undergoes such suffering yet their mind does not regress, they are called a bodhisattva in name [only].
When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they never seek the fruits of those six pāramitās; rather, they take the benefit of sentient beings as their sole task."

The Bodhisattva deeply understands the faults and afflictions of birth and death, yet he delights in dwelling therein for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and bestowing peace and happiness upon them.

That the Bodhisattva fully realizes both the peace and happiness of liberation and the faults and afflictions of birth and death, yet is able to dwell within them, is called the inconceivability of the Bodhisattva.
The conduct of a bodhisattva does not seek gratitude or recompense;
yet, toward those from whom they have received kindness, they always contemplate how to repay it. Good son!
All sentient beings constantly seek their own benefit, whereas the conduct of a bodhisattva always seeks the benefit of others; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, though fully possessed of afflictions, bestows equal benefit upon both enemies and kin; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva.
“Good son! When various non-Buddhists transform sentient beings, they may do so by using harsh words, flogging, reviling, or banishing them, and only thereafter subduing them.”

The Bodhisattva is not like this; when transforming sentient beings, he has no harsh speech, no angry speech, and no frivolous speech, but only gentle speech and truthful speech. Once sentient beings have heard them, it is as if blue lotuses encounter the moon, or red lotuses encounter the sun.
"Good son!

When a bodhisattva practices giving, although his wealth and goods may be meager, he does not give rise to a mind of weariness upon seeing many who beg; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva."

When a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings who are blind, deaf, mute, or dumb, as well as those who are ignorant, those from borderlands, and those of evil nature, their mind never grows weary or exhausted; this is called the inconceivability of a bodhisattva.
“Good son! A bodhisattva has four inconceivable qualities:

first, being able to give away even those things most dearly cherished; second, being able to endure evil deeds despite being possessed of all manner of afflictions; third, being able to reconcile and harmonize a community that has fallen into discord; and fourth, being able to transform the perception of one facing death who sees evil teachings by preaching the Dharma to them.”
These are called the four inconceivable qualities of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are three other inconceivable matters:

first, reproaching all afflictions; second, remaining amidst afflictions without abandoning them; and third, remaining free from negligence despite possessing afflictions and the karma of afflictions.
These are called the three inconceivable qualities of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are three other inconceivable matters:

first, when first intending to give, the mind gives rise to joy; second, while giving, one acts for the sake of others without seeking karmic retribution; third, after having given, the mind remains joyful and free from regret.
These are called the three inconceivable qualities of a bodhisattva.
"Good son, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, he observes his own mind:
"Am I called a Bodhisattva by name,
or am I a Bodhisattva in meaning?
If sentient beings can act in this manner, you should know that such persons are Bodhisattvas in meaning.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For an ordained bodhisattva to perform such deeds is not difficult;
for a lay bodhisattva to perform such deeds is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Ten: Benefiting Oneself and Others. From the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Ten: Benefiting Oneself and Others.
Sujāta said: "World-Honored One!"
"What is enlightenment?
What is the path to enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If one is apart from bodhi, there is no path to bodhi; if one is apart from the path to bodhi, there is no bodhi.
The path to bodhi is itself bodhi, and bodhi is itself the path to bodhi.”
That which transcends all the fruits of the path attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called bodhi and the path to bodhi. Sujāta said,
“World-Honored One!
“The fruits of the path attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are themselves bodhi, and they are themselves the bodhi-path;
how can you say they are superior? “Good son!
The paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not vast and are not the awakening of all; therefore, bodhi and the path to bodhi are called supreme.
It is just as, among all the secular scriptures of the world, the twelve divisions of the sūtras are the most preeminent.
Why is this? Because what has been taught is not erroneous and is free from inversion.
The path of the two vehicles compared to the path of Bodhi is likewise so.
“Good son! The path to bodhi is itself training, and it is itself the fruit of training.
What is meant by ‘training’?
To practice the path to enlightenment while not yet possessing the mind of non-retrogression is called "learning";
to have already attained non-retrogression is called the "fruit of learning.
To have not yet attained definitive existence is called "learning."
Having already attained certainty of existence, that which occurs during the third *kalpa* is called the fruit of training.
During the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one is still unable to practice giving with all wisdom, at all times, and to all sentient beings;
during the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, although one practices universal giving, one is still unable to give at all times and to all sentient beings.
These two stages are called "training.
During the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, being able to practice all forms of giving—giving at all times and to all sentient beings—is called the "fruit of training."
"Good son!
When a bodhisattva practices giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, this is called 'learning';
reaching the other shore is called the 'fruit of learning'."

“Good son! There is that which is giving but not a pāramitā; there is that which is a pāramitā but is not called giving; there is that which is both giving and a pāramitā; and there is that which is neither giving nor a pāramitā.”

Good son! That which is giving but not a pāramitā refers to the giving practiced by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, all ordinary worldlings, those of external paths and divergent views, and by bodhisattvas during the first and second asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
That which is a *pāramitā* but not giving is, for example, the *śīla-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
That which is both giving and a *pāramitā* is the giving practiced by a bodhisattva during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
That which is neither giving nor a perfection refers to the precept-keeping, meditative cultivation, patience, loving-kindness, and compassion of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Good son!
That which is neither giving nor a pāramitā is called "learning";
that which is both giving and a pāramitā is called the "fruit of learning. "Good son!
Now, awakening (bodhi) is precisely the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
To diligently cultivate and accumulate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment for the sake of these two knowledges is called "training" (śaikṣa);
having attained awakening, it is called the "fruit of training" (śaikṣaphala).
"To discipline one's own faculties first, and subsequently to discipline sentient beings, is called training;
to attain liberation for oneself and cause sentient beings to attain it as well, is called the fruit of training."
"To cultivate and gather the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three mindfulnesses is called 'training';
to fully attain the eighteen unique qualities is called the 'fruit of training.'"
"To perform various karmas for the benefit of oneself and others is called 'learning';
to be able to benefit others is called the 'fruit of learning.
To practice and study worldly dharmas is called 'learning';"
To study the supramundane Dharma is called the fruit of training.
To be unrelenting regarding one's body and wealth for the sake of all sentient beings is called training;
to likewise not begrudge one's body, wealth, or even life for the sake of all sentient beings is called the fruit of training.
"To be able to transform sentient beings so that they perform the deeds of humans and devas is called 'learning';
to perform untainted (anāsrava) deeds is called the 'fruit of learning.
To be able to bestow all manner of material wealth upon sentient beings is called 'learning';"
To be able to practice the gift of Dharma is called the fruit of training.
To be able to personally destroy one's own stinginess, greed, and envy is called training;
to destroy the stinginess, greed, and envy in the minds of others is called the fruit of training.
To uphold the five faculties and practice mindfulness is called "learning";
to teach others to cultivate, accomplish, and fulfill them is called the "fruit of learning. "Good son!
Once the Bodhisattva’s faculty of faith has brought about self-benefit, he further benefits others.
What constitutes self-benefit is not called true benefit;
rather, benefiting others is what is truly called self-benefit.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for the sake of benefiting others, does not give rise to stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth; this is called self-benefit.

The Bodhisattva knows with certainty that if one attempts to teach and transform sentient beings using the enlightenment of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and they do not accept it, then one should instead teach them the worldly pleasures of devas and humans;
this is called benefiting others. To benefit others is itself to benefit oneself.
If a bodhisattva is unable to benefit both self and others, seeking only their own benefit, this is termed the inferior grade.
Why is this? Because such a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment toward dharmas and wealth; for this reason, they are unable to benefit themselves.
If a practitioner causes others to suffer while dwelling in personal ease and comfort, such a bodhisattva cannot benefit others.
If one does not personally cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning, yet teaches others to do so, this is called benefiting others but being unable to benefit oneself.
If one personally fulfills the five faculties, such as faith, and subsequently teaches others, this is called a bodhisattva’s benefiting of self and others. "Good son,
there are two kinds of benefit:
First is the present life, and second is future lives.
If a bodhisattva performs beneficial acts only for the present, it is not called true benefit;
if they perform them for future lives, they are able to provide benefit for both.
“Good son! There are two kinds of happiness—the first is worldly happiness, and the second is supramundane happiness—and merit is likewise twofold.”
If a bodhisattva can personally possess these two kinds of happiness and two kinds of merit to transform sentient beings, this is called benefiting oneself and others. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with one dharma, he is able to benefit both himself and others; that is, heedfulness.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that can benefit both oneself and others:
first, extensive learning, and second, reflection.
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas that can benefit both oneself and others:
first, compassion for sentient beings; second, diligent application of vigor; and third, the possession of mindfulness."
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas that can benefit both oneself and others, namely, the four modes of deportment.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that can benefit both oneself and others:
first, the faculty of faith; second, upholding the precepts; third, extensive learning; fourth, generosity; and fifth, wisdom.”
“Furthermore, there are six dharmas that can benefit both oneself and others, namely, the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas that can benefit both oneself and others, namely, the destruction of the seven types of pride (*saptavidha-māna*).”

“Good son! If there are faults among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, men, women, or those within a great assembly, the bodhisattva, having seen them, first accords with their inclinations and then teaches the Dharma so that they may be tamed.”
If one cannot first comply with their wishes and instead preaches the Dharma to them immediately, this is called a bodhisattva of the lowest grade.
"Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
First, one delights in associating with virtuous friends; second, one does not so delight.
One who delights in virtuous friends is able to benefit both self and others;
one who does not delight in such association cannot achieve the mutual benefit of both self and others.
“Good son! There are two kinds of delighting in associating with virtuous friends:
first, delighting in making offerings; second, not delighting in making offerings.”
Those who delight in making offerings are able to benefit both themselves and others;
those who do not delight in making offerings cannot benefit both.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who delight in making offerings:
First, those who are able to listen to the Dharma; second, those who are unable to listen.
Those who listen with a sincere mind are able to benefit both themselves and others;
those who do not listen with a sincere mind derive no such dual benefit.
"Listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind further has two aspects:
first, being able to inquire; second, being unable to inquire.
One who can inquire is able to benefit both self and others; one who cannot inquire is unable to attain the benefit of self or others."
"Regarding those capable of inquiring into the meaning, there are further two types:
first, those who uphold it with a sincere heart; second, those who cannot so uphold it.
Those who uphold it with a sincere heart are able to benefit both themselves and others."
Those who do not maintain a sincere mind cannot attain benefit for themselves or others.
There are two kinds of those who maintain [the teaching] with a sincere mind:
first, those who contemplate it; second, those who do not contemplate it.
Those capable of contemplation can benefit both themselves and others;
those who do not contemplate cannot be said to benefit themselves or others.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those capable of contemplation:
First, those who understand the meaning; second, those who do not understand the meaning.
Those who can understand the meaning are able to benefit both themselves and others;
those who do not understand the meaning cannot be said to be able to benefit themselves and others.
“Furthermore, there are two kinds of persons who understand the meaning:
first, those who abide in accordance with the Dharma; second, those who do not abide in accordance with the Dharma.
Those who abide in accordance with the Dharma are able to benefit both themselves and others.”
"One who does not abide in accordance with the Dharma cannot be said to benefit themselves or others.
There are two kinds of those who abide in accordance with the Dharma:
first, those who are fully endowed with the eight knowledges; second, those who are not so fully endowed."
What are the eight knowledges? First, knowledge of phenomena;

second, knowledge of meaning; third, knowledge of time; fourth, knowledge of contentment; fifth, knowledge of self and others; sixth, knowledge of assemblies; seventh, knowledge of faculties; eighth, knowledge of the superior and inferior.
This person, being fully endowed with these eight kinds of knowledge, possesses sixteen qualities in whatever they preach:

first, speaking at the proper time; second, speaking with a sincere mind; third, speaking in proper sequence; fourth, speaking in harmony; fifth, speaking according to the meaning; sixth, speaking with joy; seventh, speaking according to the listeners' inclinations; eighth, not disparaging the assembly; ninth, not rebuking the assembly; tenth, speaking in accordance with the Dharma; eleventh, speaking for the benefit of both oneself and others; twelfth, speaking without distraction; thirteenth, speaking in accord with the truth; fourteenth, speaking with authenticity; fifteenth, not giving rise to arrogance after having spoken; and sixteenth, not seeking worldly rewards after having spoken.
"Such a person is able to listen from another; when listening from another, they possess sixteen qualities:

First, listening at the proper time; second, listening with joy; third, listening with a sincere mind; fourth, listening with reverence; fifth, listening without seeking faults; sixth, listening not for the sake of debate; seventh, listening not for the sake of victory; eighth, not disparaging the speaker while listening; ninth, not disparaging the Dharma while listening; tenth, never disparaging oneself while listening; eleventh, remaining far removed from the five hindrances while listening; twelfth, listening for the purpose of receiving, upholding, and reciting; thirteenth, listening for the purpose of eliminating the five desires; fourteenth, listening for the purpose of perfecting faith; fifteenth, listening for the purpose of harmonizing sentient beings; and sixteenth, listening for the purpose of severing the roots of [worldly] hearing.
"Good son!
One who possesses the eight kinds of wisdom is able to both speak and listen; such a person is able to benefit both themselves and others.
One who does not possess them cannot be said to benefit either self or others."
“Good son! There are two kinds of those who can preach the Dharma:
first, the pure; second, the impure.”
Furthermore, there are five things that constitute impurity:

first, speaking for the sake of profit; second, speaking for the sake of recompense; third, speaking to surpass others; fourth, speaking for the sake of worldly rewards; and fifth, speaking with doubt.
"Furthermore, there are five matters regarding pure exposition:

first, to provide food before preaching; second, to preach for the sake of increasing the Three Jewels; third, to preach for the sake of severing the afflictions of oneself and others; fourth, to preach for the sake of distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox; and fifth, to preach so that the listeners may attain the most supreme [attainment]."
“Good son! To speak impurely is called defilement; it is called selling the Dharma, and it is also called disgrace, as well as error and loss of the intended meaning.”
"Pure speech is called 'purity,' and it is also called 'right speech,' 'true words,' and 'the aggregate of Dharma. Good son!

If one fully understands the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the science of phonetics, and the science of logic—including knowledge of logical reasons, analogies, and the positions held by oneself and others—this is called "correct exposition."
There are four types of listeners:

first, those who understand much from hearing only a brief summary; second, those who understand by means of sequential analysis; third, those who understand according to their own original intent; and fourth, those who understand each individual word and each individual phrase.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is intended precisely for three types of persons, not for a fourth.
Why is this? Because they are not suitable vessels.
These four types of persons are divided into two kinds:
first, the mature; second, the immature.
The mature are those who are tamed in the present life.
"Those who are to be born" refers to those to be tamed in the future. "Good son!
It is like a forest, which generally has four kinds:"

First, those that are easy to fell but difficult to extract; second, those that are difficult to fell but easy to extract; third, those that are easy to fell and easy to extract; fourth, those that are difficult to fell and difficult to extract.
There are also four types of householders: first, those who are easy to discipline but difficult to cause to leave the home life;

second, those who are difficult to discipline but easy to cause to leave the home life; third, those who are easy to discipline and easy to cause to leave the home life; and fourth, those who are difficult to discipline and difficult to cause to leave the home life.
These four types of persons are divided into three categories:
first, those who are disciplined through reprimand; second, those who are disciplined through gentle speech; and third, those who are brought to subjection through both reprimand and gentle speech.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, being able to discipline oneself without relying on others; second, if one is unable to do so oneself, requesting others to bring about such discipline.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
First is taming through giving, and second is taming through incantations.
This method of subduing further involves two occasions:
first, the occasion of joy, and second, the occasion of suffering.
When preaching the True Dharma for these four types of people, there are two skillful means:
first, being well-versed in worldly affairs; second, serving as their attendants.
"Good son!

If a bodhisattva understands these two skillful means, they can benefit both themselves and others; if they do not understand them, they will be unable to attain self-benefit or the benefit of others."
“Good son! For the sake of benefiting others, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva first studies external treatises and only thereafter analyzes the twelve divisions of the sūtras;
when sentient beings hear these twelve divisions of the sūtras, they then develop a sense of revulsion and disdain for external treatises.”

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he speaks of the faults of afflictions and liberation from afflictions; he praises the virtues of good friends and censures the faults of evil friends; he extols the merit of giving and denounces the failings of stinginess.
The Bodhisattva is always tranquil and praises the merit of tranquility; they constantly cultivate the practice of the Dharma and praise the virtue of practicing the Dharma.
If one can act in this way, it is called benefiting both oneself and others.
"A lay bodhisattva first disciplines themselves; if they do not discipline themselves, they will not go forth into homelessness.
A lay bodhisattva is able to deliver many people, whereas a renunciant bodhisattva is not so."

Why is this? If there were no laypeople, there would be no followers of the Three Vehicles who have left the household life; the renunciation, cultivation of the path, observance of precepts, recitation of sutras, and practice of meditation of those in the Three Vehicles who have left the household life are all adorned by the presence of laypeople.
Good son! There is the Path and there is the adornment of the Path;
the Path refers to what is called the practice of the Dharma.
The adornment of the Path refers to those who remain at home.
A renunciant bodhisattva practices the Path for the sake of those who remain at home, while those who remain at home perform the practice of the Dharma for the sake of renunciants.
Householders mostly cultivate two dharmas:
first, receiving; second, giving.
Those who have left the household life also cultivate two dharmas:
First is recitation, and second is instruction.
"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva further possesses four dharmas:
Receiving, giving, reciting, and teaching—
these are called benefiting oneself and others.

If a bodhisattva wishes to explain the profound meaning of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) to sentient beings, they should first explain worldly dharmas and only thereafter explain the profound dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because they are easy to transform.
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should protect the minds of all sentient beings; if he does not protect them, he will be unable to discipline all sentient beings."
A bodhisattva should likewise protect his own person; for if he does not protect his person, he will be unable to discipline sentient beings.
A bodhisattva does not protect his body, life, or wealth out of craving for them; rather, he protects his body, life, and wealth solely for the sake of disciplining all sentient beings.

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva first eliminates evil within themselves and afterwards teaches others to eliminate it; it is impossible for one who does not eliminate it themselves to be able to teach others to eliminate it!
Therefore, a bodhisattva should first personally practice giving, maintain ethical discipline, be content, and exert diligent effort, and only thereafter transform others.
If a bodhisattva does not personally practice these dharmas, they will be unable to teach and transform sentient beings.
“Good son! There are three kinds of faculties among sentient beings, and the faculties of Bodhisattvas are likewise of three kinds: namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
A Bodhisattva with inferior faculties can transform those with inferior faculties, but cannot reach those with middling or superior faculties;”
“Bodhisattvas of middling capacity can transform those of middling and lower capacities, but not those of superior capacity;
Bodhisattvas of superior capacity can perform the three kinds of transformation. Good son!
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.
For a bodhisattva who has left the home life, benefiting both self and others is not difficult.
For a lay bodhisattva to cultivate these two benefits is indeed difficult.
Why is this? Because a lay bodhisattva is frequently entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Eleven: Adornment of Self and Others. In the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Eleven, "Adornment of Self and Others," Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
“By how many dharmas is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva endowed so as to be able to benefit both self and others?
“Good son! By being endowed with eight dharmas, one is able to benefit both self and others.”
What are these eight? First, a long life span;

second, possession of supreme and wondrous physical form; third, a body endowed with great strength; fourth, possession of a noble lineage; fifth, abundance of wealth and treasures; sixth, possession of a male body; seventh, eloquence and clarity of speech; eighth, freedom from fear of the great assembly.
Sujāta said: “World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva obtain a long life, and even so that the great assembly does not give rise to fear?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have practiced non-killing with a mind of loving-kindness throughout immeasurable lifetimes, by virtue of these causes and conditions, they obtain long life."
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly gave clothing and lamps; by this causal condition, he obtained a superior complexion.
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly destroyed arrogance; by this causal condition, he was born into a noble lineage.
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly gave food and drink; by this causal condition, his physical strength is fully endowed.
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he always delighted in preaching the Dharma; by this causal condition, he possesses abundant wealth and treasures.
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he reviled the female body; by this causal condition, he obtained a male body.
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he maintained the precepts with a sincere mind; by this causal condition, his speech is eloquent and lucid.
Having made offerings to the Triple Gem throughout immeasurable lifetimes, by virtue of these causes and conditions, one has no fear of great assemblies.
These eight matters have three underlying causes and conditions:
first, purity of material things; second, purity of mind; and third, purity of the field of merit.
What is purity of material goods?

It is that which is not obtained through theft, not an object prohibited by the Noble Ones, not a communal property, not a property belonging to the Triple Gem, not something given to one person and diverted to many, nor something given to many and diverted to one; it is obtained without causing distress to others, without deceiving others, and without cheating others—this is called purity of material goods.
What is purity of mind?

When giving, one does not do so for the sake of favorable karmic fruits within saṃsāra, nor for fame that surpasses others, nor to obtain physical beauty, strength, or wealth; nor to ensure the continuity of family traditions or to have many and abundant kinsmen.
Rather, one gives solely for the purpose of adorning bodhi and with the desire to subdue sentient beings. This is called purity of mind.
What is the purity of the field of merit?
A recipient who is free from the eightfold wrong paths is called a pure field of merit. Good son!
By means of these three causes and conditions, one is fully endowed with the eight dharmas.
"Good son! The reason a bodhisattva seeks long life is that they wish to praise non-killing for the sake of sentient beings."
The reason a bodhisattva seeks a superior physical appearance is to cause sentient beings to see it with joy.
The reason a bodhisattva seeks a superior lineage is to cause sentient beings to give rise to reverence.
The reason a bodhisattva seeks the perfection of power is for the sake of upholding the precepts, reciting the sūtras, and practicing dhyāna meditation.
The reason a bodhisattva seeks abundant wealth and treasures is for the sake of taming and converting all sentient beings.
The reason a bodhisattva seeks a male body is to become a vessel and to perfect wholesome dharmas.
The reason a bodhisattva seeks eloquence in speech is so that all sentient beings may receive the teachings of the Dharma.
The reason a bodhisattva seeks to be fearless in the great assembly is that they desire to discern the true Dharma.
"Good son! Therefore, when a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these eight dharmas, they are able to benefit both themselves and others; to practice in this way is called 'true practice.'"
"Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses eight dharmas fully upholds and maintains the ten wholesome paths of action, delighting in transforming others;
he fully upholds and maintains the upāsaka precepts, delighting in transforming others."
Although they may obtain exquisite physical form, they never give rise to arrogance on that account;

although they may maintain pure precepts, possess great learning, be diligent, have great strength, belong to a noble lineage, or abound in wealth and treasures, they never give rise to arrogance because of these things.
They do not deceive or delude sentient beings with illusions, they do not give rise to negligence, and they cultivate the six points of harmonious respect.
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with such qualities as these, although they remain a householder, they are no different from one who has gone forth.
In this way, a bodhisattva never creates the causes and conditions for others to commit evil.
Why is this? Because their sense of shame and remorse is firm. "Good son!

If a layperson observes such Upāsaka precepts for even a single lifetime, although they may later be reborn in a place where the Three Jewels do not exist, they will ultimately never create the causes and conditions for various evils.
Why is this so? Because of two causes and conditions:
first, wisdom; second, heedfulness.
"Good son!
There are four causes and conditions for not committing evil deeds in subsequent evil places:

first, because of understanding the faults of the afflictions; second, because of not following after the various afflictions; third, because of being able to endure all evil sufferings; and fourth, because of not giving rise to a mind of fear."
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they cannot be shaken by any suffering or any afflictions.
Good son, there are five causes and conditions for a bodhisattva to be immovable:

First, delighting in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas; second, discerning between the wholesome and the unwholesome; third, drawing near to the True Dharma; fourth, feeling compassion for sentient beings; and fifth, constantly remembering past lives.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva is endowed with these eight dharmas, if he hears slander or defamation, his mind is able to endure it;
if he hears praise, he instead gives rise to a sense of shame and remorse.”
When practicing the path, one rejoices and celebrates within oneself, yet does not give rise to arrogance.
One is able to discipline wicked people; seeing a community that is divided or disintegrating, one is able to bring them into harmony.
To proclaim the good deeds of others while concealing their faults; never to speak of what others feel shame for; and upon hearing the private matters of others, not to disclose them to anyone else.
One does not make oaths or incantations for the sake of worldly affairs.
When someone bestows even small kindness upon oneself, one desires to repay it greatly;
toward those who harbor enmity toward oneself, one constantly generates thoughts of goodness; and when both enemies and kin suffer, one rescues the enemy first.
When seeing those who revile him, he instead gives rise to compassion;
when seeing others stealing, he remains silent and unmoving;
when seeing those coming to strike him, he conceives a heart of pity.
He regards all sentient beings as his own parents; he would rather lose his own body and life than ever utter a false word.
Why is this? Because he understands the law of karmic retribution.
One should conceive of all afflictions as enemies and regard wholesome dharmas as old friends.
If one gives rise to a mind of craving toward external phenomena, one should immediately examine the faults and transgressions of that craving;
it is the same for all afflictions.
Although one may dwell for a long time among evil people, one never conceives thoughts of intimacy or affection toward them;
although one does not reside together with virtuous people, one never conceives thoughts of distance toward them.
Although they may provide for their parents and teachers, they never commit evil deeds for their sake.
Even when destitute of wealth, upon seeing a petitioner, they do not give rise to malicious thoughts.
Although they do not associate with those who are wicked and cruel, their inner hearts constantly give rise to compassion; when evil is directed toward them, they repay it with goodness.
When they experience happiness themselves, they do not disparage others;
seeing others suffer, they do not feel joy.
With purity of physical action, they maintain the four modes of deportment and transform sentient beings by means of these dharmas;
with purity of verbal action, they recite the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures and transform sentient beings by means of these dharmas;
with purity of mental action, they cultivate the four immeasurables and likewise transform sentient beings through these dharmas.
Willingly undergoing suffering for oneself so that others may experience happiness, one takes joy in doing so.
Regarding worldly affairs, even those that offer no personal benefit, one studies them for the sake of sentient beings;

and regarding the matters studied, which are the most excellent in the world, though one attains mastery, the mind remains free from pride. One diligently employs what one knows to transform others, desiring that these teachings continue through the ages without interruption.
Among friends and kin, he does not cause them to commit evil deeds; he delights in teaching and transforming sentient beings through the aforementioned eight dharmas.
He explains causes and effects without error.
When separated from those he loves, his mind does not give rise to affliction, for he contemplates impermanence.
When experiencing pleasant sensations, the mind does not become attached or intoxicated, but contemplates suffering and impermanence.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with the eight dharmas mentioned above, he is then able to perform such deeds as these.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a renunciant bodhisattva to cultivate these eight dharmas is not difficult;
for a householder to cultivate and assemble them is indeed difficult. Why is this?
“Because a lay bodhisattva is entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Twelve: The Two Adornments. From the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: The Two Adornments. Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
"What is meant by 'the adornment of oneself and others' for a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
"Bodhisattvas who are endowed with two dharmas are able to adorn both themselves and others:
first, merit; second, wisdom.
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition does one obtain these two adornments? "Good son!
When a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates the six pāramitās, they thereby obtain these two kinds of adornment."
Generosity, ethical discipline, and diligence are called the adornment of merit;
patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom are called the adornment of knowledge.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas that serve as the causes for these two adornments, namely the six recollections:
Mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha is called the adornment of wisdom;
mindfulness of the precepts, generosity, and the devas is called the adornment of merit. "Good son!

When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these two adornments, they are able to benefit both themselves and others; even while undergoing the sufferings of the three evil realms for the sake of all sentient beings, no anxiety or regret arises within their inner mind.
If one can be fully endowed with these two adornments, one will attain subtle and wondrous skillful means, and come to understand both worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas.
Good son!
The adornment of merit is itself the adornment of wisdom, and the adornment of wisdom is itself the adornment of merit. Why is this?

For wisdom enables one to cultivate wholesome dharmas and fulfill the ten virtuous actions, thereby attaining wealth and great sovereignty. Because these two are attained, one is able to benefit both oneself and others.
A person of wisdom excels among those who study worldly dharmas; by this cause and condition, they obtain wealth and great sovereignty.
When a Bodhisattva is fully endowed with these two dharmas, they are able to benefit both themselves and others in both worlds.
If a wise person can differentiate between mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas:
mundane dharmas refer to all worldly discourses and all worldly concentrations;
supramundane dharmas refer to the knowledge of the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).
Because the bodhisattva understands the causal conditions of these two dharmas, he is able to benefit both himself and others in the two periods [of this life and the next]. Good son!
Although the bodhisattva knows that worldly happiness is illusory and not real, he is nevertheless able to create the causal conditions for worldly happiness.
Why is this? It is because one desires to benefit all sentient beings. "Good son!
These two adornments have two primary causes:
first, a mind of loving-kindness; second, a mind of compassion.
By cultivating these two causes, even while wandering through the ocean of suffering in birth and death, the mind does not give rise to regret.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva, by being endowed with two dharmas, is able to adorn unsurpassed enlightenment:
first, not delighting in birth and death; second, deeply contemplating liberation.

Therefore, it can also bring benefit to both present and future lives; by thoroughly understanding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one attains great wisdom and is able to cause the increase of wealth and life-span for oneself and others. Good son!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with two dharmas, they do not give rise to sorrow or regret when practicing all-encompassing giving, and they are able to endure the sight of various evil matters.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they contemplate two kinds of fields:
first, the field of merit; second, the field of poverty.
A bodhisattva gives to those who are poor and suffering in order to increase their merit;
they give to fields of merit in order to increase their unsurpassed, wondrous wisdom;
and they give to fields of merit in order to repay their kindness.
Out of compassion, one bestows gifts upon the poor;
out of the relinquishing of afflictions, one gives to the field of merit;
and for the sake of accomplishing spiritual qualities, one gives to the poor.
One gives to the field of merit in order to increase all causes and conditions for happiness;
one gives to the poor in order to abandon all causes and conditions for suffering.
If a bodhisattva gives to those who are dear and beloved, it is for the sake of repaying their kindness.
If one gives to enemies, it is for the sake of eliminating their evil.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees a seeker coming, they conceive of them as an only son; therefore, they give according to the measure of their own power. This is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
When a bodhisattva practices giving, being free from a mind of stinginess, it is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
Being able to endure all the words of those who come seeking, it is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
To personally hand over the object of giving with one's own hands is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
To focus the mind with utmost sincerity and contemplate liberation is called the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Not discriminating between the characteristics of all enemies and kin is called the Prajñāpāramitā. Good son!
Just as when sentient beings kill with a mind of greed, they fully possess the twelve links of dependent origination in a single thought-moment.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, it is likewise so: in a single thought-moment, they fulfill these six matters.
This is called the adornment of merit and wisdom.
"Furthermore, good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas create the causes and conditions for the unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*), it is called the adornment of merit;
when they teach and transform sentient beings so that they all attain the three kinds of enlightenment (*bodhi*), it is called the adornment of wisdom.
Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva is able to subdue sentient beings, it is called the adornment of wisdom;
if they undergo all manner of suffering and affliction together with sentient beings, it is called the adornment of merit.
That a bodhisattva can cause all sentient beings to be free from evil views is called the adornment of wisdom;
that they can teach sentient beings to abide in faith, generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom is called the adornment of merit.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with five dharmas, he is able to adorn unsurpassed bodhi.
What are these five?

First is the mind of faith; second is the mind of compassion; third is courage and vigor; fourth is reading and reciting worldly treatises without becoming weary or fatigued; fifth is learning various worldly occupations without ever growing weary of them.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with the two kinds of adornment, there are seven characteristics.
What are these seven?

First, knowing one's own faults; second, not speaking of the faults of others; third, delighting in attending to the sick; fourth, delighting in giving to the poor; fifth, protecting the bodhicitta; sixth, maintaining heedfulness of mind; seventh, at all times constantly cultivating the six pāramitās with a sincere heart.
Good son! Furthermore, there are seven characteristics. What are these seven?
First, delighting in transforming enemies;
second, never growing weary while transforming them;
third, ensuring they reach maturity and liberation.
Fourth, exhausting all that one knows of worldly discourse and worldly affairs to transform sentient beings, with a mind free from greedy attachment;
fifth, being able to endure all evil matters;
sixth, never proclaiming to others anything that is unpleasant to them.
Seventh, upon seeing those who break the precepts or those who are wicked and evil, their minds do not give rise to anger, but they constantly produce compassion.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows these seven signs, they are then able to benefit themselves and others.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a renunciant bodhisattva, these two adornments are not difficult to achieve;
for a householder to cultivate and accumulate them is truly difficult. Why is this?
"Because those living at home are entangled by many evil causes and conditions.
*Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Volume Two;
*Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: On Gathering. Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
Once a bodhisattva has perfected the two adornments, how does he come to maintain a retinue of disciples? “Good son!
One should embrace them through the four means of integration, causing them to leave all evils behind and increase all wholesome dharmas;
one should instruct and admonish them with a sincere heart as if they were an only child, seeking no reward for their kindness, no fame, no gain or support, and no personal pleasure.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva keeps disciples without such qualities as these, he is called a wicked person; he is a bodhisattva in name only, not a bodhisattva in truth.
He is called a caṇḍāla, foul, stinking, and impure; he destroys the Buddha-dharma, and such a person is not cherished or remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions."

“Good son! If a bodhisattva can provide instruction and admonition according to the occasion—where ‘occasion’ refers to the occasions of greed, anger, and delusion—then when the fetter of greed arises, he should preach various methods of counteraction to enable the removal of that greed; it is the same for the other two.
Next, he should teach the twelve divisions of the scriptures, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), samādhi, and the discernment of profound meanings.”
He shall harmonize his body and mind, causing them to cultivate the six recollections and the dharma of heedfulness;

he shall care for those suffering from illness without giving rise to weariness, and be able to endure abusive speech, slander, and insults; he shall likewise be capable of enduring hardships inflicted upon his body and mind;
and should there be suffering, he shall provide relief and liberation, removing their base, evil, and doubting minds.

He skillfully knows those of sharp faculties, middling faculties, and dull faculties; he teaches those of dull faculties to give rise to faith, enables those of middling faculties to become pure and refined, and causes those of sharp faculties to attain liberation. One who can diligently instruct and exhort others in this way is called a Bodhisattva in name and meaning; such a person is called a virtuous man, a *puṇḍarīka* flower, a fragrant elephant among men, a charioteer of men, and a great master mariner.

“Good son! It would be better to accept evil precepts and, within a single day, sever the life-faculties of immeasurable beings, than to nurture and maintain a base and wicked disciple who cannot be tamed.”
Why is this? Good son! The calamity of such improper conduct (akuśala-vinaya) extends only to oneself;

however, by taking on evil disciples whom one cannot instruct, one causes immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil, enables them to slander immeasurable wholesome and sublime dharmas, destroys the harmony of the Saṃgha, and causes many sentient beings to commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya). For these reasons, it is more grievous than the offense of improper conduct itself.
"Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life."
The renunciant bodhisattva has two kinds of disciples:
first, those who have renounced the world; second, those who remain at home.
The lay bodhisattva has one kind of disciple, namely, those who remain at home.
"The renunciant bodhisattva teaches the twelve divisions of the sūtras to those who have left the household life, and according to whatever offense they may commit, he instructs them to repent.
He teaches and trains them in the eight knowledges; what are these eight?"

First is the knowledge of phenomena; second is the knowledge of meaning; third is the knowledge of time; fourth is the knowledge of contentment; fifth is the knowledge of oneself; sixth is the knowledge of the assembly; seventh is the knowledge of the faculties; eighth is the knowledge of discernment.
"Good son!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can thus instruct and discipline his ordained disciples, both the teacher and the disciple will attain immeasurable benefit; in this way, such a teacher and disciple can cause the Three Jewels to increase."

Why is this? Because once such a disciple has realized these eight knowledges, they are able to diligently make offerings to their teachers, preceptors, elders, and those of virtuous merit; they are able to accept wholesome words and diligently engage in recitation; furthermore, they practice the giving of the Dharma, remain heedful in mind, subdue sentient beings, tend to the suffering of the sick, and provide for the poor and destitute.
“Good son! If an ordained bodhisattva has lay disciples, he should also first teach them the dharma of heedfulness.
Heedfulness is itself the practice of the Dharma;”
Make offerings to one's parents, teachers, preceptors, elders, and those of virtuous merit, bestowing upon them peace and happiness;
receive the precepts with a sincere heart and do not recklessly violate them;
and do not deny what has been entrusted to you.
Seeing anger, one is able to endure it;
one never engages in harsh speech, abusive language, or meaningless talk;
out of compassion for sentient beings, one always maintains a sense of reverence and awe toward kings, elders, and ministers.
One is able to discipline one’s own wife, children, and retinue; distinguish between enemies and kin; and not treat sentient beings with contempt;
eliminate arrogance and pride; avoid evil friends;
and practice moderation in eating, removing greed, having few desires, and being content.
In places of contention, one does not enter among them; even in jest, one does not speak evil words—this is called the dharma of heedfulness.
"If an ordained bodhisattva takes on lay disciples, he should first teach them to practice the dharma of heedfulness."
When experiencing suffering or pleasure, one should always remain together with them.
Even if they fall into poverty and have needs, one should not begrudge them anything beyond the six personal requisites.
When they are ill, one should seek out whatever they require; while attending to their illness, one should never give rise to weariness.
If one lacks property of one's own, one should seek it from the four directions;

if it cannot be obtained through seeking, one may borrow the property of the Triple Gem. Once the illness has been cured, one should repay tenfold according to worldly custom, as is the righteous law of King Prasenajit’s kingdom.
If they are unable to repay it, one should further instruct them, saying:
"Now that you owe much to the Triple Gem and cannot repay it, you should diligently cultivate practice to attain the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat."
If one can sincerely resolve to attain bodhicitta; or if one teaches a thousand people to give rise to pure faith in the Buddha-dharma; or if one destroys the grave wrong views of a single person.
“If an ordained bodhisattva can instruct a layperson in such matters as these, both the teacher and the disciple will obtain immeasurable benefit. Good son!
If a lay bodhisattva takes on lay disciples, he should first teach them the dharma of heedfulness (*apramāda*).
To be heedful is to make offerings to one’s parents, teachers, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), elders, and those of virtuous character;

furthermore, it is to provide for one’s brothers, wife, children, friends, kinsmen, and relatives, as well as for travelers and those who have come from afar. As for all servants and laborers, one must first give them food and drink, and only afterwards use them for oneself.

Furthermore, they should be instructed to place faith in and turn toward the Triple Gem; whether in suffering or joy, they shall always be shared together and never be left alone. They should be granted rewards according to the occasion so as not to suffer from hunger or cold, and they must never be subjected to beating, scolding, whipping, or physical torment; rather, they should be exhorted and taught with gentle words.
Should they fall ill, they should be cared for and treated, and whatever they may lack, one should seek to provide it for them.
He instructs them in all worldly affairs, ensuring that when they seek spouses through marriage, they do not seek those of low station;

he teaches them the five classes of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, and upon seeing those who are estranged or broken, he is able to bring them into harmony; once they have been reconciled, he causes their wholesome minds to increase;
and regarding all monastics and followers of internal or external paths, he makes offerings according to his will without ever making distinctions—why is this?

First, they are gathered through generosity, and subsequently, because they are to be disciplined, they are instructed by means of the six points of respectful harmony—whether seeking wealth through commerce, agriculture, or service to a king, one should always act with sincerity and according to the Dharma; having acquired wealth, one should protect it in accordance with the Dharma;
delighting in the performance of merit, one feels joy in the sight of others doing so—this is what is called the dharma of non-negligence.
If a lay bodhisattva can instruct another lay bodhisattva in such matters as these, both the teacher and the disciple will obtain immeasurable benefit.
“Good son! If a lay bodhisattva attains sovereignty as the ruler of a great kingdom, he should protect his subjects as if they were his only child.
He should instruct them to abandon all evils and practice wholesome dharmas.”
When seeing those who commit evil, he beats, strikes, or reviles them, yet never takes their lives.
Of their wealth and goods, he takes one-sixth as tax.
When seeing those who harbor anger and malice, he teaches them the cultivation of patience and heedfulness.

His speech was gentle and supple, and he was able to distinguish between those who were good and those who were evil; seeing those who had committed offenses, he would endure them rather than interrogate them.
According to his means, he constantly practiced the giving of wisdom.

He recited and studied the five divisions of the scriptures according to his capacity; he was skilled at protecting his body, life, and wealth; and he was able to transform sentient beings so that they would not commit evil.

Upon seeing those who were impoverished, he gave rise to great compassion; within his own kingdom, he constantly practiced contentment; he never believed or accepted the slanders of wicked people; and he did not seek or acquire wealth through unrighteous means.
"Protecting the nation in accordance with the Dharma involves staying far away from seven kinds of evils:

first, not delighting in games of chance, go-boards, or six-sided dice; second, not delighting in hunting; third, not delighting in drinking alcohol; fourth, not delighting in lustful thoughts; fifth, not delighting in harsh speech; sixth, not delighting in divisive speech; and seventh, not delighting in acquiring wealth through unrighteous means."

He constantly delights in making offerings to those who have left the household life, enabling the people of the nation to always regard the king as their own father and mother; they believe in causes and effects, do not give rise to jealousy when seeing those superior to themselves, and do not give rise to arrogance when seeing that they themselves are superior to others; they recognize kindness and repay it, responding with great gratitude even for small favors.
They are able to subdue the sense faculties and purify the three karmas.
They praise virtuous people and reproach the wicked; they speak first with a welcoming intention, and their speech is gentle and soft.
Being naturally without power or influence, he lawfully submits to others; when taking another kingdom, he does not mobilize the fourfold army.
When sentient beings are terrified, he is able to provide relief and liberation, constantly gathering them in through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Being well able to discern the various characteristics of phenomena, one who does not accept the Dharma should be disciplined with gentle words: "Good son!
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
The first is the householder, and the second is the renunciant.
For a renunciant bodhisattva to maintain two disciples is not difficult;
for a householder bodhisattva to maintain even one disciple is truly difficult.
"Why is this? Because those who live at home are entangled by many evil causes and conditions.
Chapter Fourteen: Receiving the Precepts. From the Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Chapter Fourteen: Receiving the Precepts. Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
How does a lay bodhisattva receive the upāsaka precepts? “Good son!”
If a lay bodhisattva wishes to receive and uphold the upāsaka precepts, they should first make offerings to the six directions in successive order:
the east, the south, the west, the north, the nadir, and the zenith.

What is called the "eastern direction" refers to one's parents. If a person is able to provide their parents with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, housing, and wealth, and treats them with reverence, prostration, praise, and respect, that person is then able to make offerings to the eastern direction.
Parents repay them in five ways: first, by loving and cherishing them with a sincere heart;

second, by never deceiving or betraying them; third, by relinquishing wealth to provide for them; fourth, by arranging marriages with noble families; and fifth, by instructing them in the affairs of the world.

"To speak of the south is to refer to one's teacher. If there is anyone who can provide their teacher with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites; who honors, praises, reveres, and prostrates before them; and who rises early and retires late to receive and practice their virtuous instructions—that person is truly able to make offerings to the south."
The teacher, in turn, repays them with five matters: first, teaching them swiftly so as not to let the opportunity pass;

second, teaching them exhaustively so as not to leave anything incomplete; third, not giving rise to envy or jealousy when the student excels oneself; fourth, entrusting them to strict teachers and virtuous friends; and fifth, relinquishing one's wealth to them at the time of death.

"To speak of the western direction refers to one's wife and children. If there is anyone who can provide their wife and children with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, necklaces, garments, and ornaments for adorning the body, that person is thereby making offerings to the western direction."

The wife, in turn, repays him with fourteen matters: first, she performs all tasks with her whole heart; second, she acts constantly without ever becoming indolent; third, she ensures that whatever is undertaken is brought to completion; fourth, she works diligently so as not to miss the proper time; fifth, she always attends to guests; sixth, she keeps the rooms and bedding clean; seventh, she is affectionate and respectful, speaking with gentle words; eighth, she instructs servants and attendants with soft speech; ninth, she is skilled at guarding wealth and property; tenth, she rises early and sleeps late; eleventh, she can prepare pure food; twelfth, she can endure instruction and admonition; thirteenth, she can conceal unseemly matters; and fourteenth, she can care for him in times of illness and suffering.

"To speak of the north means that it is the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). If there is anyone who can provide offerings and support to a virtuous friend, giving according to their ability, speaking with reverence and gentle words, prostrating, and praising them—that person is then able to make offerings to the north."
This spiritual friend, in turn, repays them with four things:

first, teaching the cultivation of wholesome dharmas; second, causing them to leave unwholesome dharmas behind; third, being able to provide rescue and liberation when they are in fear; and fourth, being able to cause them to abandon negligence when it occurs.

"To speak of 'the lower direction' refers to servants and slaves. If there is someone who can provide these servants and slaves with clothing, food and drink, and medicine for their illnesses and infirmities, and who neither reviles nor beats them, that person is one who can provide for the lower direction."
A servant or slave should repay their master with ten matters: first, not committing transgressions; second, acting without waiting for instruction;

third, completing whatever task is undertaken; fourth, working diligently so as not to miss the proper time; fifth, never abandoning or deserting the master even if they fall into poverty; sixth, rising early; seventh, guarding property; eighth, returning much for little kindness received; ninth, maintaining sincere respect and mindfulness; and tenth, carefully concealing the master’s misdeeds.

"To say 'the upper direction' refers to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others. If one makes offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of clothing, food and drink, dwellings, bedding, and medicine for illness; if one can rescue them when they are afraid, provide food during times of famine, and shield them from hearing evil; and if one prostrates to, reveres, respects, and praises them—such a person is able to make offerings to the upper direction."
These renunciants repay [their benefactors] through five kinds of deeds:

first, by teaching them to generate faith; second, by teaching them to generate wisdom; third, by teaching them to practice generosity; fourth, by teaching them to uphold the precepts; and fifth, by teaching them to cultivate extensive learning.
"If there are those who make offerings to these six directions, such persons shall increase their wealth and lifespan, and will be able to receive and uphold the Upāsaka precepts.
Good son!..."
If a person wishes to receive the Upāsaka precepts and increase their wealth and lifespan, they must first consult and inform their biological parents.
If the parents grant permission, they should next notify their wife, children, slaves, and servants;
once these people have given their consent, they should then inform the sovereign.

Having heard this, the lord of the land would go to whoever had gone forth and resolved their mind upon bodhicitta, prostrate with their head at their feet, and inquire after them with gentle words, saying:
"Virtuous One!..."
"I am a man, possessing a male body, and I wish to receive the bodhisattva upāsaka precepts; I only pray that the Venerable One, out of compassion, will grant me permission to receive them!
At that time, the bhikṣu should speak these words:
"Have your parents, wife and children, servants, and the ruler of your country given their consent?"
If he says he consents, one should further ask:
"Have you never misappropriated property belonging to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or the property of others?
If he says he has not, one should further ask:
"Do you not currently have any illness, either internal or external, of body or mind?
If he says there is none, one should further ask:
"Have you not committed any improper act toward a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī?"
If he says he has not done so, one should further ask:
"Have you perhaps not committed the five heinous crimes?
If he says he has not done so, one should further ask:
"Are you not one who commits acts of theft?
If he says he does not, one should further ask:

"Are you not a person with dual sexual organs or without sexual organs? Have you not violated the eightfold precepts of the fast? Have you not abandoned your parents or your teacher when they were ill?"

Will you not refrain from killing those who have awakened the bodhicitta, stealing property belonging to the Saṃgha present before you, engaging in double-tongued speech or harsh words, and committing unrighteous acts against your mother or sisters?
"Did you not tell a falsehood before the great assembly?
If he says "No," one should further say to him:
"Good son!..."
The Upāsaka precepts are extremely difficult to uphold! Why is this?
Because these precepts serve as the foundation for the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, the precepts of a mahābhikṣu, and the bodhisattva precepts, even up to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one wholeheartedly receives and upholds the Upāsaka precepts, one will be able to obtain such immeasurable benefits as these.
If there are those who violate or break these precepts, they will dwell within the three evil realms throughout immeasurable and boundless lifetimes, undergoing great suffering and affliction.
"Do you now wish to obtain immeasurable benefit? Can you receive these with a sincere heart?
If they say they can, one should further say to them:
"The Upāsaka precepts are extremely difficult to uphold!"
Once one has taken refuge in the Buddha, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever rely upon Īśvara or other such deities;
once one has taken refuge in the Dharma, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever rely upon the scriptures of non-Buddhists;
once one has taken refuge in the Saṅgha, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever rely upon the heterodox assemblies of non-Buddhists.
"Are you able to thus take refuge in the Triple Gem with a sincere heart?
If they say they can, one should further say to them: "Good son!"
The Upāsaka precepts are extremely difficult to fulfill!
If a person takes refuge in the Triple Gem, that person has already bestowed fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
if a person can bestow fearlessness, that person shall attain the Upāsaka precepts and even reach Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Are you able to bestow such freedom from fear upon all sentient beings?
If they say they are able, one should further say to them:
"There are five things that prevent a person from increasing their wealth and lifespan in the present."
What are these five?
First, taking pleasure in killing; second, taking pleasure in stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; and fifth, drinking intoxicants.

Because all sentient beings kill, they obtain in the present life an ugly appearance, weak strength, an evil reputation, a short lifespan, the depletion of wealth and property, separation from their kin, rebuke by the noble and holy, lack of trust from others, and the unjust imposition of the calamities of others' transgressions upon themselves;
these are called the fruits of evil karma in the present life.
After casting off this body, one shall fall into hell and undergo much suffering, hunger, thirst, a long life, an ugly appearance, feeble strength, ill repute, and other such matters;
these are called the fruits of evil karma in future lives.
If they obtain a human body, they will further suffer from an ugly appearance, a short life, and poverty.
By the power of the causal conditions of this evil person, all five grains, fruits, and melons outside [the realm] will diminish; the calamity of this person flows out to affect the entire world.

If a person delights in stealing, that person will likewise obtain an ugly appearance, meager strength, an evil reputation, a short life, and a depletion of wealth; they will be separated from their kin, others will suspect them of having stolen lost property, and though they associate with people, they will not be trusted; they will be constantly rebuked by the wise and holy.
These are called the fruits of evil karma in the present life.
After abandoning this body, one falls into hell, where one receives an ugly appearance, weak strength, an evil reputation, hunger, thirst, suffering, and affliction for a long duration of life;
these are called the fruits of evil karma in future lives.

If one attains a human body but is destitute of wealth and property, even what is obtained is lost immediately; such a person is not loved or cherished by parents, brothers, wives, or children, and their body constantly undergoes suffering while their mind harbors grief and affliction.

Due to the causal power of this wicked person, all the people shall find that whatever they eat provides them neither physical luster nor strength; the evil fruits of this person’s karma shall thus flow as a calamity upon the myriad subjects.
"Good son!

If there is another person who delights in false speech, that person will in the present life obtain harsh words and an ugly appearance; though what they say may be true, people will not believe or accept it, and all will loathe them, taking no pleasure in seeing them.
