This is called the retribution for evil karma in the present life."
After casting off this body, one enters hell and undergoes great suffering, tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat;
this is called the retribution for evil karma in future lives.

Even if one obtains a human body, one’s mouth will be incomplete; though what one says is true, people do not believe or accept it, and those who see one find no pleasure in it. Although one may preach the True Dharma, people take no delight in hearing it.
By the power of the causal conditions of this evil person, all external material assets will diminish. Good son!

Furthermore, if there is someone who delights in drinking alcohol, that person in the present life will be prone to losing wealth and property, suffer from many physical and mental illnesses, constantly delight in quarreling, have an ill reputation spread far and wide, lose wisdom, lack a sense of shame or remorse, possess an ugly complexion and strength, be constantly rebuked by all, be unpleasant for others to behold, and be unable to cultivate goodness.
This is called the present retribution for drinking alcohol.
After casting off this body, one dwells in hell, undergoing immeasurable suffering such as hunger and thirst;
this is called the fruit of evil karma in future lives.
If one obtains a human body, the mind will be constantly deranged and distracted, unable to maintain mindfulness or contemplate wholesome dharmas.
Due to the causal power of this evil person, all external objects and assets will become putrid and rotten.

"Good son! If there is another person who delights in sexual misconduct, that person will be unable to protect their own body or the bodies of others; all sentient beings who see them will give rise to doubt. Whatever they do, false speech will precede it. At all times they will constantly experience suffering and affliction, and their minds will always be distracted, such that they cannot cultivate goodness. They will frequently lose their wealth and property, and their wife and children will have no affection for them.
Their lifespan will be short: these are called the evil fruits of sexual misconduct in the present life."
After casting off this body, one dwells in hell, experiencing an ugly physical form and strength, enduring hunger, thirst, and a long life of immeasurable suffering;
this is called the retribution for evil karma in future lives.
If one obtains a human body, yet possesses an ugly appearance and foul speech, such that people take no pleasure in seeing him, he will be unable to protect his wife, concubines, sons, or daughters.
Due to the causal power of this evil person, he shall have no mastery over any external things.
"Good son! Regarding these five unwholesome dharmas, are you now truly able to distance yourself from them?
"If he says that he can, one should further say to him:"
“Good son! Having received the Upāsaka precepts, there are four matters that one must not do.
What are these four?
On account of greed, one should not speak falsely; on account of hatred, delusion, or fear, one should not speak falsely.
Are you able to abandon these four unwholesome states?
“If he says he is able, one should further say to him:
‘Good son! Upon receiving the Upāsaka precepts, there are five places where you must not frequent:’”
"The abodes of butchers, courtesans, taverns, kings,
and caṇḍālas— can you avoid these five places?
If they say they can, one should further say to them:
“Good son! Having received the Upāsaka precepts, there are furthermore five things that one must not do:
first, one must not sell living beings; second, one must not sell swords or blades; third, one must not sell poisonous drugs; fourth, one must not sell liquor; and fifth, one must not press oil.”
"Can you abandon these five things?
"If he says he can, one should further say to him:
'Good son!'"
Upon receiving the Upāsaka precepts, there are furthermore three things one should not do:
first, not making nets; second, not using indigo dye; and third, not tanning hides.
"Can you renounce these three things?
"If he says he can, one should further say to him:
'Good son!'"
Upon receiving the Upāsaka precepts, there are further two things that one should not do:
first, playing *chūpú*, *weiqí*, or *liùbó*; second, various forms of singing, dancing, and musical performance.
"Can you abandon these two things?
If he says he can, one should further say to him:
"Good son!..."
Upon receiving the Upāsaka precepts, there are four kinds of people whom one should not associate with:
first, those who play chess or gambling games; second, those who drink alcohol; third, those who practice deception and fraud; and fourth, those who take pleasure in selling alcohol.
"Can you, among these four types of people, remain free from them?
If he says he can, one should further say to him:
"Good son!..."
Having received the upāsaka precepts, there are certain things that one who is negligent should not do.
What constitutes negligence?
It is being distracted by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, or the state of having eaten too much and being full.
At dawn, at dusk, and during times of haste;
when working, or when first intending to work; at times of loss, at times of gain; at times of fear, and at times of joy;
during times of banditry and calamity, during times of famine, and during times of suffering from illness.
In times of youth and vigor, or when one has grown old and decayed;

in times of wealth, or in times of poverty; or when seeking wealth for the sake of one's life—during such times as these, if you do not cultivate wholesome dharmas, will you be able to remain free from them?
"If he says he can, one should further say to him: 'Good son!

Upon receiving the Upāsaka precepts, you must first study worldly affairs. Once you have mastered them, seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma. If you obtain wealth, you should divide it into four parts:"

One part should be used for making offerings to one's parents, oneself, wife, children, and kinsmen; two parts should be used for conducting trade and commerce in accordance with the Dharma; and the remaining one part should be set aside as a reserve for future use.
"Can you perform these four matters?
If he says he can, one should further say to him: "Good son!"
Wealth should not be entrusted to four types of persons:
first, the elderly; second, those who live far away; third, wicked people; and fourth, those with great power.
"These four places should not be entrusted; are you able to remain free from them?
If he says he is able, one should further say:
"Good son!..."
Having received the Upāsaka precepts, there are four types of evil persons whom one should always avoid:

first, those who delight in speaking of others' faults; second, those who delight in speaking of false views; third, those whose mouths are soft but whose hearts are evil; and fourth, those who do little but speak much.
"Can you distance yourself from these four types of evil people?

If they say they can, one should have that person attend upon and serve a wise renunciant for a full six months; the wise one, in turn, should with a sincere mind observe the four modes of deportment of that person's body.

If it is known that this person can act according to the instructions, then after six months have passed, a community of monks numbering at least twenty shall assemble and perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha!..."
Listen to this:

So-and-so now requests from the Saṃgha to receive the Upāsaka precepts; he has already completed six months [of training], maintaining purity in the four modes of deportment during that time, and with a sincere heart he upholds the Stage of Pure Adornment. This person is a man endowed with a male body. If the Saṃgha permits, let there be silence; if it does not permit, speak.
If the Sangha grants permission, the wise one should further speak as follows:
"Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
The Sangha is already in harmony and grants you permission to receive and uphold the Upāsaka precepts.
These precepts are the very root of all wholesome dharmas!

If one accomplishes such precepts, one shall attain the fruit of Srotāpanna up to the fruit of Anāgāmin; however, if one violates these precepts, at the end of life one shall fall into the three evil realms.
Good son! The Upāsaka precepts are inconceivable. Why is this?

Having received these precepts, although one may still experience the five desires, they cannot obstruct the attainment of the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of anāgāmin; therefore, they are called inconceivable.
"Will you, out of compassion for all sentient beings, accept these precepts?
If he says he can accept them, the wise person should then explain the Dharma of the Three Refuges to him, repeating this a second and a third time.
Having received the three refuges, one is called an upāsaka.
At that time, the wise person should further say:
"Good son!..."
Listen attentively, listen attentively!

The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, speaks of the upāsaka precepts: there may be those who possess one part, those who possess half a part, those who possess no part, those who possess many parts, or those who possess the full complement.
If an upāsaka, having received the three refuges, does not receive the five precepts, he is still called an upāsaka.
If, having received the three refuges, he undertakes and maintains one precept, this is called "one part.
Having received the three refuges, if he undertakes and maintains two precepts, this is called "a small part."
If one has received the Three Refuges and maintains two precepts, yet breaks one precept, this is called "incomplete.
If one has received the Three Refuges and receives and maintains three or four precepts, this is called "partially complete.
If one has received the Three Refuges and receives and maintains the five precepts, this is called "fully complete."
"Do you now wish to become a one-part upāsaka, or a full-part one?
If they speak according to their inclination, then at that time the wise one should confer the precepts according to that inclination.
“Once the precepts have been conferred, he further says:
‘Upāsaka, there are six grave dharmas.
O son of good family!...’”
Once an upāsaka has received and maintains the precepts, he must not kill any living being, from celestial maidens down to even an ant.

If, after receiving the precepts, he instructs another to kill by word of mouth or kills with his own body, this person immediately loses the upāsaka precepts. Such a person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin).
These are called the precept-breaking upāsaka, the foul-smelling upāsaka, the caṇḍāla upāsaka, the defiled upāsaka, and the fettered upāsaka.
This is called the first grave offense.
Regarding the Upāsaka precepts, even for the sake of one's own life, one must not steal so much as a single coin.
If one violates this precept, that person immediately loses the Upāsaka precepts; such a person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), let alone the stages from Srotāpanna up to Anāgāmin.
This is called a precept-breaking upāsaka, a foul, a caṇḍāla, a defiled, and a fettered upāsaka.
This is called the second grave offense.
Regarding the upāsaka precepts, even for the sake of one’s body or life, one must not falsely claim, "I have attained the contemplation of impurity" up to "I have attained the stage of an anāgāmin."

If one breaks this precept, that person immediately loses the upāsaka-precepts; such a person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin).
This is called a lay follower who has broken the precepts—a foul, outcaste, defiled, and fettered lay follower.
This is known as the "threefold [transgression].
Regarding the lay follower's precepts, even for the sake of one’s own life, one must not engage in sexual misconduct.

If one breaks this precept, that person immediately loses the upāsaka-precepts; such a person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin).
These are called the precept-breaking upāsaka, the foul-smelling, the caṇḍāla, the defiled, and the fettered upāsaka.
These are known as the four grave offenses.
Even for the sake of one’s own life, an upāsaka who has received the precepts must not proclaim the faults or transgressions of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.
If one breaks this precept, that person immediately loses the upāsaka precepts; such a person cannot even attain the stage of "warmth" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from srotāpanna to anāgāmin.
These are called the lay followers who violate the precepts: the foul-smelling, the caṇḍāla, the defiled, and the fettered lay follower.
These are known as the five grave offenses.
Regarding the precepts of a lay follower, even for the sake of one’s own life, one must not sell alcohol.

If one breaks this precept, that person immediately loses the upāsaka-precepts; such a person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin).
These are called the precept-breaking upāsakas: the foul-smelling, the caṇḍāla, the defiled, and the fettered upāsakas.
These are called the six grave [offenses]. "Good son!
If one receives such Upāsaka precepts and is able to maintain them with a sincere heart without violating them, then one will obtain the fruits of such precepts. Good son!

The Upāsaka precepts are called a necklace and are called an adornment; their fragrance is subtle and wondrous, permeating boundless realms, warding off unwholesome dharmas, and serving as the wholesome Dharma and Vinaya.
They are a treasury of unsurpassed, wondrous jewels, a noble lineage, a place of great tranquility, the flavor of nectar, and the ground for the arising of wholesome dharmas.
"If merely giving rise to this thought can yield such immeasurable benefits, how much more so for one who single-mindedly upholds it without violation? 'Good son!

As the Buddha has said, if an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts, fails to make offerings to his parents and teachers, that upāsaka incurs the offense of negligence; he is unarisen, fallen, impure, and subject to karmic action.'"

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, indulges in the pleasure of drinking alcohol, this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; he does not incur a downfall, nor is it impurity, but it is a transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts, fails to attend to those who are afflicted by illness due to filth or malice, this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and conditioned transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts, sees a beggar and is unable to give them a portion according to his means—whether much or little—but instead sends them away empty-handed, this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an arising, a falling away, an impurity, and an active transgression."

"If a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having received and upheld the precepts, sees a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an elder, or senior lay followers and lay followers (*upāsikā*), and fails to rise to greet them, pay homage, or inquire after their well-being, this lay follower incurs an offense of negligence; he has failed to rise, fallen away, become impure, and committed a transgression."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and upheld the precepts, sees a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā violating the precepts they have received, and conceives arrogance in their mind, saying, 'I am superior to them; they are not my equal,' this lay follower incurs an offense of mental transgression (manodauḥśilya); it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and conditioned [fault]."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, is unable within each month to observe the eightfold fast for six days and make offerings to the Triple Gem, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; he has failed to rise, he has fallen, he is impure, and his actions are defiled."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, does not go to hear the Dharma being expounded within a distance of forty li, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and active transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts, accepts bedding, seats, or couches belonging to the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and active transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, drinks water because he suspects it contains insects, this upāsaka incurs the offense of transgression of mind (manodūṣaṇa); it is an arising offense, a falling offense, an impure offense, and an active offense."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, travels alone through dangerous and difficult places without a companion, this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an arising [offense], a falling away, an impurity, and an act that must be performed."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, stays overnight alone in a bhikṣuṇī monastery, this upāsaka incurs an offense of transgression; it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and conditioned fault."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, beats or reviles his slaves, servants, or outsiders for the sake of wealth or livelihood, this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an arising [of transgression], a falling away, an impurity, and a conditioned act."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and upheld the precepts, gives leftover food to a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, that lay follower incurs an offense of negligence (āpatti-pratikṣepaṇa); it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and conditioned transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, keeps a cat or a wildcat, this upāsaka incurs an offense of transgression of mind (manodūṣaṇa); it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and conditioned offense."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and maintained the precepts, raises elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, or any other domestic animals, and fails to perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*) by giving them to those who have not received the precepts, that lay follower incurs an offense of negligence (*āpatti-daurmanasya*); it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and active transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, does not store away the saṃghāṭī robe, the alms bowl, and the mendicant’s staff, this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen falling away, an impurity, and a transgression."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and maintained the precepts, for the sake of his body and life requires field labor, yet does not seek out pure water or land suitable for cultivation, this lay follower incurs an offense of negligence; it is an arising [of fault], a falling away, an impurity, and an active transgression."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and maintained the precepts, engages in trade by buying and selling goods with measures and scales for the sake of his body and life, once he has stated a price, he must not subsequently change it to abandon the cheap and pursue the expensive;
he may use measures and scales as they are originally leveled, but if they are not level, he should speak up to have them made level."
If it is not thus, this upāsaka incurs an offense of transgression; he has failed to rise, he has fallen, he is impure, and he has committed an act.

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, engages in sexual desire at an improper place or at an improper time, this upāsaka incurs an offense of transgression; he has failed to rise, he has fallen, he is impure, and he has committed an act."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and maintained the precepts, engages in trade and commerce but fails to pay government taxes, and instead steals and abandons them, this lay follower incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen downfall, impure, and a transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, violates the laws of the state, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an arising [of fault], a falling away, an impurity, and an active transgression."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and maintained the precepts, obtains new grain, fruits, melons, or vegetables, and does not first offer them as a gift to the Triple Gem before consuming them himself, that lay follower incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and active transgression."

"If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and maintained the precepts, should personally preach the Dharma or offer praise when the Sangha has not authorized him to do so, that lay follower incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and active transgression."

"If a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having received and maintained the precepts, walks on a road ahead of the bhikṣus or ahead of the śrāmaṇeras, that lay follower incurs an offense of negligence (*duṣkṛta*); it is an arising [of fault], a falling away, an impurity, and an act of commission."

"If an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts, is served food within the Saṃgha, and if he shows partiality toward his teacher by selecting the finest portions and giving them to him in excess, that upāsaka incurs an offense of mental transgression (manodūṣaṇa); it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and conditioned fault."
"If an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts, raises silkworms, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen, fallen, impure, and active transgression."

"If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, encounters a sick person while traveling and fails to stay to look after them, failing to provide skillful means or entrust them to someone else before departing, this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; it is an unarisen downfall, impure, and constitutes a formal transgression."

“Good son! If an upāsaka can wholeheartedly receive and uphold such precepts as these, this person is called a *pundarīka* flower among upāsakas, a subtle and supreme fragrance among upāsakas, a pure lotus among upāsakas, a true and precious jewel among upāsakas, and a true man (*mahāpuruṣa*) among upāsakas!”
“Good son! As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
A bodhisattva who has left the household life is called a bhikṣu; a bodhisattva who remains at home is called an upāsaka.
For a bodhisattva who has left the household life to observe the monastic precepts is not difficult;
for a bodhisattva who remains at home to observe the lay precepts is indeed difficult.
"Why is this? Because those who live at home are entangled by many unwholesome causes and conditions. 15.
Chapter on Pure Precepts, Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Chapter Fifteen: Pure Precepts. Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
If there are people who have received and upheld such precepts as these, how should they cause these precepts to be pure?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! There are three dharmas that can purify this precept:
first, faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; second, deep faith in cause and effect; and third, the mind of understanding.”
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, a mind of loving-kindness; second, a mind of compassion; third, a mind free from greed; and fourth, bestowing kindness upon those who have not yet shown one kindness."

"Furthermore, there are five dharmas: first, to benefit those who have been one's enemies with kindness; second, to provide protection for those who are terrified; third, to open one's heart and give to those who seek before they even ask; fourth, to be impartial and without distinction in all instances of giving; and fifth, to extend universal compassion to all beings without depending on specific causes or conditions."
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, never disparaging oneself by saying, 'I cannot attain the fruit of Bodhi';
second, when proceeding toward Bodhi, maintaining a firm and resolute mind;"
Third, to diligently cultivate all wholesome dharmas with vigor;
fourth, to undertake great undertakings without weariness or regret in the mind.
"Furthermore, there are four other matters:
First, one studies the wholesome dharmas oneself and, having studied them, teaches others;
second, one distances oneself from unwholesome dharmas and teaches others to distance themselves from them as well;
third, one is skillfully able to discern between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Fourth, one does not grasp at or cling to any phenomena.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:

first, knowing that conditioned phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self; second, knowing that all karma inevitably has its retribution; third, knowing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; and fourth, knowing that suffering arises from pleasure and pleasure arises from suffering.
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, having no attachment in one's mind toward any sentient beings; second, bestowing happiness upon sentient beings with an impartial mind; third, acting according to what one has spoken."
“Furthermore, there are three dharmas:

first, being able to bestow upon sentient beings the causes of happiness; second, not seeking gratitude or recompense for what one has done; third, knowing with certainty that one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Furthermore, there are three qualities:

first, undergoing great suffering and affliction for the sake of all sentient beings; second, undergoing them in successive order; third, not ceasing in the interim—though undergoing such suffering, the mind never regrets it.”
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, though one has not yet eliminated the mind of attachment, one is able to renounce what is loved and bestow it upon others;
second, though one has not yet eliminated anger, one is able to endure when evil is inflicted upon them."
Third, although they have not yet eliminated deluded thoughts, they are able to discern between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, being skillfully proficient in expedient means, they are able to teach sentient beings to distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas;
Second, knowing skillful means, they are able to teach sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas;
third, when transforming sentient beings, their minds are free from weariness or regret.
"Furthermore, there are three more dharmas:
First, when causing sentient beings to be free from physical suffering, one does not begrudge one's own body, life, or mind;
second, when causing sentient beings to be free from mental suffering, one does not begrudge one's own body, life, or mind;
third, when teaching and transforming sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas, one does not begrudge one's own body, life, or mind.
“Furthermore, there are three qualities:
first, setting aside one’s own affairs to attend first to the affairs of others;
second, when attending to the affairs of others, not being selective about the timing.”
Third, one never looks back with concern toward hardship, toil, or distress.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas:
first, the mind is free from envy and jealousy;
Second, seeing others experience happiness, one gives rise to joy in one’s heart; third, one’s wholesome mind continues in succession without interruption.
Furthermore, there are three things:
first, seeing even a small amount of goodness in others, one does not forget it from the very beginning.
Second, with even the slightest wisdom, one immediately thinks of receiving abundant rewards;
third, having undergone immeasurable suffering throughout immeasurable lifetimes, one’s mind remains firm and free from any thought of regression.
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, although one deeply understands that birth and death are replete with many faults and transgressions, one nevertheless does not abandon all karmic activities;
second, seeing sentient beings who have no refuge, one acts as their refuge."
Third, upon seeing evil sentient beings, one gives rise to compassion in one's heart and does not reproach them for their faults.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, associating with virtuous friends; second, never growing weary of hearing the Dharma; and third, receiving the instructions of spiritual mentors with a sincere mind.
"Furthermore, there are nine dharmas:
distancing oneself from three dharmas, having no regrets at the three times, and practicing impartial wisdom in giving to the three types of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."
“Good son! If a bodhisattva seeks to purify the mind through pure dharmas, it must be at two times:
first, when a Buddha appears in the world; second, when a pratyekabuddha appears.”
"Good son! There are three ways in which the wholesome dharmas of sentient beings arise:
first, arising from hearing; second, arising from reflection; and third, arising from cultivation."
Regarding the two types—listening and reflection—they exist during those two periods; however, that which arises from cultivation does not necessarily do so.
"Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
The first is the householder, and the second is the renunciant.
For a renunciant bodhisattva, such pure precepts are not difficult;
for a householder, pure precepts are indeed difficult.
"Why is this? Because those who live at home are entangled by many evil causes and conditions.
Chapter Sixteen: Ceasing Evil. In the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen: Ceasing Evil, Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva has already received the upāsaka precepts, how can they become free from internal and external evil and impure causes and conditions? “Good son!”
If a bodhisattva possesses internal or external causes and conditions for various evils and impurities, that person should cultivate the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.

If one cultivates mindfulness of the Buddha with a sincere heart, that person will then be able to leave behind internal and external evil and impure causes and conditions, and increase their compassion and wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
How should one practice? “Good son!”
One should contemplate that the Tathāgata possesses seven superior qualities:

first, superiority of body; second, superiority of abiding in accordance with the Dharma; third, superiority of wisdom; fourth, superiority of endowment; fifth, superiority of sphere of activity; sixth, superiority of inconceivability; and seventh, superiority of liberation.
"What is meant by 'superiority of body'?

The body of the Tathāgata is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. The strength of each joint equals that of eighteen thousand airāvata fragrant elephants. Sentient beings delight in beholding it without ever feeling satiety; this is called superiority of body."
"What is the excellence of abiding in accordance with the Dharma?

Having already attained one's own benefit, the Tathāgata is further able to have compassion for, rescue, and benefit immeasurable sentient beings; this is called the excellence of abiding in accordance with the Dharma."
"What is the superiority of wisdom?
The Tathāgata possesses the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, which are not within the reach of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this is called the superiority of wisdom."
"What is excellence of endowment?
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with conduct, livelihood, precepts, and view; this is called excellence of endowment.
What is excellence of sphere of activity?"

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cultivates the three samādhis, the nine successive attainments, and so forth, which are beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is called the excellence of the sphere of practice.
"What is meant by 'inconceivable superiority'?
The six supernormal powers possessed by the Tathāgata cannot be attained even by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
likewise, the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and three foundations of mindfulness—these are called inconceivable superiority."
"What is the excellence of liberation?

The Tathāgata is fully endowed with two kinds of excellence in liberation: he has removed the cognitive obscurations and the afflictive obscurations, eternally severed all habitual tendencies of the afflictions, and attained mastery over both wisdom and its objects; this is called the excellence of liberation."

Therefore, Śāriputra, in the sūtras, the Tathāgata is praised for being endowed with seven superior qualities. From his contemplation of impurity up until his attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and from the Ground of Adornment (*vyūha-bhūmi*) up to the Ground of Liberation (*vimukti-bhūmi*), he surpasses the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others; for this reason, the Tathāgata is named the Unsurpassed Honored One.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cultivates the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of cessation, the four dhyānas and great compassion, and contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination—all for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
The Tathāgata’s perfect awakening is such that his speech is non-dual; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, just as former Buddhas emerged from the stage of adornment and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is therefore called the Tathāgata.
Having fully attained the subtle and sublime True Dharma, he is named Arhat; because he is able to receive the offerings of all humans and devas, he is named Arhat;
because he has awakened to and understood the two truths—the conventional truth and the ultimate truth—he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having cultivated and maintained pure precepts and being fully endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge, he is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna).
Because he will never again be born within the realms of existence, he is called "Well-Gone" (Sugata).
Because he knows the two worlds—the world of sentient beings and the world of the physical realm—he is called "Knower of the World" (Lokavid).
Skillfully knowing the means to discipline sentient beings, he is called the "Tamer of Men.

Being able to cause sentient beings not to give rise to fear, and using skillful means to teach and transform them so they may leave suffering behind and attain happiness, he is called the "Teacher of Gods and Humans."
Because he knows all phenomena and all modes of conduct, he is called a Buddha.
Because he is able to destroy the four māras, he is called Bhagavat.
Furthermore, one observes that the Tathāgata practices morality, concentration, and wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, he has benefited enemies and kin equally, without distinction.

He has completely severed all immeasurable afflictions and knows them one by one; he knows that for each and every sentient being, a single affliction causes them to undergo great suffering and distress throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
"For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is able to give what is difficult to give and endure what is difficult to endure.
The Buddha possesses two kinds of purity:
first, the purity of adornment; second, the purity of karmic fruition."
By the power of these two causes and conditions of purity, from the first ten-tens to the final ten-tens, no human or deva can speak of any fault in him.

The Tathāgata is endowed with eighty thousand tones; when sentient beings hear them, they do not give rise to weariness or revulsion. For this reason, the Tathāgata excels all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
“Good son! If a person who upholds the Upāsaka precepts wishes to purify those precepts, they should cultivate the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha in this way.

If they cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha, that person will leave behind all internal and external evil and impure causes and conditions; their compassion and wisdom will increase, greed, anger, and delusion will be severed, and they will fully accomplish all wholesome dharmas.”
"Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life."
For an ordained bodhisattva to cultivate the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is not difficult;
for a layperson to cultivate and accumulate it is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Seventeen: Honoring the Triple Gem From the Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Chapter Seventeen: Honoring the Triple Gem Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
“Having already received the Upāsaka precepts, how should a Bodhisattva further make offerings to the Triple Gem?
“Good son! There are generally three kinds of fields of merit in the world:”
First, the field of gratitude; second, the field of merit; third, the field of poverty.
As for the field of gratitude, it refers to one's parents, teachers, and preceptors.
The field of merit refers to those from the attainment of the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) up until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The field of poverty refers to:
For all those who are destitute, suffering, and in distress, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is a field of merit of two kinds:
first, the field of gratitude; second, the field of merit.
The Dharma is likewise, constituting two kinds of fields.
The Saṃgha consists of three kinds:
first, the field of gratitude; second, the field of merit; and third, the field of poverty.
For this reason, a bodhisattva who has already received the upāsaka precepts should, with a sincere mind, diligently make offerings to the Triple Gem.
"Good son! The Tathāgata is the treasury of all dharmas; therefore, the wise should, with a sincere and diligent mind, make offerings to the living body, the parinirvāṇa body, images, and stūpas!"
If there is a place in a wilderness where no stupa or image exists, one should always maintain mindfulness, showing respect and offering praise;

whether acting on one's own initiative or encouraging others to do so, and upon seeing others doing so, one should feel joy in one's heart. If one possesses the power of merit, one must extensively instruct many people to work together upon it.
Having made the offering, one should not give rise to thoughts of self-deprecation regarding one's own person; one should likewise act toward the Triple Gem.

In all acts of offering, one should not have others perform them on one's behalf, nor do so for the sake of surpassing others. While performing the offering, one should feel no regret, nor experience anxiety or distress in the mind; rather, one should join the palms in praise, showing reverence and respect.

Whether it be with a single coin up to immeasurable jewels; whether it be with a single thread up to immeasurable threads; whether it be with a single flower up to immeasurable flowers; whether it be with a single fragrance up to immeasurable fragrances; whether it be with a single verse of praise up to immeasurable verses of praise; whether it be with a single prostration up to immeasurable prostrations; whether it be circumambulating once up to immeasurable circumambulations; whether it be for a single moment up to immeasurable moments; whether performed alone or together with others.
"Good son!
If one can thus make offerings with a sincere heart to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, there is no difference whether it is during my present lifetime or after my parinirvāṇa."
"When seeing a stupa or temple, one should make offerings with gold, silver, copper, iron, chains, banners, canopies, music, fragrant oil, and lamps."
If one sees birds or beasts trampling and destroying [the sacred sites], one must certainly plaster, repair, sweep, and clean them until they are pure;

likewise, for places damaged by violent winds, water, or fire, one should also repair them oneself—if one lacks the strength to do so, one should encourage others to repair them—using gold, silver, copper, iron, earth, or wood.
If there is dust or soil, sprinkle water and sweep it away; if there is grime or filth, wash it with scented water.
If one constructs a jeweled stūpa or a jeweled image, once completed, one should offer various banners, canopies, incense, and flowers.

If one lacks the power of genuine jewels and is unable to provide them, one should next construct [the image] using earth and wood; once completed, one should likewise offer it worship with banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and various kinds of music.

If there are weeds, grass, impurities, the carcasses of birds or beasts, or their excrement within the stupa, as well as withered flowers that have become foul and rotten, all of these must be removed;
holes made by snakes and rats must be plugged and repaired.

Whether they be images of bronze, wood, stone, or clay, or images made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and so forth, one should always wash and clean them, and apply incense upon them according to one's ability.
According to one's capacity, one should fashion various kinds of necklaces and ornaments, even as elaborate as those for the stūpa of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
The interior of the vihāra should be smeared with incense.
Once the stūpa or image has been fashioned using white clay or mud, one should make offerings to it with lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, silk, brocade, bells, chimes, and cords.

When painting an image of the Buddha, one must not mix glue or egg whites into the pigments. One should instead make offerings with various flower garlands, scattered flowers, exquisite ribbons, bright mirrors, powdered incense, unguents, loose incense, burning incense, and all kinds of music, song, and dance.
As it is by day, so it is by night;
as it is by night, so it is by day.
Unlike the non-Buddhists who offer sacrifices by burning ghee and barley, one must never smear the body of a stūpa or an image with ghee, nor wash them with milk.
One should not create an image of the Buddha that is incomplete in its upper body;
if there is an image whose body is not complete, one should cover it up secretly and urge others to repair it. Once it has been repaired and made complete, only then should it be displayed.
If one sees that an image has been damaged, one should with a sincere heart offer worship and pay respect to it as if it were intact and no different.
Such worship must be performed by oneself; if one lacks the personal strength to do so, one should employ others for the task and also exhort others to provide assistance.

"If a person were to offer the treasures of the four continents to the Tathāgata, and another person were to honor and praise him with various merits, revering him with a sincere heart—these two forms of merit would be equal and without distinction."
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s perfection of body and mind?

His body possesses the subtle thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and is endowed with great power; his mind possesses the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, the three mindfulnesses, the five wisdoms and samādhis, the three dharma-gates, the eleven kinds of emptiness, the wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, and immeasurable meditative concentrations. He is fully endowed with the seven wisdoms and has already been able to cross over to the further shore of the six pāramitās.
If a person can praise the Buddha with such dharmas as these, that person is said to truly make offerings to the Buddha.
What is meant by making offerings to the Dharma?
"Good son! If one can make offerings to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, this is called making offerings to the Dharma.
How does one make offerings to the twelve divisions of the scriptures?"

If one can with a sincere heart believe in and rejoice in, receive and uphold, read and recite, explain and expound, and practice according to the teachings—both for oneself and further encouraging others to do so—this is called making offerings to the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
If one is able to transcribe the twelve divisions of the sutras, and having transcribed them, makes various offerings to them as if making offerings to the Buddha—
except for the bathing ceremony— then whoever makes such offerings, upholds, and recites these sutras is said to be making an offering to the Dharma.
When making offerings to the Dharma, one should do so as if making offerings to the Buddha.

Furthermore, there is another method: if a bodhisattva honors a single root, or a pratyekabuddha honors three roots and the three truths, and if one has faith in this, it is called making offerings to the Dharma.

If one makes offerings to those who have set their minds on bodhicitta and uphold the precepts—whether they be renunciants or those progressing from the stage of stream-enterer up to the fruit of arhatship—it is called making offerings to the Sangha.

If there are those who can make such offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, you should know that these people shall never be separated from the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, but will always walk, stand, sit, and lie down together with all the Buddhas.
"Good son!

If there is anyone who can provide even a small amount of offerings to these three fields of merit as described, you should know that this person will receive great benefit throughout immeasurable lifetimes."
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For an ordained bodhisattva to make offerings to the Triple Gem is not difficult;
for a layperson to do so is truly difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
*Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter 18: The Six Pāramitās. Chapter Eighteen on the Six Pāramitās.
Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha previously taught that one should make offerings to the six directions, and that these six directions are the six *pāramitās*, such a person is able to increase their wealth and lifespan. What are the characteristics of such a person?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!

If one can disregard all wealth and property, constantly perform deeds that benefit others, keep in mind the practice of giving, and delight in practicing giving—giving whatever one has regardless of whether it is much or little—and when performing the act of giving, not conceive a sense of disdain for one's own body or possessions, and practicing pure giving without discriminating between those who observe the precepts and those who violate them; [then one shall attain the perfection of giving]."

They praise the practice of giving; seeing others practicing giving, they rejoice without envy; seeing those who come seeking, their hearts are filled with joy; they rise to welcome them and prostrate before them, offering a seat and inviting them to sit. Whether the person asks for it or not, they spontaneously praise the fruits of giving.

Seeing those who are terrified, they are able to provide protection; living in an age of famine, they delight in giving food and drink. Although they perform such acts of giving, they do so not for the sake of karmic retribution, nor do they seek gratitude or reward in return.
They do not deceive sentient beings, but are able to extol all the merits of the Triple Gem; they do not use scales or measures adulterated with other, inferior, or base substances to cheat others.
He takes no pleasure in wine, gambling, or a mind of covetous desire;

he constantly cultivates the virtues of shame, modesty, and remorse; even though he is immensely wealthy, his mind is not heedless; he practices extensive giving and does not give rise to arrogance. Good son!
One who possesses these marks should be known as a person capable of practicing the perfection of giving and making offerings. "Good son!

If there is a person who can purify body, speech, and mind, constantly cultivates a gentle heart, and does not commit transgressions; even if they should err and commit one, they always feel shame and remorse, believing that such karmic offenses will result in evil retribution."

Regarding the wholesome deeds they cultivate, their hearts give rise to joy; they conceive a sense of extreme gravity toward even minor transgressions, and having committed them, they feel dread, sorrow, and remorse. They never strike, revile, or provoke anger in sentient beings;

they speak first with kindness, their words are always gentle, and upon seeing sentient beings, they give rise to a heart of loving-kindness. Knowing gratitude and repaying kindness, their minds are free from stinginess, and they do not deceive sentient beings.

They seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma, delight in performing meritorious deeds, and constantly use the merit they have created to transform others. When they see those who are destitute and suffering, they are willing to take it upon themselves in their own bodies.

Constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for all beings; when seeing those who commit evil, be able to protect them from it; when seeing those who perform good deeds, praise their virtues and explain the fruits of their actions, and further assist them with one's own physical strength;
even when the body lacks autonomy, enable others to act with ease;
constantly cultivate a state of mind that remains far removed from anger, and should it ever arise even momentarily, recognize it and feel shame and regret.
Speaking truthful words and gentle words, and remaining far removed from divisive speech and meaningless speech:
O son of good family!
One who possesses these marks should be known as a person capable of making offerings to the *śīlapāramitā*.

“Good son! If a person can purify the actions of body, speech, and mind, even if sentient beings inflict great evil upon them, they will not give rise to a single thought of anger, nor will they ever retaliate with evil. If others come to repent and apologize, they accept it immediately;
when seeing sentient beings, their minds are always joyful, and when seeing those who commit evil, they give rise to a heart of compassion.”
He praises the fruit of patience and rebukes anger, explaining that the retribution for anger consists largely of bitter suffering;
when practicing generosity and patience, he first directs them toward his enemies;
and he correctly contemplates the five aggregates as a convergence of various conditions, asking: "If they are formed through such a convergence, why does anger arise?"

One should deeply contemplate that anger is the cause and condition for suffering in immeasurable evil realms in the future; if anger should arise even momentarily, one should immediately give rise to shame, remorse, and a sense of dread;
and seeing others excel through patience, one should not harbor envy or jealousy. Good son!
One who possesses these marks should be known as a person capable of making offerings to the perfection of patience. "Good son!

If there is a person who does not become indolent, and who does not accept or crave the pleasures of sitting or lying down—just as when performing great meritorious deeds with power or when attending to minor tasks, their mind remains likewise; [this is one who practices patience]."
In all actions one undertakes, one must ensure they are brought to completion. While acting, one does not regard hunger or thirst, cold or heat, or whether it is the proper time or not;
nor does one disparage oneself. Before a great task is finished, one does not give rise to regret; once it is completed, one rejoices in having accomplished it.

One praises the karmic fruits obtained through diligence—such as acquiring wealth in accordance with the Dharma and using it with reason—and when seeing those who engage in wrong effort, one explains to them the evil consequences thereof.
He skillfully teaches sentient beings to cultivate diligence, so that they do not rest midway until what they have undertaken is completed;
when practicing wholesome dharmas, he does not follow the words of others. Good son!
One who possesses these marks should be known as a person capable of making offerings to the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

"Good son! If there is a person who can purify body, speech, and mind; who delights in dwelling in solitude—whether in a cave, on a mountain, in a forest, or in an empty house; who does not delight in clamor and bustle, nor in attachment to bedding and seats; who does not delight in hearing or discussing worldly matters; and who does not delight in lust, anger, or delusion; [such a person is one who can make offerings to the perfection of vigor]."
First, they speak with gentle words and always delight in teaching and transforming sentient beings outside the household life;
all their afflictions are light, soft, and thin, and they are free from evil thoughts and observations;
they cultivate loving-kindness toward those who harm them and delight in explaining the rewards of meditative concentration.
If the mind becomes distracted or agitated, one gives rise to fear, shame, and remorse;
seeing those settled in wrong concentration, one explains their faults and evils to them, skillfully transforming sentient beings and establishing them in right concentration:
"O son of good family!"
One who possesses these marks should be known as a person capable of making offerings to the dhyāna-pāramitā. "Good son!
If there is a person who can purify body, speech, and mind, who learns all worldly affairs, yet does not take pleasure in greed, hatred, or delusion, and is neither crazed nor distracted;
They have compassion for sentient beings; they are skillfully able to make offerings to their parents, teachers, preceptors, elders, the aged, and those of virtue;
they cultivate heedfulness;
they speak first and with gentle words, do not deceive sentient beings, and are able to distinguish and explain the wrong path and the right path, as well as the retributions of good and evil.
They always delight in tranquility, leaving the household life to cultivate the Way;

they are able to use worldly affairs to teach sentient beings; seeing those whose learning surpasses their own, they do not give rise to envy; being superior to others themselves, they do not give rise to arrogance;
they do not grieve when suffering, nor do they rejoice when experiencing pleasure.
“Good son!
One who possesses these marks should be known as a person capable of making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā. Good son!”
Within each of these directions, there are four matters.
Regarding the four matters of the direction of giving:
the first is:
First, taming sentient beings; second, being free from opposites; third, self-benefit; and fourth, benefiting others.

If a person does not give rise to stinginess or attachment toward wealth, nor discriminates between the marks of enemy and friend, or between the appropriate and inappropriate time, such a person is able to tame sentient beings.
Because one does not begrudge material wealth, one is able to practice giving; thus, one attains freedom from the evil of stinginess, which is called "separation from its opposite.

To feel joy when desiring to give, while giving, and after having given, such that no regret arises, leads to the attainment of human and celestial pleasures up to supreme bliss in the future; this is called "self-benefit."
Because it enables others to be free from the affliction of the suffering of hunger and thirst, it is called "benefiting others.
Regarding the four aspects of morality (*śīla*):
first, adorning enlightenment; second, being free from opposition; third, self-benefit; and fourth, benefiting others.

Regarding the adornment of bodhi: from the upāsaka precepts up to the bodhisattva precepts, these can serve as the foundational ground for the first stage of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called "adornment."
Having already received the precepts, one further attains freedom from evil precepts and the absence of precepts; this is called "separation from opposites.
Having received and maintained the precepts, one attains the bliss of humans and devas up to the unsurpassed bliss; this is called "self-benefit."
Having already received the precepts, one bestows freedom from fear and dread upon all sentient beings, causing everyone to be free from suffering and attain peace; this is called benefiting others.
"The four aspects of patience are:
first, adorning bodhi; second, being free from opposition; third, self-benefit; and fourth, benefiting others."

To adorn bodhi means that because of patience one is able to cultivate wholesome qualities; because of cultivating wholesome qualities, one attains the first stage up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is called "adornment."
Having cultivated patience, one is able to abandon anger and malice; this is called "leaving behind opposition.
By means of the causes and conditions of patience, one attains the happiness of humans and devas up to the unsurpassed bliss; this is called "self-benefit."
Due to the causes and conditions of patience (*kṣānti*), a person gives rise to a joyful mind, a virtuous mind, and a disciplined mind; this is called benefiting others.
The four aspects of progress (*vīrya*) are:
first, adorning enlightenment (*bodhi*); second, distancing oneself from opposition; third, self-benefit; and fourth, benefiting others.

To adorn bodhi means that through diligence one attains the cultivation of wholesome qualities; by cultivating wholesome dharmas, one attains the first stage up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is called adornment.
When practicing wholesome dharmas, one abandons evil and indolence; this is called "separation from opposites.
Because of these wholesome dharmas, one attains the happiness of humans and devas up to the unsurpassed bliss; this is called "self-benefit."
To teach sentient beings to cultivate wholesome qualities and cause them to leave unwholesome dharmas behind is called benefiting others.
Regarding the four aspects of dhyāna:
first, adorning bodhi; second, being free from opposites; third, self-benefit; and fourth, benefiting others.
Regarding the adornment of bodhi: because one cultivates such power of meditative concentration, one attains the first bhūmi and even up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called adornment.
By means of this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one cultivates immeasurable goodness and abandons evil thoughts and observations; this is called "separation from opposites" (*viveka*).

By the power of the causal conditions for cultivating *śamatha*, one constantly delights in tranquility, attaining the bliss of humans and devas up to the unsurpassed bliss; this is called "self-benefit" (*svārtha*).
To sever the minds of all sentient beings from greed, hatred, and delusion is called benefiting others.
"Wisdom has four aspects:
first, adorning bodhi; second, transcending opposition; third, self-benefit; and fourth, benefiting others."
To adorn bodhi means that by cultivating wisdom, one attains the first stage up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called adornment.
By cultivating wisdom, one distances oneself from ignorance and renders the various afflictions powerless; this is called "separation from opposition.
Eliminating the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to wisdom is called "self-benefit."
To teach and transform sentient beings so that they attain subduement is called benefiting others.
"Good son! Some may say:
'Without precepts there is no patience; without wisdom there is no concentration. Therefore, it is said that there are four pāramitās.'"
If one can endure evil without retaliating, this is called precept;
if one cultivates meditative concentration with a mind free from negligence, this is wisdom. Therefore, precept is itself patience, and wisdom is itself concentration.
Apart from wisdom there is no concentration; apart from concentration there is no wisdom. Therefore, wisdom is itself concentration, and concentration is itself wisdom.

Apart from ethical discipline there is no diligence; apart from diligence there is no ethical discipline. Therefore, ethical discipline is itself diligence, and diligence is itself ethical discipline.
"To say that there is no diligence apart from giving and no giving apart from diligence, and therefore giving is itself diligence and diligence is itself giving,
such that one knows there are not six pāramitās— this interpretation is incorrect!"
Why is this? Wisdom is the cause and generosity is the fruit;
diligence is the cause and the observance of precepts is the fruit.
Samādhi is the cause and patience is the fruit.
However, cause and fruit cannot be one and the same; therefore, there must be six pāramitās.
If someone were to say, "Precepts are identical to patience, and patience is identical to precepts," this meaning would not be correct.
Why is this? Precepts are obtained from others, but patience is not like this;

there are those who, without having received the precepts, are nonetheless able to endure evil, cultivate goodness for the sake of the multitude, and endure immeasurable suffering by taking upon themselves great afflictions on behalf of all sentient beings throughout countless lifetimes, their minds never regretting or retreating. For this reason, there must be patience even apart from the precepts.
Good son! Samādhi is precisely śamatha, and wisdom is precisely vipaśyanā;

śamatha is defined as focusing on a single object without distraction, while vipaśyanā is defined as the ability to discern. For this reason, I have taught in the twelve divisions of the scriptures that concentration and wisdom are distinct; you should know that within concentration there are six pāramitās.
The reason the Tathāgata first taught the dānapāramitā was to discipline sentient beings.
Since they become free from greed at the time of giving, he next taught the śīlapāramitā.
Because one is able to endure and relinquish the mind [of attachment] at the time of giving, the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) is taught next.
Because the mind finds joy in giving and does not regard the timing, the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) is taught next.
At the time of giving, the mind is single-pointed and free from distracted signs; therefore, the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramitā) is taught next.
At the time of giving, one does not act for the sake of experiencing the pleasures of birth and death; therefore, the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) is taught next.
“Good son! What is meant by ‘pāramitā’? When giving, one does not seek internal or external rewards;

one does not discriminate between a field of merit and what is not a field of merit; one gives all manner of wealth without stinginess in heart and without selecting specific times or seasons. For this reason, it is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).”
Even regarding minor offenses, one does not transgress them even at the cost of one's own life; therefore, it is called the *śīlapāramitā*.
Even when wicked people come to cut one’s body, one endures it without anger; therefore, it is called the *kṣāntipāramitā*.
To praise the Buddha with a single verse throughout the three months, without ceasing or resting, is therefore called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
To fully attain the vajra-samādhi is therefore called the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
"Good son!
When one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one fully accomplishes the six pāramitās; therefore, it is called the jñāna-pāramitā."
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For one who has left the household life to purify the six pāramitās is not difficult;
for one remaining at home to purify them is truly difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Nineteen: Miscellaneous, The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra. Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
“Having already cultivated the six pāramitās, what kind of deeds can a bodhisattva perform for the sake of sentient beings?
“Good son! Such a bodhisattva is able to pull out from the ocean of suffering those sentient beings who have sunk beneath its waves.”
"Good son!

If there are those who give rise to stinginess regarding wealth, the Dharma, or food, you should know that such persons will receive the retribution of delusion and poverty for immeasurable ages. Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they must bring about both self-benefit and the benefit of others."
"Good son!

If a person delights in giving, all enemies will regard them with affection, and those who lack self-mastery will all attain it. By believing in the cause and effect of giving and believing in the cause and effect of the precepts, such a person shall achieve the fruits of giving."
"Good son!
Some people say:
'Generosity is itself the mind.'"
"Why is this so? Because the mind is the root of giving.
This interpretation is not correct.
Why is this? Giving is itself the five aggregates. Why is that so?
Because giving is perfected through body, speech, and mind.

If giving is performed for one's own benefit, for the benefit of others, or for the benefit of both oneself and others, it then comprises the five aggregates; such giving is able to adorn the path to enlightenment.
Being free from afflictions and possessing great wealth and vast riches is called the primary fruit of giving;
longevity, physical form, strength, well-being, and eloquence are called the secondary fruits of giving.
There are three kinds of fruits of giving:
obtaining a superior fruit because the gift itself is superior;
and obtaining a superior fruit because the field [of merit] is superior.
Because the donor is superior, they obtain a superior fruit.

From those who are candidates for the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) up to bodhisattvas in their final birth, and even until the attainment of Buddhahood—these are called "superior fields" (*kṣetra*). By giving to such fields, one obtains a superior fruit.
If there is a gift that is fully endowed with excellent color, fragrance, flavor, and texture, this is called "superior material"; by giving such an object as a gift, one obtains a superior fruit.
If there is a donor whose faith is pure and intense, and who possesses generosity, morality, learning, and wisdom, they shall obtain a superior fruit.
"Good son! For a person of wisdom, there are five kinds of giving:
First, giving with a sincere mind; second, giving with one's own hands; third, giving with faith; fourth, giving at the proper time; fifth, giving things acquired in accordance with the Dharma.
"Good son! What kind of fruit does one who gives with a sincere heart obtain?

If one gives with a sincere heart, that person will obtain abundant wealth and many treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and coral; elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; fields, houses, slaves, and servants—and will have a great retinue of followers."
One who gives with a sincere heart obtains such fruits as these.
What kind of fruit does one obtain by giving with one's own hands?
Having given with one's own hands, the retribution obtained is as described above.
Having obtained [wealth], one who is able to use it and gives it with their own hand receives such a reward.
As for the donor who gives with faith, what kind of fruit do they obtain?
Having given with faith, the retribution obtained is as described above.
They shall always be cherished and remembered by their parents, brothers, kinsmen, and all sentient beings; those who give with faith shall receive such a reward.
Regarding the giving at the proper time: what kind of fruit does it yield?
As for the retribution obtained from giving at the proper time, it is as described above;
one obtains whatever is needed according to the season. Giving at the proper time yields these fruits as well.
What kind of fruit is obtained from giving wealth in accordance with the Dharma?
The retribution obtained from giving wealth in accordance with the Dharma is as previously described;
having obtained such wealth, it cannot be encroached upon by kings, thieves, water, or fire.
"If one gives beautiful forms as a gift, by this causal condition, that person obtains exquisite and superior physical appearance;
if one gives fragrances as a gift, by this cause, that person's fame will be heard far and wide;
if one gives flavors as a gift, by this cause, that person will be joyfully seen and heard by the multitude, and once they have seen and heard them, they will give rise to affection and respect."
If one gives a gift of pleasant touch, that person will, by reason of this, obtain exquisite touch;
once the recipient has received it, they will be able to obtain longevity, physical form, strength, ease, and eloquence.
"Good son! Some may say:
'Making offerings to a stūpa or an image does not result in longevity, physical beauty, strength, peace, or eloquence, because there is no recipient. This argument is not correct."
Why is this? Because they possess faith; when a donor practices giving with a faithful mind, they shall therefore obtain these five kinds of retribution. Good son!

For example, when a bhikṣu cultivates and accumulates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), although such a mind of loving-kindness has no actual recipient, he nevertheless obtains immeasurable karmic rewards;
making offerings to stūpas, images, and the like should be understood in the same way, whereby one obtains the five kinds of rewards.
"Good son! Just as when a person sows grain, it will never produce cucumbers;

so it is with making offerings to a stūpa or an image. Because they are fields of merit, one obtains various fruits. Therefore, I say that the field receives the retribution, the object receives the retribution, and the donor receives the retribution."
"Good son! There are two kinds of giving:
first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of material wealth."
The gift of Dharma yields two rewards: the reward of wealth and the reward of the Dharma; the gift of material wealth yields only the reward of material treasures.
When a Bodhisattva practices these two kinds of giving, it is for two purposes:
first, to cause sentient beings to distance themselves from suffering and affliction; second, to cause the minds of sentient beings to attain subduing and mastery.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are three kinds of giving:
first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of fearlessness; and third, the gift of material wealth.”
As for giving the Dharma, it consists of instructing others to receive the precepts, leave the household life, cultivate the Path, and perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*;

preaching the True Dharma to destroy false views; being able to analytically explain what is real and what is unreal; and proclaiming the four inversions and heedfulness—this is called the gift of Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who fear kings, lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, or bandits, and the Bodhisattva, having seen them, is able to provide rescue and relief, this is called the gift of fearlessness (abhaya-dāna).

Regarding one’s own wealth and treasures, one overcomes stinginess and does not begrudge them—whether they be beautiful or ugly, many or few; whether they be cattle, sheep, elephants, horses, houses, bedding, groves, springs, or wells; whether they be male or female slaves, servants, oxen, camels, or donkeys; whether they be carriages, litters, or palanquins; whether they be jars, basins, cauldrons, or cooking pots; whether they be rope-beds, seats, copper, iron, or earthenware vessels; whether they be clothing, necklaces, lamps, incense, flowers, fans, parasols, hats, or shoes; whether they be tables, staffs, ropes, plows, hoes, axes, chisels, grass, wood, water, or stone—one gives such things to those who seek them, according to their wishes and as required. This is called the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).

If one constructs a monastic dwelling or a separate room and bestows them upon those who have left the household life as described above, with the sole exception of elephants and horses: "Good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who do not observe the precepts; [2] giving to those who do not practice meditation; [3] giving to those who do not cultivate wisdom; and [4] giving to those who do not seek liberation. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four kinds of giving that bring great merit: [1] giving to those who uphold the precepts; [2] giving to those who practice meditation; [3] giving to those who cultivate wisdom; and [4] giving to those who seek liberation. Good son, these are the four kinds of giving that bring great merit. Furthermore, good son, there are four kinds of giving that bring immeasurable merit: [1] giving to a Pratyekabuddha; [2] giving to a Buddha; [3] giving to a Bodhisattva; and [4] giving to the Three Jewels. Good son, these are the four kinds of giving that bring immeasurable merit. Furthermore, good son, there are four kinds of giving that bring inexhaustible merit: [1] giving to one's parents; [2] giving to one's teachers; [3] giving to one's preceptors; and [4] giving to one's fellow practitioners. Good son, these are the four kinds of giving that bring inexhaustible merit. Furthermore, good son, there are four kinds of giving that bring supreme merit: [1] giving to a sick person; [2] giving to one who is suffering; [3] giving to one who is in danger; and [4] giving to one who is about to die. Good son, these are the four kinds of giving that bring supreme merit. Furthermore, good son, there are four kinds of giving that bring unsurpassed merit: [1] giving to a Dharma-preacher; [2] giving to a person of noble character; [3] giving to a person of great virtue; and [4] giving to a person of great wisdom. Good son, these are the four kinds of giving that bring unsurpassed merit. Good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] stinginess; [2] jealousy; [3] attachment to wealth; and [4] lack of faith. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving with a distracted mind; [2] giving with a contemptuous mind; [3] giving with a regretful mind; and [4] giving with a mind seeking only worldly reward. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are arrogant; [2] giving to those who are deceitful; [3] giving to those who are hypocritical; and [4] giving to those who are ungrateful. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who break the precepts; [2] giving to those who engage in evil conduct; [3] giving to those who harbor malice; and [4] giving to those who are envious. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are attached to their own views; [2] giving to those who are attached to their own practices; [3] giving to those who are attached to their own reputation; and [4] giving to those who are attached to their own gain. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not mindful; [2] giving to those who are not wise; [3] giving to those who are not diligent; and [4] giving to those who are not compassionate. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not learned; [2] giving to those who are not virtuous; [3] giving to those who are not disciplined; and [4] giving to those who are not self-controlled. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not sincere; [2] giving to those who are not respectful; [3] giving to those who are not humble; and [4] giving to those who are not reverent. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not pure; [2] giving to those who are not clean; [3] giving to those who are not neat; and [4] giving to those who are not orderly. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not upright; [2] giving to those who are not honest; [3] giving to those who are not straightforward; and [4] giving to those who are not truthful. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not steadfast; [2] giving to those who are not firm; [3] giving to those who are not resolute; and [4] giving to those who are not courageous. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not patient; [2] giving to those who are not enduring; [3] giving to those who are not tolerant; and [4] giving to those who are not forbearing. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not gentle; [2] giving to those who are not mild; [3] giving to those who are not harmonious; and [4] giving to those who are not conciliatory. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not kind; [2] giving to those who are not benevolent; [3] giving to those who are not compassionate; and [4] giving to those who are not sympathetic. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not grateful; [2] giving to those who are not appreciative; [3] giving to those who are not mindful of kindness; and [4] giving to those who are not mindful of favors. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not faithful; [2] giving to those who are not devoted; [3] giving to those who are not respectful; and [4] giving to those who are not reverent. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving.
