Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not sincere; [2] giving to those who are not honest; [3] giving to those who are not upright; and [4] giving to those who are not truthful. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not pure; [2] giving to those who are not clean; [3] giving to those who are not neat; and [4] giving to those who are not orderly. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not disciplined; [2] giving to those who are not self-controlled; [3] giving to those who are not restrained; and [4] giving to those who are not guarded. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not wise; [2] giving to those who are not learned; [3] giving to those who are not intelligent; and [4] giving to those who are not discerning. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not diligent; [2] giving to those who are not energetic; [3] giving to those who are not persistent; and [4] giving to those who are not persevering. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not mindful; [2] giving to those who are not attentive; [3] giving to those who are not focused; and [4] giving to those who are not concentrated. Good son, these are the four obstacles to giving. Furthermore, good son, there are four obstacles to giving: [1] giving to those who are not virtuous; [2] giving to those who are not moral; [3] giving to those who are not ethical; and [4] giving to those who are not righteous. Good
First, a mind of stinginess and greed; second, not practicing giving; third, disparaging small things; fourth, seeking worldly rewards.
These four hindrances can be destroyed by two methods:
first, cultivating the realization of non-self; second, cultivating the realization of impermanence.
“Good son! If you wish to delight in giving, you should destroy five things:
first, anger; second, stinginess; third, envy; fourth, attachment to body and life; and fifth, lack of faith in cause and effect.”
Having abandoned these five things, one constantly delights in giving.
A person who delights in giving obtains five things:

first, they are never separated from any of the noble ones; second, all sentient beings delight in seeing and hearing them; third, when entering a great assembly, they do not give rise to fear; fourth, they acquire a good reputation; and fifth, they adorn their bodhi.
“Good son! A bodhisattva is called ‘One Who Gives All. Why is he named ‘One Who Gives All’?
Good son!...”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and gives it as an act of giving, it is called "giving everything";
when one constantly gives to recipients with a pure mind, it is called "giving everything";
and when one is able to give even a small amount of things, it is called "giving everything."
To be able to relinquish beloved objects by breaking through stinginess is called "universal giving";
to give without seeking recompense is called "universal giving";
to give at the time of offering without discriminating between a worthy field and an unworthy field is called "universal giving."
Giving impartially to both enemies and kin is called "giving all.

When a bodhisattva gives wealth, there are generally two kinds of recipients—first, sentient beings, and second, non-sentient things—and because they do not begrudge even their own bodies within these two categories, it is called "giving all.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices giving out of a heart of compassion, it is called "giving all."
To have no regret before giving, while giving, or after having given is called "giving everything.

Even if one occasionally gives an impure object in order to cause another person to feel joy, one must never give things such as alcohol, poison, weapons, staffs, or shackles—whether one has mastery over them or not;
nor does one give impure food or medicine to the sick.
He does not steal the property of others, even as much as a single coin, but instead takes it to practice giving.
Although the Bodhisattva possesses mastery when giving, he never scolds or strikes his servants and attendants to cause them to give rise to anger or suffering.
In giving material gifts according to the Dharma, one does not seek rewards in the present or future lives.

Having given, one constantly contemplates the faults and transgressions of the afflictions and deeply contemplates the subtle and wondrous merits of Nirvana; with the exception of Bodhi, there is nothing else sought.
When giving to the poor and destitute, one should give rise to a mind of compassion;
when giving to fields of merit, one should generate a mind of joy and reverence;
and when giving to friends and relatives, one should not harbor a mind of indifference.
If one sees a beggar, one should know what they require and provide it according to their needs without making them speak. Why is this?
Because by giving without waiting for a request, one attains immeasurable fruit.
“Good son! There are three kinds of donors: namely, the inferior, the middling, and the superior.

One who does not believe in the results of karma, is deeply attached to stinginess, fears that their wealth will be exhausted, and gives rise to thoughts of anger and obstruction upon seeing a seeker come—this is called the inferior donor.

Although one believes in the law of karma and its fruits, one gives rise to stinginess regarding wealth, fearing its depletion; yet, upon seeing a seeker come, one develops a mind of relinquishment—this is called the middling [level].

One has deep faith in the law of karma and its fruits and does not give rise to stinginess regarding material things; one contemplates all wealth as being impermanent; upon seeing a seeker come, one rejoices if there is something to give and feels distress if there is nothing to give; one even uses one's own body as collateral to provide for them—this is called the superior [level].
Furthermore, there are those of inferior quality who, upon seeing a seeker come to them for alms, turn their faces away and do not look at them, reviling and insulting them with harsh abuse.
Again, there are those of middling quality who, although they do give gifts, treat the recipient with contempt and lack respect.
Furthermore, there is the superior kind, which gives spontaneously without being asked, bestowing with a heart of reverence.
Again, there is the inferior kind, which gives for the sake of immediate retribution;
and there is the middling kind, which gives for the sake of future retribution.
Furthermore, there is the superior kind of giving, which is out of compassion;
the inferior kind, which is for the sake of repaying a kindness;
and the middling kind, which is for the sake of karma.
Furthermore, there is the superior [giving], which is giving for the sake of the treasury of the Dharma.
Again, there is the inferior [giving], which is giving out of fear of being surpassed;
and again, there is the middling [giving], which is giving because [the recipient] is equal to oneself.
Furthermore, those who are superior do not discriminate between enemies and kin.
Moreover, those who are inferior claim they have no wealth when they possess it;
those who are middling claim they have little when they possess much.
Furthermore, as for the superior [type of donor], they give much even when asked little.
Regarding the donor who possesses no wealth, there are likewise three types:
the lowest type, upon seeing a petitioner come, responds with an evil mind, anger, and reproach;
A person of middle capacity, upon seeing a petitioner, speaks directly, saying they have nothing;
a person of superior capacity, upon seeing a petitioner, feels self-reproach for having nothing and gives rise to sorrow and distress in their heart.
Good son! Furthermore, those who are inferior are constantly rebuked by sages and worthies;
furthermore, those who are middling are constantly pitied by sages and worthies.
Furthermore, as for the superior [giver], the noble ones, upon seeing them, feel joy in their hearts.

"Good son! When a wise person practices giving, it is for the benefit of both self and others; because they know that wealth and treasures are impermanent; to cause sentient beings to give rise to a joyful mind; out of compassion; to destroy stinginess; because they do not seek future retribution; and because they desire to adorn the path to Bodhi."

Therefore, having given all things as alms, a bodhisattva does not give rise to regret; they do not worry about the exhaustion of wealth, do not disparage material objects, do not disparage themselves, do not consider the timing, and do not scrutinize the seeker; they always regard the beggar as one who is hungry and longs for food.

One draws near to virtuous friends and receives their correct teachings; upon seeing those who come to seek [the Dharma], one gives rise to joy in the heart, like a person who has escaped with wealth from a house on fire, rejoicing and praising it while speaking of the many perils of that wealth.
Having given the gift, he feels joy as if entrusting it to a virtuous person;
he further says to the beggar:
"You are now truly the cause of my merit!"
"I have now distanced myself from the mind of stinginess and greed entirely due to the causal condition of your coming to beg.
Thus, he gives rise to a heart of affection and intimacy toward the seeker.
Having bestowed the gift, he further instructs the beggar to protect it according to the Dharma and to diligently cultivate offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.

When a bodhisattva has thus delighted in the practice of giving, they become far removed from all negligence; even when giving their own limbs to a beggar, they never give rise to a single thought of malice, and because of this, their loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity further increase.

One does not treat the recipient lightly, nor does one exalt oneself; rather, one rejoices in possessing wealth and accords with the wishes of the seeker, thereby increasing their faith and causing them to have no doubt regarding the law of karmic cause and effect.
"Good son!..."

If one can contemplate wealth as having the characteristic of impermanence and regard all sentient beings with the thought of them being as one's only child, such a person is then able to give to beggars. Good son!
Such a person is not moved by the fetter of stinginess, just as Mount Sumeru cannot be shaken by the wind.
Such a person can serve as a refuge for sentient beings; such a person is able to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā.
“Good son! A person of wisdom delights in practicing generosity for four reasons:

first, because through giving one can destroy afflictions; second, because through giving one gives rise to various vows; third, because through giving one attains peace and happiness; and fourth, because through giving one becomes abundant in wealth and treasures.”
“Good son! A mind free from greed is called giving.
What is meant by being free from greed?
Giving is itself the action, and the object is the instrument; when one performs the act of giving with both the action and its instrument complete, it is called non-attachment.
As for "destroying afflictions by means of giving": once one practices generosity, one destroys stinginess, greed, envy, hatred, and delusion.
How does one give rise to various vows through giving?
Having given this gift, one is able to give rise to various vows, both wholesome and unwholesome; by virtue of these wholesome and unwholesome vows, one obtains wholesome and unwholesome fruits.
Why is this? It is because of the power of their vow.
How is it that one attains peace and happiness by means of giving?
By virtue of this giving, one receives the pleasures of humans and devas, up to the unsurpassed bliss.
How does giving cause an abundance of wealth and treasures?
By virtue of this giving, whatever one seeks—be it gold, silver, or even livestock—is obtained according to one's wishes.
“Good son! If a person delights in giving, that person will destroy five harmful and evil dharmas:
first, wrong view; second, lack of faith; third, negligence; fourth, stinginess; and fifth, anger and resentment.”
Having abandoned these evils, the mind gives rise to joy; because of this joy, one eventually attains true and perfect liberation.
In the present life, such a person obtains four rewards: first, everyone—even enemies—delights in seeing them;

second, their good reputation spreads throughout the four quarters; third, when entering a great assembly, their heart is free from fear; and fourth, all virtuous people delight in coming near and associating with them.
“Good son! Having practiced giving, his mind is free from regret.

Even if this person should fall into hell due to adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), though he dwells in that evil place, he experiences neither hunger nor thirst. By these causes and conditions, he is freed from two kinds of suffering:”
First, the suffering of iron balls; second, the suffering of iron gruel.
If one has the body of an animal, what is required is easily obtained and there is no lack.
If one has the body of a hungry ghost (preta), one does not experience hunger or thirst, but is always fully satiated.
If one attains a human body, one's lifespan, physical form, strength, ease, eloquence, as well as faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, shall surpass all others;
though dwelling in an evil age, one shall not commit evil deeds; when unwholesome dharmas arise, one shall never follow or accept them;
and in places of fear, one shall not give rise to terror.
If one receives a celestial body, it is superior in ten respects.
"Good son! A person of wisdom practices giving for two reasons: [the first is to benefit others, and the second is to cultivate their own roots of goodness]."
First, he tames his own mind; second, he destroys the minds of enmity and anger.
Because of these, the Tathāgata is named the Unsurpassed Honored One. Good son!

After giving, the wise person does not seek the affection or fond regard of the recipient, nor do they seek fame or the avoidance of fear, nor do they seek for virtuous people to come and associate with them, nor do they hope for the karmic rewards of gods or humans.
They contemplate two matters:
first, exchanging non-durable wealth for durable wealth; second, never following after a mind of stinginess.

Why is this? Such wealth and possessions, when I eventually pass away, will not follow me; therefore, I ought to give them with my own hands. I should not give rise to distress at their loss, but rather give rise to joy in accordance with my giving.
“Good son! A giver should first test his own mind by giving external objects;
once he knows his mind is disciplined, he should next give internal objects.”
"By means of these two kinds of giving, one obtains two dharmas:
first, eternal liberation from all states of existence; second, the attainment of right liberation. Good son!"
Just as a person traveling a long distance, burdened by heavy loads and exhausted by extreme toil, finds joy in laying them down;
so too it is with one who practices giving: upon seeing a seeker come, they lay aside their wealth and give it to them, their heart giving rise to joy and happiness.
“Good son! The wise person always reflects in this way:
‘If one wishes for these things to follow one’s body into future lives, there is nothing that precedes giving.’”
Furthermore, one should deeply contemplate the suffering of poverty and the joy of noble status; therefore, fix the mind and always delight in practicing generosity. "Good son!
If a person possesses wealth but, upon seeing a seeker, says they have nothing or speaks with trepidation."
You should know that such a person has already declared their own poverty and lack of merit in future lives; such a person is called "heedless.
"Good son! It is not correct to say that a person who possesses no wealth speaks of having no wealth."

Why is this? Regarding all water and grass, there is no one who does not possess some; thus, though one may be a sovereign of a nation, it is not necessarily the case that they can give, while though one may be poor, it is not that they cannot give.
Why is this? Even a poor person has their share of food; after eating, if they wash their vessels and give away the rinsed water to those who ought to eat it, they too will obtain merit and virtue.
If one gives even a speck of dust or a grain of flour as an offering to an ant, one will likewise obtain immeasurable fruits of merit and reward.
Among those who are the poorest in the world, who would not possess at least this much of a speck of flour?
"Who is there whose life would not be preserved if they ate only three morsels of flour for a single day?
Therefore, all people should give half of their food to beggars. Good son!"
Among those who are extremely poor, who is there so destitute as to be naked and without clothing?
If one possesses clothing, would it not be possible to give even a single thread to someone to bind a wound, or a piece of wealth the size of a finger to serve as a wick for a lamp?
"Good son! Among the people of the world, who is so poor as to be without a body?

If one possesses a body, upon seeing another person performing meritorious deeds, one should go to assist them with joy and without weariness; such a person is also called a donor and shall likewise obtain merit—whether it be a portion, equal to that of the other, or even superior."
For this reason, when I accept the meal offered by King Prasenajit, I likewise offer prayers for the king and for the poor, so that the merit they obtain is equal and without distinction.
Good son!

It is like a person buying incense—ointment incense, powdered incense, scattered incense, and burning incense. When these four types of incense are encountered by someone, purchased by someone, or measured by someone, they are all smelled equally without distinction, yet none of these various incenses loses even a hair’s breadth of its fragrance.
The cultivation of the virtue of giving is likewise so:

whether it be much or little, coarse or fine, whether one assists with body and mind out of sympathetic joy, or feels joy in the heart upon seeing or hearing from afar—the fruit and retribution obtained are without distinction because the mind is equal.
“Good son! If one lacks wealth and, upon seeing another give, feels no joy or faith but instead harbors doubts regarding the field of merit, this is called poverty.
If one possesses abundant riches and is free from constraints, yet encounters a noble field of merit and, lacking internal faith, is unable to offer a gift, this too is called poverty.”

Therefore, a wise person should give according to their means and to the best of their ability; for apart from giving, there is nothing else that can cause one to attain the happiness of humans and devas, up to the unsurpassed bliss.
Therefore, in the sūtras I have said:

"If a wise person observes that by eating one final morsel of food they will survive, whereas by giving it to another they will die, they should still give it away; how much more so when there is more?"
"Good son! A wise person should contemplate that wealth is impermanent; because it is impermanent, throughout immeasurable lifetimes it has been lost, destroyed, and diminished, yielding no benefit.
Although it is impermanent, it can nevertheless bring about immeasurable benefit—how then can one be stingy and fail to practice giving?"

The wise person further contemplates the world: if there are those who maintain the precepts and possess extensive learning, by the power of the causes and conditions of maintaining the precepts and extensive learning, they may even attain the fruit of arhatship;

yet, though they have attained this fruit, they cannot eliminate sufferings such as hunger and thirst—if an arhat finds it difficult to obtain housing, clothing, food and drink, bedding, or medicine for illness, it is all due to the causes and conditions of not having practiced giving in previous lives. Conversely, if a person who has broken the precepts delights in practicing giving, that person, even if they fall into the realms of hungry ghosts or animals, will always be fully satisfied and lack nothing.
Good son! Apart from giving, one cannot attain two fruits:
first, sovereignty; second, liberation.
If a person who upholds the precepts is reborn in heaven, because they did not cultivate the practice of giving, they will not obtain superior food or exquisite necklaces and ornaments.
If one desires worldly happiness as well as unsurpassed bliss, one should take delight in giving.

The wise person should contemplate that birth and death are boundless, and that the experience of pleasure is likewise so; therefore, one should practice giving for the purpose of severing birth and death, not seeking the enjoyment of pleasure.

Furthermore, one should reflect: "Even if one possesses the lands of the four continents and experiences immeasurable pleasure, one still knows no satisfaction; therefore, I should practice giving for the sake of supreme bliss, not for the realms of humans or devas."
Why is this? Because it is impermanent and because it has limits. "Good son!
If someone were to say:

"The donor, the recipient, and the one who experiences the pleasure are all the five aggregates; since these five aggregates are impermanent, when one gives away the five aggregates, who is it that receives them?"
Although there is no recipient, the wholesome fruit does not perish; therefore, there is neither giver nor recipient.
One should instead ask: "Are there a giver and a recipient?"
If one says, "The gift is indeed the gift, and the recipient is I," then one should further say to them, "I am also like this: the gift is indeed the gift, and I am the five aggregates."
If one says that the aggregates (skandhas) are given as an offering, and these are impermanent, who is it that receives them there?
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you:
Is the seed permanent,
or is it impermanent?
If you say it is permanent, how can the seed perish and yet give rise to a sprout?

If you see this fault and further claim it is impermanent, one should then say: "If it is impermanent, how could the labor of applying manure, water, soil, and so forth at the time of the seed cause the sprout to grow?"
If you say, "Although the seed is impermanent, it produces sprouts and fruit by virtue of its karmic activity," then one should say that the five aggregates are likewise so.
If you say, "The sprout already exists within the seed beforehand, and human effort, water, and fertilizer act as the manifesting causes," this argument is not tenable.

Why is this? That which is revealed by the revealing cause (vyakti-hetu) undergoes neither increase nor decrease in the object itself; if it is much, it remains much, and if it is little, it remains little.
Yet now, the water, the manure, and the sprout increase. Therefore, that which was originally non-existent has now come into being.
If it is said: "The revealing cause is of two kinds:
first, much; second, little.
When much, one sees large; when little, one sees small."
"It is like lighting a lamp: when the light is great, what is seen is large; when the light is small, what is seen is small. This meaning is not so. Why?
It is like a single seed: even if given much water and fertilizer, it cannot grow to the size of a man or exceed a man all at once or in a single day.

If you say, "Although there are two kinds of revealing causes, they must depend on time and season; when the object is small, the result is small, and when the object is large, the result is large; therefore, I say that the revealing cause does not increase," this argument is not correct.
Why is this? Because in your doctrine time is eternal; therefore, you should not speak in such a manner.
"Good son!..."
The seed is different from the sprout; although they arise as distinct entities, they are similar and continuous. The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are likewise. Good son!

Just as the activity of the seed increases the sprout, the activity of the sprout increases the stem, the activity of the stem increases the leaf, the activity of the leaf increases the flower, and the activity of the flower increases the fruit; so it is with the aggregates.
The same applies to the five aggregates of one path increasing the aggregates of the five paths.
If you say that such a thing is "one acts and another receives," this principle belongs to you; it is not what I teach.
Why is this? According to your doctrine, the agent is the self and the experiencer is the body, yet you do not say that the agent and the experiencer are distinct.

Since the one who receives the precept against killing is the self, and by this cause and condition the body attains a wondrous complexion, it follows that in your doctrine the experiencer has no cause and the agent has no fruit; thus there is such a fault.
If one says, "I am the one who performs the action and the body is what receives it; I am likewise such that this person acts and that person receives," one should further ask:

"Your body and your self are distinct. When the body receives food, drink, clothing, and ornaments, through the condition of excellent food it acquires a fine complexion and strength, and through the condition of poor food it acquires a wretched complexion and strength. If these good and bad complexions belong to the conditions, what do you yourself obtain?"
If one says, "I have attained sorrow or joy," how is this not a case of one person performing an action and another receiving its result?
For example, suppose there is a person who consumes ghee for strength; after consuming it for a long time, his body attains great power and a most excellent complexion.
If another person, who is emaciated and weak, sees him and feels joy in his heart, would that person immediately attain such great physical power and complexion?
If you say that [the self] does not obtain it, I am also like this:
how could the self obtain what is done by the body? Why is this so?
Because they are dissimilar.
My Dharma is not thus; the aggregates act and the aggregates receive, being similar and uninterrupted. "Good son!
If one says, "The five aggregates are impermanent; they do not pass from this [life] to that [life] to receive retribution," this meaning is not so.

Why? Because in our teaching, there may be cases where the very same agent acts and receives the result, or cases where one acts and another receives, or cases where there is neither acting nor receiving.
Regarding "the one who acts is the same as the one who experiences": this refers to the aggregates (skandhas) acting and the aggregates experiencing.
Regarding "the one who acts is different from the one who experiences": this refers to a human acting and a deva experiencing.

Regarding "no actor and no experiencer": since karma arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions and is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), how could there be an actor or an experiencer?
"If you think, 'If one acts and another receives [the result], how can it be said that the continuity is unbroken?'—
this interpretation is incorrect. Why is this so?"

For example, if poison is placed in milk, it is able to kill when it has reached the stage of *ghṛta* (clarified butter). Although the milk is different [from the *ghṛta*] and the *ghṛta* is likewise different, even though there is this difference, they arise in succession and continue in a similar manner;

thus, it is able to harm people. The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are also like this: although they are different, they arise in succession and continue in a similar manner. Therefore, one may say: "one acts and another receives [the fruit]," or "one acts and that very same one receives," or "there is no acting and no receiving."
If one were separate from the five aggregates, there would be no self or what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
However, the minds of all sentient beings are shrouded by perversion; some say that form (*rūpa*) is the self, and so on up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) being the self.
Others say, "Form is the self, while the other four aggregates are what belongs to the self," and this applies likewise up to consciousness.
If anyone were to say, "Apart from the five aggregates, there exists a separate self," such a thing is impossible. Why?
Because in my Buddha-dharma, form is not the self.
Why is this? Because they are impermanent, uncreated, and lack self-mastery, these four aggregates are not called "mine";
the same applies even to consciousness.
Through the combination of various conditions, distinct phenomena arise; thus they are called "action," yet in reality there is no separate action.
Through the combination of various conditions, distinct phenomena arise; thus they are called "experiencer," yet in reality there is no separate experiencer.
Therefore, it is said to be without action and without experiencer.
"If you think, 'If one acts and another receives, why is it that when this person performs an action, another person does not receive its result,
given that both possess the five aggregates?'—
this argument is not tenable."
Why is this? There are two kinds of difference:
first, difference of body; second, difference of name.
The first is "Attained by the Buddha" (Buddhalabdha) and the second is "Attained by Heaven" (Devalabdha).
Since the bodies and names of "Attained by the Buddha" and "Attained by Heaven" are each distinct, their physical and verbal actions must also be distinct due to these causes and conditions;
because their bodies and speech are distinct, the karma they create is likewise distinct.

Because the karma created differs, there are differences in lifespan, physical appearance, strength, well-being, and eloquence; therefore, it cannot be that "Buddhadatta" performs the action while "Devadatta" receives the result.
Although both possess the five aggregates, while "form" and "name" are identical, "feeling," "perception," and "volitional formations" differ.

Why is this? Because "Buddhadeva" experiences pleasure while "Devasharma" experiences suffering; because "Buddhadeva" gives rise to greed while "Devasharma" gives rise to hatred. For these reasons, they cannot be said to be similar.
Although "form" (rūpa) and "name" (nāman) are one in designation, in reality they are distinct; for instance, there may be a "Buddha-attained" white [form] and a "Heaven-attained" black [form].
If one were to treat identical names as having a single meaning, then when one person is born, everyone should be born, and when one person dies, everyone should die.
If you do not wish to accept this principle, then it follows that one cannot perform an action and experience its result as distinct entities.
If you think, "You also perform an action and experience its result as distinct entities, and I am likewise performing an action and experiencing its result as distinct entities;

if this were the case of performing an action and experiencing its result as distinct entities, you should share my fault. Why then do you fail to see your own fault and instead reproach me?"—this argument is not tenable.
Why is this? Because "I" is of two kinds:
first, that which arises in succession and also ceases in succession; second, that which arises in succession but does not cease in succession.

Since birth is distinct, cessation is likewise distinct; therefore, when I say "one acts and another experiences" or "this one acts and this one experiences," it does not share the same fault as yours.

"It is like a person who wishes to burn down a village; if they cast a single spark of fire onto dry grass, that fire, through the successive causes and conditions of its arising, can burn for a hundred li or even two hundred li."
The village headman found him and immediately questioned him:
"You wicked man, for what reason and by what cause did you burn down this great village?
The man replied:
"In truth, it was not I who burned it. Why is this?
The fire I released was extinguished immediately; what was burned was but a single handful of grass."
"I shall now return to you two handfuls to repay you; as for the rest of the goods, I ought not to repay them.
At that time, the village headman spoke again, saying:
"Foolish man!"
"Because of your small fire, a succession of fires was produced, which eventually burned for a hundred li to two hundred li.
The guilt lies with you; why do you not pay reparation?
Although one knows that this fire is produced by one thing and burns another, because the continuity is uninterrupted, the person incurs the offense.
The five aggregates of good and evil are likewise:
although it is said that the aggregates at the time of receiving retribution did not perform the action, they arise through a continuous succession; therefore, one receives the retribution.

"It is, for example, as if someone were to make a wager with another, carrying a torch and traveling far to a place a hundred *li* away, stipulating: 'If I do not arrive, I shall pay the penalty; but if I do arrive, you shall pay me.'"
When the man carrying the torch had traveled a hundred *li*, the owner immediately demanded his property back.
The other replied, "Your torch was extinguished as soon as it left its starting point; why do you now demand your goods from me here?"
The torch-bearer said:
"Although that fire has been extinguished, it has arisen in successive succession and reached this point.
Thus, both men speak with reason.
Why is this? Because these two meanings are both identical and different; therefore, neither of the two persons incurs any fault.

If one were to say, "The five aggregates are likewise: that which acts is the same as that which receives, and that which acts is different from that which receives," in either case there would be no fault.

"For example, the two banks and the middle current are collectively called the Ganges. In summer, the distance between the two banks is very great; in autumn, the distance between the two banks is close. There is no fixed characteristic; it may be large or small. Although it increases and decreases, everyone still calls it a river."
Some may say: "This is not a river; yet the wise also speak of it as being both different and non-different.
The five aggregates are likewise: the wise also speak of the one who acts being the same as the one who experiences, and the one who acts being different from the one who experiences."
If you think that "the two banks are earth, the middle current is water, and the river deity is the river," this interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?

If the spirit were the river, why would one further speak of the river being clear or turbid, of this bank, that bank, and the depth or shallowness of the middle current, of its reaching the great ocean, or of it being fordable or not fordable?
For example, where there is a tree, a deity dwells therein; if there were no tree, where would the deity dwell?
The relationship between the river and the deity should be understood in the same way.
Therefore, the two banks—this side and that—and the middle current, being continuous and uninterrupted in succession, are collectively called a "river.
Thus, one may speak of identity and difference; the five aggregates are likewise so.

"For example, suppose there is a person who insults someone of noble rank; because of that harsh speech, his feet are bound with shackles. Although these feet actually possess no guilt for the harsh speech, they are nonetheless shackled. Therefore, one cannot definitively say that 'the one who acts is different from the one who experiences' or 'the act and its experience are simultaneous. Only a wise person can rightly say both: 'the act and its experience are simultaneous,' and 'the one who acts is different from the one who experiences.'"
"For example, when the conditions—the vessel, the oil, the wick, the flame, and the person who protects it—are combined, it is called 'lamp-light.
If you think that 'the lamp-light increases or decreases,' this interpretation is not correct."
Why is this? Because it ceases, it does not increase; because it comes, it does not decrease. Since they arise in succession, one speaks of the lamp increasing or decreasing.
If you think, "The lamp is impermanent, but the oil is permanent; when the oil is much, the light is much, and when the oil is little, the light is little," this meaning is not so.
Why is this? Because oil is impermanent, it can be exhausted and it can be burned.
If it were permanent, it would have to abide for two moments; [but it does not].
If these two abide for two moments, who could burn them away?

Therefore, the wise also say: "The lamp and its light are distinct; the five aggregates are likewise. The light is the six sense bases, and the oil is karma. Due to the causal conditions of the oil and karma, the five aggregates undergo increase and decrease, such that 'that' exists and 'this' exists."

"It is like when someone speaks the Aṭṭhiya language; although this Aṭṭhiya has long since passed away and does not exist today, because it has been transmitted by the people of the world in succession without being lost, it is called the 'Aṭṭhiya language'."
The wise also speak of this as being both the language of "attiya" and not the language of "attiya"; although it is both "is" and "is not," neither loses its principle.
The five aggregates are likewise:
one may say that the same agent acts and receives the fruit, or that the agent who acts is different from the one who receives.
“Suppose there is a man of great wealth whose lineage has been cut off and who himself has passed away; his property would then be confiscated by the state.
Someone might say:
‘Such wealth and goods ought to belong to me.’”
The official said,
"How can this wealth be produced by one person and belong to another?
The man replied again:
"I am the seventh-generation descendant of this deceased man, following in succession without interruption; why then would these assets not belong to me?
The official immediately replied, "So it is, so it is;
it is just as you have said."
The wise say: "The five aggregates are likewise; that which acts is the same as that which receives, and it is not the case that one acts while another receives.

If you think, "The five aggregates perform an action and, once completed, pass away; yet this body still remains, and the karma has no basis. If karma has no basis, then there is effectively no karma. Once this body is discarded, how can one obtain retribution?"
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because all past karma depends upon its substance and depends upon time.
For example, a tangerine arises from a tangerine and becomes sweet through its sourness.

A person plants this seed for the sake of the tangerine; yet the seed, root, stem, leaves, flowers, and the fruit while it is growing are all not sour. Only when the time comes and the fruit ripens does the sour flavor manifest.
In this way, the sour taste was not originally non-existent and now existent, nor did it arise without conditions; rather, it is due to past causal conditions of the original fruit.
The same applies to the actions of body, speech, and mind.
If one asks where this karma abides, it abides within the past; awaiting the proper time and the proper vessel, it receives its retribution.
It is like a person taking medicine: although the medicine has been digested after the passage of time, when the time arrives, it produces excellent strength and a healthy complexion.
The karma of body, speech, and mind is also like this: although it has passed and ceased, when the time arrives, it is experienced.
For example, when a child first learns a task, although it perishes moment by moment and has no place of abiding, it is not lost even after a hundred years;
past karma is likewise: although it has no place of abiding, when the time arrives, one experiences its fruit spontaneously.
Therefore it is said:
"The aggregates do not create [karma] and the aggregates do not receive [its fruit], yet one cannot say that it is received by something other than the aggregates.
If one can clearly and thoroughly penetrate this matter, such a person will be able to attain the unsurpassed fruit.
The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Volume Four;
The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Remainder of the Miscellaneous Chapter: Good son!
Furthermore, if there is a person who is stingy regarding their body, life, and wealth, and does not practice giving, this is called stinginess (*mātsarya*).

To cherish and guard a stingy person’s mind that refuses to give, lacking compassion, and instead waiting for a field of merit; to seek out a field of merit and, once found, search for faults in it; to contemplate how wealth is difficult to obtain and thus suffer on its account;
or to preach that there is no fruit, no giving, and no recipient; to cherish one's wife, children, and kin;
to accumulate wealth and seek fame; to feel joy upon seeing much wealth; and to view wealth as permanent—this is called the defilement of stinginess (*mātsarya-mala*).
This defilement can pollute the minds of all sentient beings; for this reason, they are unable to give even from the property of others, let alone from their own.

When the wise practice giving, they do not do so to repay kindness, nor to seek worldly gain, nor to protect those who are stingy and greedy, nor to be born among gods or humans to enjoy pleasure, nor to cause a good reputation to spread abroad, nor out of fear of the sufferings of the three evil realms, nor because others request it, nor to surpass others, nor to avoid the loss of wealth, nor because they have much, nor because they have no other use for it, nor as a matter of family custom, nor to curry favor with others.

When a wise person practices giving, it is out of compassion; it is because they desire to bring peace and happiness to others; it is because they wish to inspire the mind of generosity in others; it is because it is the fundamental path practiced by all noble ones; it is because they desire to destroy all afflictions; and it is because they wish to enter nirvana and sever the cycle of existence.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva practices giving, he remains far removed from four evils:
first, breaking the precepts; second, the net of doubt; third, false views; and fourth, stinginess.”
Furthermore, one should avoid five things:

first, not discriminating between those with virtue and those without virtue when giving; second, not speaking of good or evil when giving; third, not selecting based on lineage when giving; fourth, not slighting the solicitor when giving; and fifth, not using harsh words or abuse when giving.
Furthermore, there are three things by which one does not obtain a superior and wondrous karmic reward after having given:

first, to have initially generated a great resolve but later give only a little; second, to select inferior items to bestow upon others; third, to feel regret in one's heart after having performed the act of giving.
"Good son! Furthermore, there are eight things by which one does not achieve the supreme fruit after having given a gift:

first, seeing faults in the recipient after giving; second, giving with an uneven mind at the time of giving; third, seeking to have the recipient perform work after giving; fourth, rejoicing in self-praise after giving; fifth, speaking [of the gift] and then giving it only later; sixth, reviling and abusing others with harsh words after giving; seventh, seeking two-fold repayment after giving; eighth, conceiving a mind of doubt after giving."
A donor such as this cannot attain proximity to the Buddhas and the worthy sages.
If one bestows upon others that which is complete in color, fragrance, flavor, and texture, it is called a pure gift;
if one can obtain wealth in accordance with the Dharma and bestow it, it is called a pure gift.
To practice giving while contemplating that wealth is impermanent and cannot be preserved for long is called pure giving;
to practice giving in order to destroy afflictions is called pure giving;
to give for the sake of purifying the causes and conditions of one's own mind is called pure giving.

If one contemplates who gives, who is the recipient, what object is given, for what reason it is given, and what fruit is obtained through the causes and conditions of such giving—such giving consists of the twelve bases (*āyatana*). The recipient, the donor, the causes and conditions, and the retribution are all the twelve bases. One who practices giving while being able to contemplate in this way is said to perform pure giving.

When practicing giving, one should give rise to a heart of joy toward the field of merit, seeking the same virtues sought by those fields of merit without ceasing. One gives to wives, children, relatives, and servants with a heart of compassion; one gives to the poor in order to destroy their suffering and affliction. When giving, one does not seek worldly rewards;

one gives by breaking down pride, gives with a gentle and supple mind, and gives while remaining detached from all states of existence (*bhava*). One gives for the sake of seeking unsurpassed liberation, giving while deeply contemplating the many faults and transgressions of birth and death, and giving without discriminating between a field of merit and a non-field of merit.
If one can practice giving in this manner, the karmic reward will follow that person like a calf follows its mother.
"If one gives with the expectation of a fruit, it is no different from a commercial transaction.

Just as when one plows and sows for the sake of one's own livelihood and reaps a harvest according to the seeds sown, so too is it for a donor who has given: they obtain a reward of merit according to what was given."
Just as the recipient of a gift, having received it, obtains life, physical form, strength, peace, and eloquence, the donor likewise obtains these five rewards.

If one gives to an animal, one obtains a hundredfold reward; if one gives to a person who has broken the precepts, one obtains a thousandfold reward; if one gives to a holder of the precepts, one obtains a hundred-thousandfold reward; if one gives to a non-Buddhist practitioner who is free from desire, one obtains a millionfold reward; if one gives to one who is heading toward the Path, one obtains ten billionfold reward; if one gives to a *srotāpanna*, one obtains immeasurable reward; for one who is heading toward the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, there is likewise immeasurable reward; and even up to the attainment of Buddhahood, the reward is immeasurable.
“Good son! Now, for the sake of distinguishing various fields of merit for you, I have spoken thus regarding the attainment of a hundredfold reward up to an immeasurable reward.
If one can give rise to a heart of great compassion toward animals with utmost sincerity, and with single-minded reverence give to the Buddhas, the merit is exactly equal and without distinction.”

Regarding the term "a hundredfold": if one bestows longevity, physical form, strength, well-being, and eloquence upon another, the donor will subsequently obtain each of these—longevity, physical form, strength, happiness, and eloquence—in a hundredfold measure;
this remains true even up to an immeasurable degree.
Therefore, in the sūtras I have said:
"I give to Śāriputra, and Śāriputra also gives to me; yet I obtain much more, while Śāriputra does not obtain as much merit."
"If some say, 'When the recipient commits evil, the sin reaches the donor,' this meaning is not so.
Why? When the donor gives, it is for the purpose of destroying that person's suffering, not for the purpose of committing a sin; therefore, the donor should obtain wholesome fruit."
If the recipient commits evil, the retribution falls upon themselves alone and does not reach the donor.

If a donor gives pure and exquisite things, they will later obtain a beautiful appearance that others delight to behold, their good reputation will spread, their wishes will be fulfilled, and they will be born into a noble lineage; this is not called evil. Why, then, do you say that the donor incurs guilt?

When a donor has given, they feel joy and have no regrets; they associate with virtuous people, possess wealth and sovereignty, and are born into noble families. They obtain the happiness of humans and devas, culminating in unsurpassed bliss, and are able to free themselves from all fetters of affliction. Since the donor thus attains such sublime fruits, how can you say that they receive an evil retribution?

If a donor, having given with their own hands, is reborn into a noble family, encounters virtuous friends, possesses abundant wealth and jewels, achieves a circle of kinsmen, and is capable of both utilizing and giving; if all sentient beings joyfully behold them, and upon seeing them, pay homage, respect, and praise—since the donor receives such rewards as these, how can it be said that they obtain an evil retribution?

If a donor has already purified their offerings and given them away, by virtue of these causes and conditions, they will possess abundant wealth and treasures, be born into a noble lineage, have immeasurable kinsmen, be free from physical illness and suffering, and be without mental anxiety or fear. Their property cannot be encroached upon by kings, thieves, water, or fire; even if they should lose their wealth, they will not give rise to grief or distress. Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, their body and mind will remain peaceful and happy. How, then, can it be said that they receive evil retributions?

If one gives rise to faith when about to give, feels joy while giving, and experiences peace after having given; if one suffers no distress when seeking, guarding, or using the gift; if by giving clothing one obtains exquisite beauty, by giving food one obtains unsurpassed strength, by giving lamps one obtains pure and wondrous eyes, by giving vehicles one’s body receives comfort and ease, and by giving dwellings one lacks for nothing—then how can it be said that such a donor receives an evil retribution? It is only through such virtuous rewards that the donor attains these results. How, then, can you say they receive an evil fruit?
"Furthermore, once a donor has given to the Buddha, the karmic fruit is already determined, whether it is used or not.
When giving to persons and the Saṃgha, there are two kinds of merit:
first, that which arises from usage; second, that which arises from acceptance."

Why is this? When the donor gives, they personally destroy their own stinginess; when the recipient uses [the gift], they destroy the stinginess of others. Therefore, it is said that merit arises from usage.

Furthermore, by employing others to employ [the Dharma] and by causing the Sangha to increase, one gives without seeking worldly retribution and does not give with the intent of giving rise to the causes of affliction; therefore, one is able to attain the unsurpassed pure fruit, which is called Nirvana.

If there is anyone who can establish a vow day by day, first giving food to others before eating it themselves, and who pledges to forfeit their own share to the Buddha should they violate this vow, feeling shame at the transgression;
and if they do not violate it, this becomes a causal condition for subtle and wondrous wisdom—such a donor is the foremost among all donors, and such a person may also be called a supreme patron.
If one can practice giving in accordance with the wishes of the supplicant, that person will have their requests fulfilled as desired throughout immeasurable future lifetimes.
If one possesses a pure mind, and both the material wealth and the field of merit are entirely pure, that person shall obtain immeasurable karmic rewards.
If one provides food and clothing for one's wife, children, servants, and slaves, always giving with a heart of compassion and joy, one will obtain immeasurable merit in the future.
Furthermore, when observing that there are many rats and sparrows in the fields and granaries that ravage the grain and rice, one should constantly give rise to compassion;
and further, one should form this thought:
"Thus, these mice and sparrows have their lives sustained because of me.
Having thought this, he feels joy and harbors no thought of irritation; you should know that such a person attains immeasurable merit.

If one fashions for oneself garments, necklaces, bracelets, and other ornaments for adorning the body, as well as various utensils, and having completed them, feels joy and gives them away to others before using them oneself, that person will obtain a wish-fulfilling tree in the future.
"If anyone were to say, 'One can obtain a wholesome fruit apart from giving,' such a thing is impossible;
likewise, it is impossible that 'there is giving without material wealth, there is giving without a recipient, or that one accomplishes the perfection of giving without abandoning stinginess.'"

If one gives without being asked, gives when resources are scarce, gives much when little is requested, gives what is excellent when something inferior is sought, encourages others to seek out gifts, or personally goes forth to practice giving—know that such a person will, in future lives, obtain many treasuries of jewels, and all things that are not jewels will be transformed into jewels.
Giving for the sake of jest, giving to those who are not fields of merit, or giving without faith in cause and effect—such acts of giving are not truly called "giving.

If a person gives only to excellent fields of merit and does not delight in constant giving, then when that person receives the retribution of their fruit in the future, they will not delight in practicing generosity.

If a person, after having given a gift, gives rise to a mind of regret, or if they take the property of others to offer as a gift, that person will obtain wealth in the future, yet it will constantly diminish and never accumulate.
If one gives gifts by distressing one's kinsmen to acquire wealth, although such a person may obtain great rewards in the future, their body will constantly suffer from illness.

If one first fails to provide for one’s parents, and instead distresses one’s wife, children, servants, or slaves to perform a painful act of giving, this is called a wicked person; it is a gift in name only and not a gift in principle.

Such a giver is devoid of compassion and ignorant of repaying kindness; though they may obtain wealth and treasures in the future, they will constantly lose them before they can accumulate them, unable to utilize them, and their bodies will be plagued by much suffering and disease.
If a person gives wealth as an offering in accordance with the Dharma, that person will obtain immeasurable merit in the future and will possess wealth that they can utilize.

If one does not give wealth as an offering in accordance with the Dharma, although that person may obtain karmic rewards in the future, they will always depend on others for their gain; should those others perish, they will immediately fall into poverty.

A person of wisdom deeply contemplates that although the pleasures of humans, devas, and universal monarchs (cakravartin) are subtle and exquisite, they are all impermanent; therefore, when practicing giving, one does not do so for the sake of human or celestial rebirth.
“Good son! There are two kinds of giving:
first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma.”
The gift of material wealth is called "inferior," while the gift of the Dharma is called "superior.
What is the gift of the Dharma?

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who can instruct others to be fully endowed with faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom; or if they cause others to transcribe the Tathāgata’s true scriptures using paper and ink, or transcribe them themselves, and subsequently give them to others so that they may read and recite them—this is called the gift of the Dharma.
A donor who gives in this manner will obtain a superior physical appearance for immeasurable future lives. Why is this?

Because sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma, eliminate their hearts of anger; by virtue of these causes and conditions, the donor will attain a superior appearance throughout immeasurable future lifetimes.

When sentient beings hear the Dharma, they cultivate a heart of compassion and refrain from killing; by this causal condition, the donor shall obtain a long life throughout immeasurable future lifetimes.

When sentient beings hear the Dharma, they refrain from stealing the wealth of others; by this causal condition, the donor shall abound in riches and treasures throughout immeasurable future lifetimes.
When sentient beings hear this, their hearts open and they delight in giving; by this cause and condition, the donor will attain great physical strength throughout immeasurable future lives.
When sentient beings hear the Dharma and sever all forms of negligence, by this cause and condition, the donor will attain peace and happiness throughout immeasurable future lives.
When sentient beings hear the Dharma and eliminate their deluded minds, by this cause and condition, the donor will attain unimpeded eloquence throughout immeasurable future lifetimes.
When sentient beings hear the Dharma and give rise to faith without doubt, by this cause and condition, the donor’s confidence will become clear and lucid throughout immeasurable future lifetimes;
the same applies to precepts, giving, hearing, and wisdom.
Therefore, the gift of Dharma is superior to the gift of material wealth.

"As for those who say, 'If a son cultivates wholesome dharmas while his father performs unwholesome deeds, because of the son's cultivation of wholesomeness, the father will not fall into the three evil realms'—this meaning is not so."
Why is this? Because the actions of body, speech, and mind are each distinct.
If a father has passed away and fallen among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), one should know that if his son performs meritorious deeds on his behalf, the father will immediately receive the benefit.
If one is born among the devas, one does not think of human things at all.
Why is this? Because the deva realms are endowed with superior and wondrous jewels.
If one enters hell, the body undergoes such suffering and affliction that there is no leisure for reflection; therefore, [the Dharma] cannot be attained.
It is the same among animals and human beings as well.
If one asks why hungry ghosts alone obtain [these things],
it is because they originally possessed craving, greed, and stinginess, and thus fell into the realm of hungry ghosts;
once they have become hungry ghosts, they constantly regret their past transgressions and long for what they desire, and for this reason, they obtain them.
If the one for whose sake [the merit] was performed has been reborn in another realm, while his remaining kinsmen have fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts, they shall all receive it.
Therefore, the wise should diligently cultivate merit and virtue for the sake of hungry ghosts.

If one gives clothing, food, dwellings, bedding, and other necessities of life to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others who are poor and mendicants, and they perform incantations and prayers on their behalf so that they may obtain merit—by the power of these causes and conditions of giving and prayer, those who have fallen among the hungry ghosts will gain great strength and receive whatever they give.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of their birthplaces.

The food consumed by various hungry ghosts differs: some eat pus, some eat excrement, and others eat blood, vomit, nasal mucus, or saliva; yet once they receive this offering, it all transforms into the most exquisite color and flavor.
Even if one gives impure wash-water and the like to those who ought to eat, if there is someone present who prevents them from eating,
the donor nonetheless obtains merit.
Why is this? It is because the donor’s mind is characterized by compassion and pity.
If there is a sacrificial offering, who is it that receives it?
The recipient is determined according to the location of the sacrifice:
if it is near a grove of trees, the tree deity receives it; the same applies to houses, rivers, springs, wells, mountain forests, and mounds.
When such a person has completed the sacrifice, they too obtain merit. Why is this?
Because it causes the recipient to give rise to a joyful mind.
The merit of such sacrifices can protect one's person and wealth.
However, the claim that one obtains blessings by performing sacrifices involving the killing of living beings is incorrect. Why is this so?
One does not see worldly people planting *eranda* seeds and growing sandalwood trees, nor do they obtain merit by taking the lives of sentient beings!
If one wishes to perform a sacrifice, one should instead use incense, flowers, milk, curd, ghee, and medicinal herbs.
In performing meritorious deeds on behalf of the deceased, there are three seasons:
the second month of spring, the fifth month of summer, and the ninth month of autumn.

If a person gives dwellings, bedding, medicinal decoctions, gardens, ponds, wells, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, and various other necessities of life to others, and then passes away after having given these gifts, that person’s merit will constantly arise for as long as those gifted items remain in use. This merit follows the person just as a shadow follows a form.
Some may say, "It is lost immediately upon death," but this meaning is not correct.
Why? Because an object is lost at two times: when it is destroyed and no longer used, or when life comes to an end; it is not lost solely through the exhaustion of life.
If those who have left the household life emulate householders by abstaining from food and drink on festival days, they do so in accordance with worldly customs and thus it is not the ultimate truth;
yet, this is done because they place equal faith in both worldly and world-transcending dharmas.
If one can constantly delight in giving according to what one possesses at home, whether good or bad, it is called "universal giving.
If one gives away parts of one's own body, as well as one's wife and children, or things held most dear, this is called "inconceivable giving."

If there are those who are evil persons, violators of the precepts, enemies, those who do not recognize kindness or righteousness, those who do not believe in cause and effect, those who beg or solicit by force, those of great power, those who are aggressive in their abuse, those who become angry after receiving a gift, those who falsely manifest signs of goodness, and those of great wealth and status—giving to these eleven types of people is called "inconceivable."
Good son! All acts of giving have three roots:
giving to the poor out of compassion;
One gives to an enemy because one does not seek a reward;
one gives to a person of merit because of a heart of joy and reverence.
"Good son!..."

If a person possesses great wealth and makes offerings to the Triple Gem for immeasurable ages, although they may thereby obtain immeasurable fruits of merit, it is not equal to encouraging others to join together in cooperation.
If a person treats small or inferior things with contempt and, out of shame, refuses to give them away, that person increases their poverty and suffering in future lives.
If two people give together, and their wealth, the field of merit, and the intention to give are all equal, there will be no difference in the fruits they obtain.
If their wealth and intentions are equal, but one’s field of merit is superior, the resulting retribution will be superior.
If the field and the mind are both inferior, yet the material object is superior, the fruit obtained will be superior;
if the field and the material object are both inferior, yet the mind of giving is superior, the fruit obtained will likewise be superior;
if the field and the material object are both superior, yet the mind of giving is inferior, the fruit obtained will not be as excellent.
“Good son! When the wise give, they do not do so for the sake of karmic retribution. Why is this?
This is because one knows with certainty that this cause will necessarily yield its fruit.

If a person lacks compassion, does not recognize kindness or righteousness, does not covet the merits possessed by the sages, cherishes wealth, body, and life, and possesses heavy attachment through greed—such a person is unable to practice giving.

When the wise person deeply contemplates how all sentient beings, when seeking wealth and property, do not spare even their own bodies or lives, and having obtained such wealth, are able to give it away to others, they should know that such a person is capable of sacrificing their own body and life.
If a person is stingy and unable to relinquish wealth, one should know that this person also cherishes their own body and life.
If one relinquishes body and life to seek wealth for the purpose of practicing giving, one should know that such a person is a great donor.
If a person acquires wealth yet, out of greed and attachment, does not practice giving, you should know that this is the seed of poverty in future lives.
Therefore, in the sūtras I have said:
among the four continents, the people of Jambudvīpa excel in three respects—first, their courage and vigor; second, their mindfulness; and third, the purity of their conduct.

Without seeing the karmic retribution, one is able to pre-arrange the causes; not sparing even body or life, one seeks to obtain wealth; having obtained it, one can destroy stinginess; having thought of giving, and once having given, the mind feels no regret; furthermore, one is able to distinguish between fields of merit and non-fields of merit—this is called being brave and resolute.
“Good son! There are three causes for the arising of regret after having given:
first, craving and attachment to wealth; second, following and upholding false views; and third, perceiving faults in the recipient.”
Furthermore, there are three matters:
first, the fear of being rebuked by others; second, the fear of suffering when one's wealth is exhausted; and third, seeing others suffer various miseries after they have given in charity.
"Good son! A wise person does not give rise to regret at the three times, and there are furthermore three matters:
first, clearly understanding cause and effect; second, drawing near to virtuous friends; and third, not being greedily attached to wealth."
Regarding those who believe in cause and effect, there are two further matters:
first, hearing the Dharma from others; second, reflecting upon it within oneself.
Regarding drawing near to virtuous friends, there are likewise two matters:
First is deep faith, and second is wisdom.
Regarding non-attachment to wealth, there are further two matters:
first, contemplating impermanence; second, contemplating lack of self-mastery.
"Good son!
If a donor can observe in this way and practice giving in this way, you should know that such a person is able to fulfill the perfection of dāna."
Therefore, I have previously said:
there is giving that is not a pāramitā; there is a pāramitā that is not giving; there is that which is both giving and a pāramitā; and there is that which is neither giving nor a pāramitā.
“Good son! There are three kinds of wisdom:

first, the ability to relinquish external things; second, the relinquishing of both internal and external things; and third, having bestowed both the internal and external, further transforming sentient beings.”
How does one teach and transform others?
Upon seeing those who are impoverished, one should first say to them:
"Are you able to take refuge in the Triple Gem?"
"Will you observe the fast and precepts?
If they say they can, one should first bestow the Three Refuges and the fast and precepts, and afterwards give the gift;
if they say they cannot, one should further speak to them as follows:
"If you are unable [to do that], can you follow my lead and say that all phenomena are impermanent, selfless, and that nirvāṇa is quiescent?
If he says he can, one should further instruct him; having instructed him, one should then give the gift.
If he says, "I am now able to speak of these two matters, but I alone cannot speak of the selflessness of all phenomena," one should further say to him:
"If you cannot explain that all phenomena are without self, can you at least explain that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature?
If he says he can, then having instructed him, [the teacher] shall bestow the gift.
If one can first teach and afterwards give in this manner, they are called a great donor.
Son of good family!
If one can thus teach and transform sentient beings, as well as enemies and kin, without making any distinctions, they are called a great donor.
"Good son! When a wise person possesses wealth and treasures, they should practice giving in this manner;
if they have no wealth, they should further instruct others who do possess wealth to perform such giving."
If there are other donors who already know this method and do not require instruction, one should assist them with one’s own physical labor.

If one is destitute and has no goods, one should recite medical prescriptions and various incantations to seek money and medicinal decoctions; whatever is needed should be given. One should attend to the sick with a sincere heart, providing care and administering treatment, and should exhort those who possess wealth to compound various medicines—whether in pill, powder, or various decoction form.

Having mastered medical treatises, he traveled everywhere to attend to the sick; examining them according to the prescriptions, he identified the location of the ailments and provided treatment accordingly.

When treating illnesses, he was skilled in expedient means; though he remained amidst impurity, he did not give rise to feelings of aversion. He knew when a disease was increasing and when it was subsiding;
furthermore, he was well able to discern which foods and medicines would aggravate the suffering of illness, and which foods and medicines could eliminate such suffering.
If a patient seeks food or medicine that would increase their illness, one should employ skillful means and speak to them with appropriate metaphors;
one must not say that such things do not exist, for if one says they do not exist, the patient's suffering may become even more severe.

If one knows for certain that death is imminent, one should not even speak of dying; rather, one should only instruct them to take refuge in the Triple Gem, to mindfully recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and to diligently practice making offerings.

For their sake, one should explain that all these sufferings of illness are the bitter retributions obtained due to unwholesome causes and conditions from past lives, and that they must now perform repentance.
When the patient hears this, they may give rise to anger and revile him with harsh words; yet he remains silent and does not retaliate, nor does he abandon them.
Although he continues to care for and nourish them, he is careful never to demand gratitude; even after they have recovered, he still looks after them, fearing that they might suffer a relapse.
If you see them restored to health as they were when originally strong, your mind should give rise to joy, and you should not seek any reward for your kindness;
if they have died, you should perform their funeral rites and console their friends and relatives by preaching the Dharma.

One should not give food that increases illness as medicine to others; however, if the illness has been cured and one gives with a joyful heart, such items may be accepted. Having accepted them, one should then redistribute them to other destitute persons.
If one can thus attend to, nourish, and treat the illness, you should know that such a person is a great donor who truly seeks the path to unsurpassed bodhi. "Good son!

When a person of wisdom seeks Bodhi, even if they possess abundant wealth and treasures, they should still study and recite such medical prescriptions, establish infirmaries, and provide all necessary food, drink, decoctions, and medicines for the sick.

Where roads are narrow or uneven, he levels and widens them; he removes thorns, stones, filth, and impurities. At dangerous places, he provides whatever is required—whether planks, ladders, rafters, or ropes—and furnishes them all.

They dug wells along desolate roads, planted groves of fruit trees, and repaired springs and pools. In places where there were no trees, they erected pillars for carrying loads to rest upon, and constructed mounds as resting spots for those bearing burdens.
He constructed guest houses, providing all necessary items such as jars, basins, lamps, beds, and bedding. Where foul odors and filth flowed, he built bridges and stairs;

at fords and ferry crossings, he provided bridges, boats, and rafts. For those unable to cross, he would go himself to ferry them across; for the elderly, the young, the frail, and those lacking physical strength, he would personally take them by hand to ensure they reached the other side.
Along the way, he built stupas and planted trees bearing flowers and fruit.
Whenever he saw those who were terrified, he would immediately provide them refuge; using material goods and kind words, he would entice and persuade their captors.
If he sees a practitioner who has reached a dangerous place, he immediately goes forward to support and receive him, enabling him to pass through the peril;
if he sees someone who has lost their land or suffered ruin, he provides for them as appropriate and consoles them with kind words.
When one has traveled far and is utterly exhausted, one should provide them with a bath, massage their hands and feet, and offer them a seat;
if there is no seat, one should spread out grass as a mat.
In times of heat, one provides shade with fans, garments, and canopies; in times of cold, one bestows fire and warm clothing—whether performing these acts oneself or instructing others to do so.
In buying and selling, he instructs them to follow fair prices, not to covet small profits, and not to deceive one another.

When he sees travelers on the road, he points out the right path and the wrong path—the right path being that which abounds in water and grass and is free from bandits—and he proclaims the wrong path as being full of many dangers and hardships.
When he saw people’s boots, robes, or alms bowls that were worn out or damaged, he would immediately mend, wash, dye, or fumigate them for them;
and if they suffered from mice, snakes, bedbugs, or venomous insects, he was able to eliminate these pests for them.
One should provide others with wish-fulfilling items, tweezers, and ear-picks; one should mend and wash the property of the Saṃgha, such as bedding and seating mats;
and one should place clean water, bathing powder, and pure ash or earth in the latrines.
If one personally makes clothing or a bowl, one should first offer them to the Buddha and have one's parents, teachers, elders, and preceptors use them first before using them oneself;
if offering them to the Buddha, one may redeem them with flowers and incense.
In all matters of eating and drinking, one must first give to śramaṇas and brahmins before eating oneself.

Upon seeing those who have come from afar, one should greet them with gentle words and inquire after their well-being; one should provide pure water for bathing the body, oil for anointing the feet—along with fragrant flowers, willow twigs, cleansing powder, ash, scented oil, perfumed water, honey, *vibhītaka* seeds, small garments, and those who apply the ointment.
Having washed them, he further bestowed upon them various kinds of fragrant flowers, medicinal pills, powdered medicines, food and drink, and beverages as required;
he also gave razors, water-strainers, and so forth, as well as needles and thread, clothing and rags, paper, pens, and ink.
If one cannot give constantly, one should give according to the days of the fast.
If one sees a blind person, one should go before them and take their hand, giving them a staff and showing them the way.

If one sees those who are suffering, those who have lost their wealth, or those whose parents have passed away, one should provide them with material goods, speak to them with kind words, preach the Dharma, comfort and exhort them, and skillfully explain the two fruits of affliction and merit.
"Good son! If one can cultivate and accumulate such giving as this, they are called a pure donor. Good son!"
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.
For a bodhisattva who has left the home life to act as a pure donor is not difficult.
For a lay bodhisattva to act as a pure donor is truly difficult. Why is this?
Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter 20: Purifying the Three Refuges. *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty: Purifying the Three Refuges. Sujāta said:

“World-Honored One, as the Buddha previously stated, ‘When there is one who comes to beg, one should first instruct them to receive the three refuges, and only then give [the gift],’ for what reason and by what causes and conditions does one receive the three refuges?”
"What is meant by the Three Refuges? "Good son!
To destroy all suffering, to sever the afflictions, and to receive the unsurpassed bliss of nirvana—for these reasons, one receives the Three Refuges."
Regarding your question as to what the three refuges are:
noble son, they are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The Buddha is one who can explain the cause for destroying afflictions and attaining true liberation;
the Dharma is itself the cause for destroying afflictions and true liberation;
the Sangha is those who receive and practice the cause for destroying afflictions and attain true liberation.
Some may say, "If this is so, then there is only one refuge," but this meaning is not correct.
Why? Because whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the True Dharma (saddharma) is ever-present and without differentiation.
Once the Tathāgata has appeared, there is differentiation; therefore, one should take refuge specifically in the Buddha.

Whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the True Dharma always exists, yet it would have no recipient were it not for the community of the Buddha’s disciples who are able to receive and uphold it; therefore, one should take refuge specifically in the Saṃgha.
The liberation through the right path is called the Dharma;
the solitary awakening without a teacher is called the Buddha;
and the ability to receive [the teaching] in accordance with the Dharma is called the Saṅgha.
