If there were no Three Refuges, how could one speak of the four indestructible faiths?
Those who attain the Three Refuges may be either complete or incomplete in their observance.
What constitutes being complete?
This refers to taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
As for those who do not fulfill this, it refers to those who take refuge in the Tathāgata and the Dharma. Good son!
"Those who attain the Three Refuges do so without anything lacking, just as with the precepts of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Good son!"
Just as the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Śrāvaka are each distinct, so too the Three Jewels cannot but be distinct.
In what way are they distinct?

They are distinct because the time of generating the aspiration is different, the time of adornment is different, the time of attaining the Way is different, and their respective natures and capacities are each different; therefore, they are distinct.
For what reason is it said that the Buddha is the Dharma?
Because he is able to understand this Dharma, he is called the Buddha;
because he receives and explains it through discernment, he is called the Saṃgha.
If anyone were to say, "The Buddha is included within the Saṃgha," this meaning is not correct.
Why is that? If the Buddha were included within the Saṃgha, then there would be no Three Jewels, nor the three refuges, nor the four unshakable faiths.
Good son! The Bodhisattva and the Dharma are distinct; the Buddha and the Dharma are also distinct.
There are two kinds of Bodhisattvas:
The first is the final body, and the second is the cultivation of the path.
Taking refuge in the final body is called taking refuge in the Dharma; taking refuge in the cultivation of the path is called taking refuge in the Saṃgha.
Observing that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) abound in faults and practicing alone, one attains the flavor of the Deathless (*amṛta*); therefore, this is called the Buddha.
The entire untainted realm of unconditioned phenomena (*anāsravāsaṃskṛtadharmadhātu*) is called the Dharma.
Upholding the prohibitive precepts and reading, reciting, and explaining the twelve divisions of the scriptures is called the Saṅgha.
"If someone were to ask:
'After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, what is this "taking refuge in the Buddha"?',
O son of good family!"
Such a taking of refuge is called taking refuge in the dharmas of no-more-learning of all past Buddhas.
It is as I previously instructed the householder Trapusa:
"You should take refuge in the Sangha of future ages."
It is also thus with respect to the Buddhas of the past.
Because there are differences in the magnitude of the field of merit and its karmic retribution, they are distinguished as three types.
However, whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, there is no difference in the karmic retribution of making offerings to him.
It is the same for those who have received refuge.

Just as when the Buddha was in the world, he established essential precepts for his disciples, and even though the Buddha has passed away, those who violate them still incur the retribution of their offenses;
so it is with taking refuge in the Buddhas of the past.

It is just as when the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, all humans and devas, for the sake of his nirvāṇa, made extensive offerings; at that time, although the Tathāgata had not yet entered nirvāṇa and still remained in the world, he accepted in advance the offerings intended for future generations.
To take refuge in the Buddhas of the past is likewise so.

For example, suppose there is a person whose parents live far away; at times this person may incur demerit by scolding or reviling them, and at other times they may gain merit by showing them respect and offering praise.
Returning to the Buddhas of the past is likewise so.
Therefore, I have said:
"Whether I am in the world or after my parinirvāṇa, there is no difference in the merit received by those who make offerings. "Good son!
Whether male or female, if one can recite the Three Refuges three times, they are called an upāsaka or an upāsikā.
Although all Buddhas take refuge in the Dharma, it is because the Dharma is taught by the Buddha that it becomes manifest; therefore, one should first take refuge in the Buddha.

Purifying body, speech, and mind, one should recollect the Buddha with a sincere heart; having recollected him, one immediately becomes free from fear and suffering. For this reason, one should first take refuge in the Buddha.

The wise person deeply contemplates that the Tathāgata’s wisdom and liberation are most supreme; he is able to teach liberation and the causes of liberation, able to teach the unsurpassed state of tranquility, and able to exhaust the great ocean of the suffering and affliction of birth and death. His deportment is dignified and orderly, and his three karmas are serene; therefore, one should first take refuge in the Buddha.
The wise contemplate deeply that the phenomena of birth and death are a great mass of suffering, which the Unsurpassed Right Path can forever sever;
the phenomena of birth and death are a famine of craving and thirst, which the flavor of the Unsurpassed Ambrosia can satisfy;
the phenomena of birth and death are fearsome perils and difficulties, which the Unsurpassed True Dharma can eliminate and cut off.

The errors of birth and death, the heterodox and the unrighteous—such as perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as self, the suffering as pleasure, and the impure as pure—are all completely severed by the unsurpassed True Dharma.
For these reasons, one should take refuge in the Dharma.

The wise should observe that the followers of external paths lack shame and remorse; they do not abide in accordance with the Dharma. Although they practice the way, they do not know the correct path; although they seek liberation, they do not attain the essential method.

Although they obtain minor mundane virtues, they are stingy and protective of them, unable to explain them to others. They possess a nature contrary to wholesome conduct, yet they perceive such conduct as being virtuous.

The Buddha and the Sangha are tranquil; their minds are filled with great compassion, possessing few desires and being content. They abide according to the Dharma, cultivate the right path, and attain true liberation. Having attained it, they are further able to turn [the wheel of Dharma] and speak of it for others.
Therefore, one should next take refuge in the Saṅgha.

If one can pay homage to these Three Jewels, welcoming them upon arrival and seeing them off upon departure, honoring and praising them, abiding in accordance with the Dharma, and believing in them without doubt, this is what is called making offerings to the Three Jewels.

If there is anyone who, having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, though not having received the precepts, abandons all evil and cultivates all goodness, and even while remaining a householder dwells in accordance with the Dharma, this person may also be called an upāsaka.

If someone were to say, "One who has not previously taken refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha should be known as one who does not obtain the precepts," this meaning is not correct.
Why is this? As I previously stated:
"Welcome, bhikṣus! Although you have not yet attained refuge in the Triple Gem, your precepts are entirely complete."

Some may say, "If one does not receive [the precepts] in their entirety, then one does not obtain the precepts; the same applies to the Dharma of the Eight Precepts and the Fasting Observance. This interpretation is incorrect.
Why is this? If one could not obtain the precepts without receiving them in full, how could a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who seeks existence obtain the precepts?
In truth, he does obtain the precepts, but they are not complete.
If one does not fully receive the method of the eight precepts of fasting, although it cannot be called "fasting," it may be called "wholesome.
Good son! If one can purify the actions of body, speech, and mind to receive the Upāsaka precepts, this is called the five aggregates.
What are the five aggregates?
Not accepting wrong views, not speaking of wrong views, believing in and accepting right views, speaking of right views, and practicing the true Dharma—these are called the five aggregates.
"Having received the three refuges, one may commit acts of delusion and accept the teachings of non-Buddhists or the words of Maheśvara; by these causes and conditions, one loses the three refuges."

If a person is upright and straightforward, with a mind free from stinginess and greed, constantly cultivating a sense of shame and remorse, possessing few desires and being content, such a person will before long attain a body of tranquility.

If, however, one performs various mixed karmas and practices virtuous deeds merely for the sake of receiving pleasure—like the methods of trade in a marketplace—and their mind lacks compassion for sentient beings, such a person does not obtain the Three Refuges.
If a person, for the sake of protecting their home, property, body, or life, performs sacrifices to various deities, this person is not said to have lost the refuge in the Dharma;
however, if a person with sincere faith believes that such [deities] can rescue them from all fears and pays homage to non-Buddhist teachers, this person then loses the refuge in the Triple Gem.

If one hears that among the various devas there are those who have previously seen the Buddha and whose merit surpasses one's own, and thus pays them homage and makes offerings, such a person does not lose the dharma of taking refuge.

Or if at times one pays homage to the Sovereign Heavenly King (Īśvara), it should be as one would pay homage to the kings, elders, nobles, or venerable persons of virtue in the world; such a person likewise does not lose the dharma of taking refuge.
"Even though you prostrate yourselves, be careful not to accept the false teachings they preach.
When making offerings to the gods, you should give rise to a mind of compassion, for the sake of protecting your lives, your wealth, your lands, and your people from fear."
Regarding the false views you have described, why do you not accept them?

A wise person should observe what the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say: "All things are created by Maheśvara. If all things were created by Maheśvara, for what purpose would I now cultivate these wholesome deeds?

Some say that "by throwing oneself into a deep pool, leaping into fire, or ending one's life through fasting, one immediately attains liberation from suffering. Since these are themselves causes of suffering, how can it be said that one thereby becomes free from suffering?
All sentient beings perform good and evil deeds, and by virtue of these karmic conditions, they themselves receive the retributive fruits.

Furthermore, there are those who say, "All things are created by time, the stars, or the god Īśvara. Regarding such false teachings, how could I accept that I receive the results of deeds performed in the past while also receiving the results of deeds performed in the present?
The wise clearly understand that these are the fruits of karma; why then do you say that "seasons and constellations act with sovereign power"?

If one experiences suffering and pleasure due to the causes and conditions of seasons and constellations, then since many people in the world share the same season and the same constellation, why is it that one person suffers while another enjoys pleasure, or one is male while another is female?

Among the devas and asuras, there are those who are born at the same time and under the same lunar mansion; yet sometimes the devas prevail while the asuras are defeated, and sometimes the asuras prevail while the devas do not.

Furthermore, among various kings, there may be those who are born at the same time and under the same lunar mansion and rule their realms together, yet one loses his kingdom while the other preserves his territory.

The various non-Buddhists also say: "When evil years or evil lunar mansions appear, one should teach sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas in order to repel them. Yet if these are merely years and lunar mansions, how could the cultivation of wholesome dharmas possibly eliminate them?
For these reasons, how could a wise person accept the false and erroneous teachings of the non-Buddhists? "Good son!
All sentient beings follow their karmic actions: those who cultivate right view experience peace and happiness, while those who cultivate wrong view undergo great suffering and affliction."
By cultivating wholesome karma, one attains great sovereignty; having attained sovereignty, sentient beings draw near.

One then proclaims for them the causes and conditions of wholesome karma: it is through the causes and conditions of wholesome karma that one attains sovereignty. All sentient beings obtain peace and happiness solely by virtue of the causes and conditions of cultivating wholesome karma; it is not due to age or past destiny.
"Good son!

King Ajātaśatru and Devadatta both fell into hell due to the causes and conditions of the evil karma they committed; it was not because of their age or their past lives that they received this retribution!"
"Due to the causes and conditions of Udraka Rāmaputra’s wrong views, he shall in the future fall into the great hells. 'Good son!

All wholesome dharmas have desire as their root. By means of this desire, one attains the fruit of *samyak-saṃbodhi* and liberation; one enters the dharma of renunciation, destroys great evil karma and the karma of existence, is able to receive and uphold the precepts, draws near to all Buddhas, is able to practice total relinquishment toward beggars, is able to establish a fixed nature that destroys evil retributions, extinguishes great evil offenses, attains the stage of certainty, leaves behind the three obstacles, and is well able to cultivate and accumulate the path that destroys afflictions.'"

With this as the causal condition for desire, one is able to receive the Three Refuges; having received the Three Refuges, one is then able to receive the precepts; once the precepts have been received, one practices the path of vision and the path of cultivation, surpassing that of the śrāvakas.

If those who fear lions, tigers, wolves, and other such predatory beasts can still attain liberation by taking refuge in the Buddha, how much more so for those who give rise to a virtuous mind seeking transcendence from the world? How could they not attain liberation?

Anāthapiṇḍada instructed those within his household that all children in the womb were to receive the refuges; however, these children in the womb had not yet actually achieved [the state of being ordained]. Why was this?
This Dharma must be personally proclaimed by one's own mouth.
Even if one does not achieve [enlightenment], one can still protect it. "Good son!

The various non-Buddhist teachers claim that "all the worlds were created by Maheśvara," and they also say, "In a future age, after a hundred kalpas have passed, a phantom shall appear; that which is called the phantom is none other than the Buddha."
If Īśvara could become a Buddha, how could this Buddha then refute the ritual of taking refuge in Īśvara?
If Īśvara cannot become a Buddha, why do you say that "everything is created by Īśvara"?

The non-Buddhists further claim: "Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, and Viṣṇu, Lord of Heaven, are all one and the same. They also say: "Their places of birth are each distinct and different. As for Maheśvara, he is named Maheśvara, named Constant, named Lord, named Existence, named Rudra, and named Śiva. Each of these names has its own distinct functions; they seek liberation and are themselves liberation."
This interpretation is not correct. Why?

Because if Īśvara were able to produce sentient beings, create the various realms of existence, perform good and evil deeds along with their karmic retributions, and create greed, hatred, and delusion to bind sentient beings, [then he would be subject to those very things].
Furthermore, you say: "When sentient beings attain liberation, they all enter into [the Buddha's] body; therefore, liberation is an impermanent dharma.
This meaning is not so.
Why is this? If it were impermanent, how could it be called liberation?
It would be like a Brahmin’s son regaining his life; for this reason, it cannot be called Īśvara.
These three kinds of gods are also not one.
Why is this? Because Viṣṇu Mahādeva acts as the liberator for the Ājīvikas; for this reason, they are also not one.
If one says that liberation is impermanent, know that it is then an illusion; it is not the Buddha who is called an illusion.
If one can clearly and correctly perceive the true self, this is called liberation.
Furthermore, some say: "To perceive the subtle atoms (paramāṇu) is called liberation. Others say: "To perceive that the nature [of things] is distinct and the self is distinct is called liberation."
This interpretation is not correct! Why is this?
Because if one can cultivate the Path and perceive the Four Noble Truths, that person will then attain the vision of their nature and the vision of the Self.
If a person can receive the three refuges, that person is then able to truly perceive the Four Noble Truths.
These three refuges are the root of all immeasurable wholesome dharmas, up to and including Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.
For a bodhisattva who has left the home life, it is not difficult to purify the three refuges.”
To cultivate purity while living at home is indeed difficult.
Why is this? Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter 21: On the Eightfold Precept Fasting (Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-varga). In the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-one, "On the Eightfold Precept Fasting," Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!
If there is a person who can receive the three refuges and the fasting precepts, what kind of karmic fruit and retribution will that person obtain?"
“Good son! If there is a person who can receive the three refuges, you should know that the meritorious retribution obtained by this person is inexhaustible! Good son!”

In the kingdom of Kaliṅga there was a treasure of the seven jewels named Piṅgala; the people of that country—whether great or small, male or female—carried it away for seven days, seven months, and seven years using vehicles, elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys, yet they could not exhaust it.

If there is one who with a sincere heart receives the Three Refuges and the fast, the merit and karmic fruit obtained by that person surpasses all the treasures contained within that treasury. Good son!

In the kingdom of Videha there is a treasury of the seven precious gems called Bhaluka; the people of that country—men, women, great and small—even if they were to carry it away constantly for seven days, seven months, and seven years using vehicles, elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys, could not exhaust its contents.

If there is one who with a sincere heart receives the three refuges and the fast, the merit and karmic reward obtained by this person surpasses all the treasures contained within that treasury. Good son!

In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a treasure of the seven precious gems called Khaṅkha; the people of that country—men, women, the old, and the young—even if they were to constantly carry it away for seven days, seven months, and seven years by means of vehicles, elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys, could never exhaust it.

If there is one who with a sincere heart receives the three refuges and the fast, the merit and karmic fruit obtained by this person surpasses all the treasures contained within that treasury. Good son!

In the kingdom of Gandhāra there is a treasury of the seven precious gems called Airāvata; the people of that country—men, women, great and small—even if they were to constantly carry it away for seven days, seven months, or seven years by means of vehicles, elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys, could not exhaust it.

If there is one who with a sincere heart receives the three-refuge precepts, the merit and karmic reward obtained by that person surpasses all the treasures contained within those treasuries. "Good son!
If one receives the three refuges and the eight precepts from another person three times, this is called attaining the complete one-day and one-night *upoṣadha* of an *upāsaka*.
When the dawn appears, it is then lost; therefore, one must not receive them before a Buddha image, but must do so from a person.

Fundamental purity, purity upon receiving [the precepts], purity of adornment, purity of applied and sustained thought, purity of mindfulness and mind, and purity in seeking retribution—this is called the method of the pure fast of the Three Refuges.
"Good son!
If one can thus take refuge with purity and receive the eight precepts, all other transgressions—except for the five heinous crimes—will be entirely extinguished."
Regarding such precepts, two people may not receive them simultaneously.
Why is this? If two people were to receive them together at one time, by what cause and condition would one person violate them while the other person maintains them strictly?
By the power of this precept, one cannot commit evil when reborn in a future life; even if one commits a transgression after having received it, the precept is not permanently lost.

Suppose someone first sends a messenger intending to execute another, but the messenger arrives late. If that person subsequently resolves to observe the *upavāsa* (fasting) ceremony, and the messenger arrives just as they are about to receive the fast, then although the execution would occur at that very moment, by the power of the precept, the crime of killing is not incurred.

If there are persons of noble rank who habitually command the commission of evil, and they wish to observe the fast, they must first issue a command to cease their previous misdeeds; only then can the fast be successfully accomplished.
If they do not first cease such actions and yet abruptly undertake the fast, it cannot be said that they have attained the fast.

One who wishes to observe the fast should first issue a proclamation throughout their domain: "I wish to observe the fast; on all days of fasting, all acts of evil and punishments such as execution must be completely suspended."
If one can thus purely observe and uphold the eight precepts of the fast, that person will obtain immeasurable karmic rewards leading to unsurpassed bliss.
"When Maitreya appears in the world, observing the fast for a hundred years is not equal to observing it for a single day and night in my world."
Why is this? Because at that time, the sentient beings were possessed of the five defilements (pañca-kaṣāya).
For this reason, I spoke thus to Mṛgāramātṛ:
"O virtuous woman!
If a śāla tree can receive the eight precepts of the fast, it too shall obtain the pleasures of humans and devas, up to the unsurpassed bliss.
O son of good family!
This eightfold precept fast is indeed the jeweled necklace that adorns unsurpassed bodhi!
Such a fast is both easy to perform and capable of yielding immeasurable merit.
If there is that which is easy to do yet one does not do it, this is called negligence.
"Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
First, the householder; second, the renunciant.
It is not difficult for a renunciant bodhisattva to teach sentient beings to purify the eightfold precepts;
however, it is truly difficult for a householder bodhisattva to teach others to achieve such purity.
Why is this? It is because those who live at home are entangled by many unwholesome causes and conditions.
— *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Five Precepts. Chapter Twenty-Two: The Five Precepts.
Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of person attains the three refuges?"
"Who are those people who do not obtain the Three Refuges? "Good son!
If a person believes in causes, believes in effects, believes in the Truths, and believes that there is the attainment of the Way, such a person then obtains the Three Refuges."
If a person possesses sincere faith that cannot be defeated, draws near to the Triple Gem, and receives the instructions of virtuous friends, such a person shall obtain the Three Refuges;
the Upāsaka precepts are likewise the same.
If one can contemplate that these Upāsaka precepts possess immeasurable fruits of merit and are capable of destroying countless evil dharmas;
and that while sentient beings are infinite and their suffering is likewise boundless, it is difficult to obtain a human body;
and though one obtains a human body, it is difficult to be endowed with all the sense faculties.
Though one possesses all the faculties, it is difficult to attain faith;
though one attains faith, it is difficult to meet a virtuous friend;
though one meets a virtuous friend, it is difficult to attain self-mastery.
Although I have attained mastery, all phenomena are impermanent.

If I were now to create evil karma, I would, because of that evil karma, receive the retribution of an evil body and mind in two lifetimes; for this reason, the evils of my body, speech, and mind are my enemies.
Even if one were to assume that the three types of unwholesome karma do not result in retribution, one still ought not to commit evil in the present.

These three unwholesome karmas can produce such things as an ugly physical appearance in the present life, and at the time of death, they give rise to remorse. For these reasons, I take refuge in the Triple Gem and observe the eight precepts, distancing myself from all evil and unwholesome actions.
“The wise should contemplate that there are two kinds of precepts:
first, worldly precepts; second, ultimate precepts.
If one receives the precepts without relying upon the Triple Gem, this is called a worldly precept; such a precept is not firm, like colored paint without glue.”
Therefore, I first take refuge in the Triple Gem, and only thereafter receive the precepts—
whether for as long as life lasts or for one day and one night— namely, the Upāsaka precepts and the Eightfold Fasting Observance (Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa).
Now, worldly precepts cannot destroy prior evil karma;
however, by receiving the Three Refuges precepts, one can destroy it—such that even if one commits a great sin, one does not lose the precepts.
Why is this? It is because of the power and influence of the precepts.

Suppose there are two people who together commit a transgression; one has received the precepts and the other has not. The one who has received the precepts incurs a heavy offense upon transgressing, whereas the one who has not received the precepts incurs a light offense.
Why is this? Because they have disparaged the Buddha’s words.
"There are two kinds of offenses: [the offense of disparaging the Dharma and the offense of disparaging the Sangha]."
First, those grave by nature; second, those grave by prohibition.
These two types of offenses further possess degrees of lightness and heaviness.
There are some who can make a grave offense light and a light offense grave, such as Aṅgulimāla receiving the worldly precepts and the dragon Elāpattra receiving the ultimate precepts.
Aṅgulimāla violated what is grave by nature yet did not incur a grave offense, whereas the nāga Elāpattra violated a prohibitive precept and incurred a grave offense.

Therefore, some may turn a grave offense into a light one, while others may turn a light offense into a grave one; for this reason, one should not assume that because the precepts are identical, the resulting fruits must also be identical.
The worldly precepts also include not killing and not stealing; the ethical precepts likewise include not killing and not stealing;
this remains the same even up to the precept against drinking alcohol.

In this way, worldly precepts are fundamentally impure; they are impure upon reception, impure in their adornment, impure in their applied and sustained thought, impure in the mindfulness of the mind, and impure in their karmic fruit. Therefore, they cannot be called precepts in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-śīla), but are merely called worldly precepts.
For this reason, I shall receive the precepts of ultimate meaning.

“Good son! In future ages, sentient beings will be eight zhang tall and their lifespan will reach a full eighty-four thousand years; those who receive the precepts at that time, as well as those who receive the precepts in this present evil age—the karmic rewards obtained by these two are exactly equal.”
Why is this? Because the three roots of goodness are equal.
As for those who say, "One must take a life in order to obtain the precepts," this meaning is not correct.

Why is this? For as for the precepts, they are obtained in relation to all that may be killed and all that may not be killed; since all that may be killed and all that may not be killed are immeasurable and boundless, the karmic fruit of the precepts is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
"Good son!
Among all forms of giving, the gift of fearlessness is the most supreme. Therefore, when I speak of the five great gifts, they are none other than the five precepts."

These five precepts can cause sentient beings to leave behind the five fears; these five kinds of giving are easy to practice, are free and unimpeded, do not result in the loss of wealth or property, and yet yield immeasurable and boundless merit.
Apart from these five kinds of giving, one cannot obtain the fruit of srotāpanna, nor even attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son!

If one has already received the precepts, it should be known that such a person will be revered and protected by devas and humans, attain great renown, remain free from sorrow and affliction even when encountering adverse circumstances, and be so closely approached by sentient beings that they joyfully come to rely upon them.
Although the son of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada received the precepts for the sake of eight thousand pieces of gold, he nonetheless obtained immeasurable merit and karmic retribution. Good son!
"If even those who receive the precepts for the sake of wealth still obtain benefit, how much more so for one who possesses a sincere heart and seeks liberation—how could such a person not attain it?
"Good son! There are five wholesome dharmas that surround these precepts, causing them to constantly increase like the waters of the Ganges."
What are these five?
First, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, sympathetic joy; fourth, patience; and fifth, faith.

If a person can destroy deep-seated wrong views and their mind is free from the net of doubt, they will possess right mindfulness, be adorned with purity, be fundamentally pure, and remain free from evil thoughts and reflections.
"Good son!
If a person can distance themselves from the five evil deeds, this is called receiving the precepts, for they remain far removed from all evils of body, speech, and mind.
If anyone were to say, 'Having departed from the five precepts, one has crossed over birth and death,' such a thing is impossible."
"Good son! If a person wishes to cross the great ocean of birth and death, they should wholeheartedly receive and uphold the five precepts.
Among these five precepts, four will become 'unmanifested precepts' (avijñapti-śīla) in future lives; however, because craving alone is difficult to sever, it cannot be so realized."
For these reasons, because lustful desire is so entangling, you should with a sincere heart be careful and never be negligent!
If someone were to say:
"There are other immeasurably grave matters; for what reason did the Buddhas of the past not prohibit those, but instead prohibit alcohol?"

Good son! Because of drinking alcohol, the sense of shame and remorse is destroyed, and one does not give rise to fear regarding the three evil realms. Due to these causes and conditions, one is unable to receive the remaining four precepts; therefore, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past established the prohibition against drinking.
If someone should say, "Since the Tathāgata has already spoken of the many faults of alcohol, why was it not mentioned at the beginning of the five precepts?
this interpretation is incorrect. Why is that?
Such a precept regarding alcohol is called a "prohibitive grave" (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) and not an "inherent grave" (prakṛti-sāvadya);
the Tathāgata first established the inherent grave precepts, and subsequently established the prohibitive grave ones. "Good son!
The Tathāgata previously taught that there are three fast days (upoṣadha) in each of the white and black fortnights; this was in accordance with the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Since various non-Buddhist groups constantly make offerings to their deities on these days, the Tathāgata likewise spoke of the three fast days.

Good son! Just as a window curtain does not fall because it is secured by its fastening, so too is the Dharma of the Three Fast Days: if sentient beings resolve their minds to receive and uphold it, they will ultimately never fall into the three evil realms.

Good son! If there are those who, when wishing to give alms, when making offerings to the Triple Gem, when practicing seated meditation, when cultivating goodness, when reading the scriptures, or when supporting their parents, first establish a vow, saying:
"If I do not act accordingly, I shall surely punish myself," then that person’s merit and virtue will increase day and night, like the flow of the Ganges River.
These five precepts have five kinds of fruits:
first, the fruit of non-action; second, the fruit of retribution; third, the fruit of subsequent result; fourth, the fruit of action; and fifth, the fruit of liberation.
If there are those who fully receive and uphold the five precepts, you should know that such persons will obtain these five fruits.
If an upāsaka is constantly able to go to temples and monasteries, and having arrived, draws near to the bhikṣus;
and having drawn near, inquires about the flavor of the Dharma;
Having already inquired about the Dharma, one should listen with a sincere mind;
having listened, one should receive and uphold it, recollecting it without forgetting and being able to discern its meaning;
having discerned its meaning, one transforms sentient beings—this is called an upāsaka benefiting both self and others.

"If an upāsaka cannot practice and study as thus taught, but instead treats bhikṣus with contempt, approaches them to listen to the Dharma only to seek out their faults, lacks faith and reverence, serves non-Buddhist practitioners, perceives merit in them, and places deep faith in the sun, the moon, the five planets, and the various lunar mansions—such an upāsaka is not called one who dwells firmly in accordance with the Dharma."
If an upāsaka, though not performing the five evil deeds himself, instructs others to do so, this upāsaka does not abide in accordance with the Dharma.
If an upāsaka first takes another's property, promising to perform a service for them, this upāsaka does not abide in accordance with the Dharma.
"If an upāsaka is in charge of an official ferry or a marketplace where goods are appraised and sold, that upāsaka does not abide in accordance with the Dharma.
If an upāsaka calculates a fee for treating an illness and sells goods after the treatment has been performed, that upāsaka does not abide in accordance with the Dharma."
"If an upāsaka violates public or private regulations, he does not abide in accordance with the Dharma.
If an upāsaka does not commit evil himself, does not instruct others to do so, and does not harbor evil thoughts in his mind, he is said to abide in accordance with the Dharma."
"If an upāsaka, having committed an offense arising from adventitious afflictions, does not give rise to a sense of shame, remorse, or regret, he does not abide in accordance with the Dharma.
If an upāsaka, for the sake of his own body and life, performs various evil deeds, he does not abide in accordance with the Dharma."
“If a lay follower (upāsaka), though having obtained a human body, acts contrary to the Dharma, he is not called a human being.

If one attains faith and is able to cultivate merit and virtue, correctly practicing right mindfulness, observing that all phenomena are impermanent, non-self, and devoid of what belongs to a self; if the mind has no grasping toward any phenomenon, seeing that all phenomena lack autonomy and are subject to arising and ceasing, suffering, empty, and without tranquility;
and realizing that a human body is difficult to obtain, and though a human body is obtained, it is difficult to possess all its faculties in full—[this is true practice].”
Though one possesses all the sense faculties, it is difficult to attain right view;
though one possesses right view, it is difficult to attain faith;
though one attains faith, it is difficult to encounter a virtuous friend.
Though one may encounter virtuous friends, it is difficult to hear the True Dharma;
though one may hear the True Dharma, it is difficult to receive and uphold it.
To be able to contemplate in this way is what is called a human life.

"If a person can contemplate that the desire realm is impermanent, and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception which is entirely impermanent, by virtue of these causes and conditions, they will not seek rebirth in the three evil realms, nor even in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Having observed in this way, one perceives the three things as not firm, and exchanges the unfirm body for a firm body:

by performing prostrations and making offerings, by welcoming and seeing off others, by giving with one's own hands, and by personally attending to meritorious deeds—this is called exchanging the unfirm body for a firm body.
To exchange non-durable wealth for durable wealth:

being able to consume it oneself and also giving it in charity, providing for those who are sickly, emaciated, or traveling, and making offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others who are poor and lowly—this is called exchanging non-durable wealth for durable wealth.
They exchange their non-enduring life for a lasting life: they cultivate the six recollections, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

they realize the Four Noble Truths; they skillfully contemplate birth, old age, sickness, and death; they clearly understand the retribution of good and evil karma; they know with certainty that those they love must eventually part; they recognize that all sentient beings lack autonomy and that, until the Holy Path is attained, the power of birth and death is great; and they realize that all worldly pleasures are ever accompanied by suffering. Thus, though they experience such things, their minds remain unstained by attachment—just as one seeking warmth from fire in a cold month may do so, yet never commits evil in the process.
They cultivate patience and the two kinds of giving to nourish sentient beings, and they deeply contemplate how the nature of suffering and pleasure is equal.

Whatever words they utter, their speech is gentle; they skillfully transform sentient beings, causing them to abide in accordance with the Dharma, to distance themselves from evil friends, and to have no negligence of mind. They do not engage at all in drinking alcohol, gambling, archery, or hunting. This is called exchanging a non-firm life for a firm life.

“Good son! If one obtains a human body, possesses abundant wealth, and furthermore attains mastery, one should first make offerings to one’s parents, teachers, preceptors, elders, and those who uphold the Dharma; one should provide for those who come from afar, those who have newly set out on the path, and those in need of medical care.”

Their speech is gentle and supple, and they possess a great sense of shame and remorse. They do not place their faith and respect exclusively upon a single virtuous person; rather, when they see sages and noble ones who uphold the precepts and possess extensive learning, they are able to provide them with offerings of dwellings, food and drink, bedding, clothing, and medicinal requisites for illness.

With deep faith that within the Sangha there are many who possess merit—those who cultivate the path toward the fruit of Srotāpanna, up to those who can cultivate the path toward Arhatship and attain the fruit of Arhatship, and who cultivate the Vajra-samādhi and the Lightning-flash Samādhi.
Having contemplated in this way, one offers with equanimity;
having offered in this way, one attains immeasurable merit.
Therefore, in the *Mṛgāramātṛ-sūtra*, I said to Mṛgāramātṛ:
"Even if one invites the Buddha and five hundred arhats, it still cannot be called the merit of inviting the Saṃgha.
However, if one can give alms within the Saṃgha to even a single semblance of a most wicked bhikṣu, one will still obtain immeasurable fruits of merit."

Why is this? Although such a bhikṣu may be an evil person, lacking precepts and extensive learning, and failing to cultivate wholesome dharmas, he is still able to expound the three types of bodhi along with their causes and fruits; furthermore, he does not slander the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, upholds the unsurpassed, supreme banner of the Tathāgata, and possesses right view without error.
If one makes offerings to the Sangha, this is equivalent to making offerings to both the Buddha and the Sangha Treasures;
if one contemplates the subtle and wondrous merits of the Buddha-Dharma, this constitutes making complete offerings to the Three Jewels.

"If a person gives a gift without seeking its karmic reward, this is precisely making an offering to unsurpassed bodhi; they fully accomplish the dāna-pāramitā, cultivate the path to bodhi, can attain immeasurable merit in the future, and is able to benefit both themselves and others."
One is able to cultivate compassion, relinquishing one's own happiness to destroy the suffering of others.

Until the attainment of Bodhi, the mind remains free from sorrow or regret; even upon hearing that Bodhi is distant and difficult to attain, the inner mind never wavers, nor does one grow weary or exhausted by the immeasurable suffering endured for the sake of all sentient beings throughout countless lifetimes.

He delights in practicing according to the Dharma and does not seek worldly pleasures; he delights in dwelling in tranquility to leave the household life and cultivate the Path. Although he has not yet left the household life, even while living as a householder, he acts like one who is liberated, committing no evil deeds, and attains the threefold precepts: the precept of restraint, the precept of concentration, and the untainted precept.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a renunciant bodhisattva to practice according to the Dharma is not difficult;
for a householder bodhisattva to practice according to the Dharma is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Twenty-three: Śīlapāramitā. In the *Upāsakaśīla Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-three on Śīlapāramitā, Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva proceed toward enlightenment with a firm mind? "Noble son,
a bodhisattva is firm by being endowed with four qualities:
First, when undergoing great suffering, one never abandons practice in accordance with the Dharma;
second, having attained great mastery, one constantly cultivates patience;
third, though living in poverty, one always delights in giving.
Fourth, in the prime of youth, one always delights in leaving the household life.
If a bodhisattva is endowed with these four dharmas, they will advance toward enlightenment with a firm mind.
"When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these four dharmas, they further reflect:
'This is the primary foundational stage of the path to enlightenment; it is called morality.'"

Such precepts are called the Ground of the Beginning, the Ground of Guidance, the Ground of Levelness, the Ground of Equality, the Ground of Loving-kindness, and the Ground of Compassion; they are called the Footprint of the Buddha, the Root of All Meritorious Qualities, and the Field of Merit.
For these reasons, the wise should accept and uphold them without violating them.
Furthermore, the wise person also reflects thus:
"The precepts have two fruits:
first, the bliss of the devas; second, the bliss of bodhi."
"A wise person should seek the bliss of Bodhi, not the bliss of the heavens.

If, after having received the precepts, one intentionally performs what should not be done, intentionally contemplates what should not be contemplated, is indolent and lazy, delights in sleep, dwells upon evil thoughts and reflections, maintains a wrong livelihood, or harbors evil aspirations—this is called defiling the precepts.

If, after having received the precepts, one feels regret in one's heart, seeks the pleasures of humans and devas, indulges in much negligence, and fails to give rise to compassion, this is called defiling the precepts.

If one receives the prohibitive precepts out of fear of poverty, out of terror, for the sake of losing wealth, out of fear of forced labor, for the sake of one's own life, for the sake of gain and honor, or out of attachment to sensual desires, and having received the precepts, gives rise to doubt in one’s mind—this is called defiling the precepts.

“Good son! If a person does not delight in dwelling long in birth and death, deeply perceives the fault of transgression, views the pleasures of humans and devas and the suffering of the Avīci hell as equal and without distinction, feels compassion for sentient beings, possesses right mindfulness, and—desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings so that they may attain the Way;
for the sake of perfecting the path of unsurpassed bodhi; and for the sake of practicing according to the Dharma—receives and upholds these precepts;”
With a mind free from negligence, one is able to observe the actions of body, speech, and mind in the past, future, and present, discerning what is light and what is heavy;
in all undertakings, one should first bind the mind to cultivate non-negligence, and likewise cultivate non-negligence both while performing and after having performed them.

If one does not know beforehand and commits an offense after acting, or if one loses mindfulness and commits an offense, or if adventitious afflictions arise for a brief moment and one commits an offense, or if one is slightly negligent and commits an offense—if such a person constantly regards even minor transgressions as serious, and having so regarded them, gives rise to remorse and a sense of shame, feeling fear, distress, and a lack of delight in the act, and then sincerely repents; and having repented, their mind becomes joyful, and they carefully guard and uphold [the precepts] never daring to transgress again—this is called pure morality (*śīla*).
“Good son! Once a person of wisdom has received the precepts, they should contemplate three matters and refrain from committing evil deeds:
first, for themselves; second, for the world; and third, for the Dharma.”
“What is acting for one’s own sake?

It is when I personally realize and know: ‘This is an evil deed; I know that by performing an evil action one obtains such a fruit, and I know that by performing a wholesome action one obtains such a fruit.’”

The evil karma one has committed is not false; it will certainly result in the fruits of various evils. The good karma one has performed is likewise not false; it will certainly result in the fruits of various goods.
Since these two types of karma are not false, how could I now deceive myself?
"For this reason, having received the precepts, I should not violate them, but should uphold them with a sincere mind; this is called 'for oneself.
What is meant by 'for the world'?"

The wise person observes those in the world who have attained the pure divine ear, the divine eye, and the knowledge of others' minds, thinking: "If I were to commit evil, these people would surely see, hear, and know of me;
if they see, hear, and know of me, how could I fail to feel shame and yet continue to do evil?"

Furthermore, one contemplates that the various devas possess immeasurable merit, as well as supernormal powers, the divine ear, and the divine eye; endowed with the knowledge of others' minds, they can see and hear from afar. Although they are close to humans, humans cannot see them. If I commit evil, such devas will see, hear, and know it.
If these devas clearly perceive me in this way, how could I fail to feel shame and yet intentionally commit transgressions?
This is called the world.
What is meant by "Dharma"?

A person of wisdom contemplates the Tathāgata’s Dharma as pure and undefiled; it yields benefit in the present, can bring about tranquility and lead one to the further shore, and can effect liberation without regard for time or season.
It is for the sake of this Dharma that I uphold the precepts. If I cannot first accept the minor regulations, how could I possibly receive the major ones?
Having violated the minor regulations, one increases the suffering of the five realms of existence; if one upholds them with a sincere heart, one increases unsurpassed bliss.

"The reason I have not yet attained the realization of liberation since receiving this body is truly because I did not receive the prohibitive precepts from the immeasurable Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past;
having received the precepts now, I shall certainly encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the future."

Having contemplated this deeply, they give rise to great compassion; with a sincere heart, they receive the precepts, and having received them, they uphold them firmly for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

“Good son! Whether one is a layperson or a monastic; whether it be the three refuges, the eight precepts of fasting, or the five precepts; whether complete or incomplete; whether for a day and a night, for a single moment, or for as long as one’s life lasts—if one receives and maintains them with a sincere mind, you should know that such a person attains great merit.”
"Good son!

If, after having received the precepts, one cultivates the three wholesome karmas—extensive learning, giving, and the cultivation of meditative concentration—and practices virtue by making offerings to the Triple Gem, this is called adorning bodhi."

If, after having received the precepts, one is able to read the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras, this is called the treasury of the unsurpassed Great Dharma; one should apply oneself with diligent vigor, desiring to fully realize the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Regarding such precepts: once they have been received in this present life, even if one does not receive them again later, they become "unmanifested precepts" (*avijñapti-śīla*).

Good son! There are precepts that are not *pāramitās*; there are *pāramitās* that are not precepts; there are those that are both precepts and *pāramitās*; and there are those that are neither prohibitive precepts nor *pāramitās*.
That which is morality but not a pāramitā refers to the morality of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That which is a pāramitā but not morality refers to the dāna-pāramitā.

Regarding what constitutes this precept as a *pāramitā*: it is like when the Bodhisattva of old took the body of a *gautama* (ox-herder), and while being devoured by various insects, beasts, and ants, his body did not waver and he gave rise to no evil thoughts;
it is also like when the Rishi, for the sake of sentient beings, allowed a blue sparrow to dwell upon his head for twelve years without rising or moving.
That which is neither morality nor a *pāramitā* is like worldly giving.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the *śīlapāramitā*, who could possibly describe the manifold sufferings they undergo?"

If there is a person who, having received even the minor precepts, possesses few desires and is content, yet is unable to have compassion for sentient beings suffering in various ways, one should know that this person cannot fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

If one can cultivate patience, samādhi, and wisdom, practice diligence with vigor, and delight in extensive learning, you should know that such a person is able to increase the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), adorn awakening, and realize the fruit of awakening.

Such precepts, because they concern immeasurable sentient beings, because they result in immeasurable retributions, and because they consist of immeasurable prohibitions and observances—by these causes and conditions, they adorn bodhi.

“Good son! Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has received the precepts, he does not speak evil with his mouth, nor does he delight in hearing it; he does not delight in speaking of worldly matters, nor does he delight in hearing them. He never allows his mind to dwell on unwholesome thoughts and reflections, nor does he associate with evil friends. For this reason, he is said to possess the pure precepts of tranquility.”
If a bodhisattva sees a person who has broken the precepts and is evil, they do not give rise to an evil mind, but employ various skillful means to subdue them;
if they cannot be subdued, they should instead give rise to compassion, never breaking or abandoning the precepts for the sake of their own body or life.
Having finished eating, he first cultivates a mind of shame and remorse, as well as a mind of non-negligence, regarding the maintenance of his body and life as one treats a malignant ulcer.

If he enters a village, he does so as if entering a forest of swords; he restrains and guards his sense faculties, cultivates and accumulates right mindfulness, observes what should and should not be done, and gives rise to no negligence.

If a person performs merit, it is because of me; if a person commits a transgression, it is also because of me. Therefore, when I receive great offerings, I should not give rise to joy; when I encounter decline and suffering, I should not give rise to anger.
Upon receiving meager offerings, one should reflect thus:

"Because my faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom are now established in accordance with the Dharma only to a small degree, I have received such slight offerings; therefore, I ought not to give rise to thoughts of sorrow or distress."
I accept the faithful offerings of others for two reasons:
first, to increase the merit of the donors; second, to increase my own roots of goodness.
Therefore, even if I receive little or poor-quality items, I should not give rise to vexation.
If one dwells for a long time and receives [alms] only after delay, or is met with slight abuse before receiving them, one should then reproach oneself:
"This is my own karmic fault from past lives; it is not the fault of sentient beings. Therefore, I should not give rise to affliction now."
If, after having received the precepts, one commits a transgression for the sake of others, one should likewise declare: "What has been done in this way is truly not the Way. Why is this so?
The twelve divisions of the scriptures do not state that various evils constitute the path to bodhi.
Therefore, I have now obtained this mixed retribution.
If one can observe deeply in this manner, it should be known that such a person is able to fulfill the śīla-pāramitā.

“Good son! If there is anyone who can restrain and protect the sense faculties, who commits no evil in the four modes of physical deportment, who is able to endure various sufferings, and who does not engage in wrong livelihood, you should know that such a person is able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).”

If one gives rise to a sense of dread regarding both light and grave precepts, so that even when encountering evil times, one does not violate minor precepts and does not allow afflictions to defile the mind, but instead cultivates and accumulates patience, it should be known that such a person is able to fulfill the *śīlapāramitā*.

If one distances oneself from evil friends and causes all sentient beings to remain far removed from evil and false views, and if they recognize kindness and repay it, you should know that such a person is able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

If, for the sake of wholesome deeds, one does not begrudge body or life, setting aside one's own affairs to accomplish those of others, and gives rise to no ill will even when encountering those who revile them, it should be known that such a person is able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

If one sees that which the Tathāgata has opened up, one maintains it as it was; one protects the lives of sentient beings, not sparing even wealth or life, and does not violate even a minor precept until the end of one's life. Although one may obtain exquisite objects of the seven treasures, no greed arises in the mind. One does not bestow goodness upon others for the sake of seeking gratitude, but rather out of compassion.

One receives and upholds the prohibitive precepts, and having so upheld them, one skillfully makes great vows, wishing that all sentient beings may fully attain pure precepts. It should be known that such a person is able to fulfill the *śīlapāramitā*.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
It is not difficult for a bodhisattva who has left the household life to be endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
rather, it is difficult to be fully endowed with it while remaining at home. Why is this?
“Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.
24. Chapter on Karma, Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-four, Part One. Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!”
"When the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have not yet appeared in the world, by what do Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas take their precepts? "Good son!

When the Buddha has not yet appeared in the world, at that time there is no precept of the Three Refuges; there are only wise people who seek the path to Bodhi and cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas."

Regarding these ten wholesome dharmas, there is none other than a Buddha capable of analyzing and explaining them; spoken by past Buddhas, they have flowed down to the present without any loss or omission, and are received and practiced by the wise.

Good son! That sentient beings are unable to receive, uphold, cultivate, and accumulate the ten wholesome dharmas is entirely due to their failure in the past to draw near to, consult, and serve the Buddhas.
“Good son! All sentient beings possess a variegated mind;

due to the conditions of a variegated mind, there arise variegated afflictions. Because of variegated afflictions, they perform variegated karma; due to the conditions of variegated karma, they undergo variegated existence; and due to the conditions of variegated existence, they receive variegated bodies.”
Good son! When all sentient beings have obtained a variegated body, they perceive variegated colors;
having perceived variegated colors, they give rise to unwholesome thoughts, and these unwholesome thoughts are called ignorance.
With ignorance as a causal condition, the arising of a seeking mind is called craving;
that which is produced because of craving is called karma;
with this karma as a causal condition, one obtains retribution. A person of wisdom is able to analyze and deconstruct this.
Bound by internal afflictions and external causes and conditions, one is fettered;

having cultivated the ten wholesome paths of action, one can then be liberated from them. For this reason, when the Tathāgata first attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he analytically expounded the dharma of the ten wholesome paths.

Because of the ten wholesome actions, there exist in the world wholesome conduct and unwholesome conduct, wholesome existence and unwholesome existence, and even liberation; therefore, sentient beings should with a sincere mind discern and realize the path of the ten wholesome actions.
If there are winds and clouds, they serve to sustain the great waters;

the palaces of the asuras, the great earth, the great mountains, the hungry ghosts, animals, hell-beings, the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings, and even up to the abode of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven—all exist because of the ten paths of karma of sentient beings.

The four wheels—of gold, silver, copper, and iron—possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King, and the seven classes of people receiving the precepts and seeking supreme enlightenment (samyak-sambodhi), likewise arise due to the causes and conditions of the ten wholesome karmic paths.

Due to the causes and conditions of these ten paths of wholesome action, all sentient beings experience increase or decrease in their internal and external possessions, as well as in their physical form and life span; therefore, the wise should fully cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action.
If sentient beings experience afflictions that arise differently during their childhood, youth, and old age, as well as during spring, autumn, winter, and summer;
so too do the afflictions that arise during the small, medium, and great kalpas differ from one another.

When sentient beings first cultivate the ten wholesome karmas, they obtain immeasurable life, as well as perfect form, fragrance, and flavor; yet due to greed, hatred, and delusion, they lose all of these.
Due to the causes and conditions of these ten paths of unwholesome action, the seasons, years, constellations, sun, moon, and the four great elements undergo transformation.
If one can contemplate such matters as these, it should be known that this person is capable of attaining liberation.

All sentient beings give rise to faith by virtue of the causes and conditions of suffering; having attained faith, they are able to contemplate good and evil, and having so contemplated, they cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas.
“The mind engages in ten bases; therefore, they are called the ten paths:
the three paths of the body are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
the four paths of speech are harsh speech, lying, divisive speech, and frivolous speech.”
The three paths of the mind are envy, anger, and false views.
These ten unwholesome karmas are all the roots of every kind of transgression.

If sentient beings were categorized by different realms, different existences, different births, different forms, different lifespans, and different names, then for such causes and conditions, they should be called immeasurable; they would not be limited to just ten.
Among these ten matters, three are called karma and are not called the Path;
the seven matters of body and speech are both karma and the Path;
therefore, they are called the "ten."

These ten courses of action—whether performed by oneself, by others, or by both together—result in the two fruits of good and evil; they are also the causes and conditions for the goodness and evil of sentient beings.
Therefore, a wise person should not even contemplate them, much less physically commit them.
If a person allows karma, afflictions, and the various fetters to gain mastery, one should know that this person is practicing the ten unwholesome paths;
if there is one who can destroy the afflictions and fetters so that they do not gain mastery, this person is practicing the ten wholesome paths.
If a person first employs skillful means or does not previously deliberate, but acts impulsively at that moment, this person does not incur a transgression subsumed under karma.
Therefore, the wise should diligently cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action;
the same applies to the realization of the Four Noble Truths.
If one intends to commit an evil act but fails to carry it out at the appointed time, one does not incur the sin.

Therefore, the wise should cultivate the ten wholesome actions; once sentient beings have cultivated these ten wholesome actions, their lifespan as well as internal and external possessions will increase.
"Due to the causes and conditions of afflictions, the ten unwholesome karmas increase;
due to the absence of the causes and conditions of afflictions, the ten wholesome karmas increase. Good son!
In each of these ten courses of action, there are three constituent elements:
first, the root; second, the preliminary application; and third, the completion.

As for the "root": if one perceives another as a distinct entity, perceives them as a sentient being, and with a mind of doubt severs their life-faculty—whether by making a physical gesture or by speaking the words of killing—this is called the root.
Seeking a blade, sharpening it, placing poison upon it, and making a noose—these are called the preparatory means (*upāya*).

Having killed, touching it with one's hand, weighing it, carrying it away, eating it oneself, giving it to others to eat, using the acquired goods for one's expenses, giving them away as one pleases, experiencing joy and pleasure, lacking shame or remorse, having no regret in one’s heart, praising oneself, and giving rise to great arrogance—these are called the completion (*niṣṭhāpana*).

"It is when one regards another's property as their own and, whether taking it oneself, sending someone else to take it, or moving it to another location with a doubtful mind, this is called the fundamental [offense]."

If one breaks down a wall, consults on the plan, sets up a ladder against the wall, enters the house to search, and even touches the object with his hand—this is called the preliminary effort (*upāya*).

If, having obtained the object, he carries it away, hides it, gives it away as he pleases, sells it, uses it, or bestows it upon others; and if he experiences joy and pleasure, feels no shame or remorse, does not regret it, praises himself, and gives rise to great arrogance—this is called the completion (*niṣṭhā*).
"If it is a woman who belongs to another, and one perceives her as belonging to another, and with a mind of doubt engages in unchaste conduct, this is called the root."
Whether one sends a messenger, or sees with one's own eyes, or gives a token of trust, or touches with the hand, or speaks softly and intimately—these are called skillful means (*upāya*).

If the deed has been completed, and one leaves behind a necklace, sits together for food and drink, experiences joy and pleasure, feels no shame or remorse, praises oneself, and gives rise to great arrogance—this is called "completion."
"If one abandons the original characteristics before a great assembly, and speaks falsely during either three or two periods of time, this is called the root."

If, at an earlier time, one sequentially prepares the adornments, constructs the framework of the speech, or receives another's words and sets out to speak them to that person, this is called skillful means (*upāya*).

If, after the deed has been accomplished, one receives and takes the wealth, bestows it as one pleases, experiences joy and pleasure, feels no shame or remorse, praises oneself, and gives rise to arrogance—this is called "having completed [the act]."
"Within this false speech, there is the inclusion of divisive talk that can destroy harmony; this is called the root.

If one speaks of another's faults or other evil matters, saying that those who are in harmony will certainly encounter misfortune, whereas those who separate and break apart will find good fortune; this is called the preliminary means."

Once the union has dissolved, he takes another's wealth and gives it away as he pleases; he experiences joy and pleasure without shame or remorse, does not give rise to regret, praises himself, and conceives great arrogance—this is called "having completed [the act]."
"If one changes one's facial expression and uses harsh words to revile [another], this is called the root.
If, upon hearing of another's transgression, one composes elaborate phrases and sets out for that person's location with the intent to speak of that evil, this is called the preliminary means."

If, after having reviled others, one receives their goods back and gives them away as one pleases, experiencing joy and pleasure without shame or remorse, and without giving rise to regret, praising oneself and giving birth to great arrogance—this is called "completion."
"If one speaks of matters of desire or untimely words, this is called the root.
If one composes songs, verses, or meaningless phrases according to what others enjoy, employing a hundred different means, this is called the preliminary application."

If, having instructed another, one subsequently accepts wealth and property, bestows it as one pleases, experiences joy and pleasure, feels no shame or remorse, praises oneself, and gives rise to great arrogance—this is called "completion."
"To covet the wealth of others with the desire to obtain it is called the root.
To give rise to a mind of affliction is called the preliminary application.

Having obtained the wealth after its acquisition, to bestow it as one pleases, to experience joy and pleasure therein, to speak of it to others, to lack shame or remorse, to praise oneself, and to give rise to great arrogance—this is called the completion."
"If one strikes or reviles another, this is called the root [offense].
If one takes up a staff or a stone and interrogates them regarding their transgressions and faults, this is called the preliminary means (*upāya*).

Having struck them, to feel joy, to take their property, to give it away as one pleases, to experience delight and pleasure, to lack shame and remorse, to feel no regret, to praise oneself, and to give rise to great arrogance—this is called the completion [of the act]."
"If one slanders karma, cause and effect, the true truths, or noble sages, this is called the root.
If one reads, recites, copies, believes in, accepts, praises, or extols heterodox texts, this is called the expedient means."

Having received [the gift], one explains it to others with partisan bias, thereby increasing their wrong views; one accepts improper wealth and distributes it as one pleases, experiencing joy and pleasure without shame or remorse, not giving rise to regret, praising oneself, and conceiving great arrogance—this is called "completion."

"Furthermore, there may be a person who simultaneously commits two of the ten paths of action—false speech and divisive speech—or three at once, namely false speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech;
or again, another set of three, namely wrong view, harsh speech, and false speech."
To speak in this manner is meaningless; this is called the fourth [point].
Hatred and greed cannot coexist at the same time, whereas the remaining eight matters can coexist at the same time.
What is meant by "at one time"?

It refers to when one dispatches messengers via six different locations while personally committing two acts—first, committing adultery with another's wife; second, asserting that there are no karmic fruits—having previously made a pact to commit both simultaneously, thereby acquiring the karma at once.
Regarding these ten unwholesome karmas, some possess manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) but lack non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*); others possess both manifest and non-manifest form.
If there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) nor completion (*niṣṭhā*), then one possesses manifest form but lacks non-manifest form;
if there is both adornment (*alaṃkāra*) and completion, then one possesses both manifest and non-manifest form.
These ten paths of action have both light and heavy degrees:

killing one's father or mother, or an *pratyekabuddha*; stealing property belonging to the Triple Gem; committing unchaste acts with one's biological mother or an *arhatī* nun; and uttering false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha—these are called heavy.
“Good son! These ten courses of action each have three types:
first, those arising from greed; second, those arising from hatred; and third, those arising from delusion.”
If one takes life for the sake of greed for profit, it is said to arise from greed;
if one kills an enemy, it is said to arise from hatred;
if one kills one's aged parents, it is said to arise from delusion.
Robbing the wealth of others is likewise of three kinds:
robbing others of their property out of greed for it—whether for oneself, one's wife, children, or kinsmen—is called "arising from greed";
stealing the goods of an enemy is called "arising from hatred."
To plunder those of low caste is called arising from delusion.
Sexual misconduct is also of three kinds:
if one engages in unchaste conduct for one’s own pleasure, this is called arising from greed;
To commit sexual misconduct with one's own kinsmen is called arising from hatred;
to engage in unchaste conduct with one's own mother is called arising from delusion.
There are three kinds of false speech:
If one seeks personal pleasure for the sake of wealth and profit, this is called arising from greed;
if it is for the purpose of destroying an enemy, this is called arising from hatred;
if it is out of fear that others will die, this is called arising from delusion.
There are three kinds of divisive speech:
that which is for the sake of wealth and profit is called arising from greed;
that which is for the sake of destroying enemies is called arising from hatred.
To destroy harmony and belong to a group of wrong views is called arising from delusion (*moha*).
There are three kinds of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*):
to revile one's wife and children for the sake of wealth and profit is called arising from greed (*lobha*).
Therefore, speaking of things one dislikes to an enemy is called arising from hatred;
speaking of the past transgressions and faults of others is called arising from delusion.
Unwholesome speech is also of three kinds:
If one engages in singing and clamorous noise for the sake of pleasure, it is called arising from greed;
if one engages in singing and clamorous noise for the sake of overcoming others, it is called arising from hatred;
if one engages in singing and clamorous noise for the sake of increasing wrong views, it is called arising from delusion.
That which arises from greed is called envy;
that which arises from hatred is called anger;
that which arises from delusion is called wrong view.
"Having cultivated the ten wholesome paths of action, one attains the three liberations within each and every matter.
These ten unwholesome karmas will certainly result in the retribution of the hells, or as hungry ghosts, or as animals;

as for their secondary results, they lead to a short life among humans, poverty and lack of wealth, unchaste wives, having one's words disbelieved by others, lacking close friends, being constantly slandered, never hearing pleasant or good words with one's ears, causing the four great elements of external objects to become frail and decay, lacking reality, encountering evil winds and torrential rains that cause rot and ruin, uneven terrain, an absence of the seven treasures, an abundance of stones, sand, thorns, and malignant brambles, shifting seasons that lack constancy, and fruit and melons that yield few seeds and lack full flavor."
If one wishes to destroy such matters as these, one should practice the ten wholesome paths of action with a sincere mind.
These ten wholesome dharmas are fully present in the three continents; some are subsumed under the precepts, while others are not.
In Uttarakuru, there are only four of these matters.
There are five [types of karma] in the hells;
among the hungry ghosts, animals, and devas, all ten are present, yet they are not encompassed by the precepts.
Among the six heavens of the desire realm, there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*); there are only two matters: the fundamental act (*maula*) and its completion (*niṣṭhā*).
"Furthermore, regarding the paths of action, they are accomplished within a single thought-moment.
For instance, if the killer and the victim die simultaneously, then the fundamental karmic fruit of the action is not obtained."
If one prepares the adornments but the act is not ultimately accomplished, one only incurs the offense of preparatory means (*upāya-karma*), and does not incur the fundamental offense (*mūla-karma*).
If, after having prepared the adornments, one actually kills, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, after having killed, one does not pursue the completion of the act, there is no offense of non-action (*avijñapti*).
If the killer dies within a single thought-moment while the victim dies in the subsequent thought-moment, the killer does not incur the fundamental karmic offense.
If one dispatches a messenger to kill, the messenger incurs the offense of action (*karmavastu*), while the one who issues the verbal command incurs the offense of non-action (*avijñapti*);
if one issues a harsh verbal command, one likewise incurs both the offense of action and the offense of non-action.
If, after having killed, one’s mind is wholesome or neutral, one still incurs both the active transgression (*karmavijñapti*) and the non-active transgression (*akarmavijñapti*).
If someone were to say: "The past has already ceased, the future has not yet arisen, and the present does not abide; how, then, can it be called 'killing'?"
"If one does not kill for even a single thought-moment, not even a mote of dust can be destroyed; if one cannot kill even once, one cannot do so many times either—how then can you say 'killing'?
This interpretation is not correct.
Why is this? Although one does not kill for even a single moment in the present, because this can prevent killing from arising in the future, it is nonetheless termed "killing.
For this reason, one cannot conclude that because there is no killing in one place, there is therefore no killing in all places.
There are those who die upon having their hands pierced, while others may have their feet cut off yet survive;
the head is not like this, for death occurs whether it is pierced or severed.
If one commits an act and incurs great demerit, this is called a path of action (*karmapatha*).
The three types of karma are acquired through oneself; the seven types of karma are acquired through both self and others.
If there were no active karma (*vijñapti*), there would likewise be no non-active karma (*avijñapti*).
"Some may say that 'among the three matters of bodily karma, there are both active and non-active [karmas], but it is not so for vocal karma'—this interpretation is incorrect."

Why is this? If there were only manifest action (*vijñapti*) in speech and no non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), then after one has commanded another to kill, one should not incur the offense; therefore, vocal karma must also possess both manifest and non-manifest action.
The mind is not like this; why is that?
Because noble and holy persons do not incur offenses.
For what reason and by what conditions are they called "manifest" (karma) and "unmanifest" (avijñapti)?
