The Remainder of Chapter Twenty-Four on Karma:
"Good son! There are two kinds of offenses committed by sentient beings: [the first is those committed intentionally, and the second is those committed unintentionally]."
The first is the person of evil precepts; the second is the person without precepts.
A person of evil precepts incurs the sin of killing constantly, even when they have killed only a single sheep or when they are not killing at all.
Why is this? Because of their prior vows.
A person without precepts incurs sin at the moment they kill even a thousand people, but incurs no sin if they do not kill.
Why is this? Because no vow has been made.
Therefore, for all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, the mind is the root.
Based on the root cause, it is said that there are two kinds of offenses committed by bhikṣus:
first, offenses of the body; second, offenses of speech. There are no offenses committed unintentionally.
Regarding such precepts, if the time is incomplete or the constituent parts are incomplete, then one does not obtain the precepts.

It is like drilling for fire: only when there is a fire-drill, physical strength, and dry grass or wood will fire be obtained; if even one of these factors is lacking, fire cannot be produced. The same applies to the dharma of the precepts.
Regarding such precepts, whether they are acquired or discarded, maintained or violated, all depend upon the mind;
the Tathāgata clearly understands the nature of all phenomena, and for this reason he established them.
"If there is another person who, by virtue of the power of reflection on wholesome karma, refrains from committing various evils, this is called the precept according to the Dharma;
if it is obtained from another, it is called the received precept."
If there were merit in receiving [the precepts] apart from the precepts themselves, then all predatory beasts—lions, tigers, and wolves—should obtain merit; yet in reality, they do not.
By these causes and conditions, those who receive the good precepts obtain immeasurable merit, while those who receive the evil precepts obtain immeasurable transgression.
Therefore, the sutras speak of the evil disciplines (*akuśala-saṃvara*): first, raising sheep;
second, raising poultry; third, raising pigs; fourth, fishing with hooks; fifth, fishing with nets.
Sixth, killing oxen; seventh, being a jailer; eighth, keeping hunting dogs;
ninth, making long snares; tenth, being a hunter; eleventh, casting spells on dragons;
twelfth, killing people; thirteenth, being a thief; fourteenth, engaging in double-tongued speech; fifteenth, using whips to inflict pain.
Flogging, shackling, branding the forehead, iron nails, and being roasted alive— those kings and ministers who receive deposits and then deceive them,
those who are ungrateful, those of evil nature and malicious intent, those village headmen and tax collectors who are exceedingly wicked,
and those bhikṣus who have violated the precepts and lack shame or remorse— all such persons as these possess no precepts.
Furthermore,
although it is not termed an unwholesome path of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*),
one incurs great demerit. Why is this?
Because it is undertaken for as long as life lasts.
Such matters as these are not accomplished unless one makes a vow or receives them from another.
Thus, the unwholesome precepts are relinquished at four times:
First, when obtaining the two sexual organs; second, when relinquishing the life-span; third, when receiving the wholesome precepts; and fourth, when severing the fetters of desire.
"Furthermore, some may say: 'Just as good precepts are fully possessed, so too are evil precepts. This meaning is not correct.
Why is this? Because evil precepts are easily acquired and are obtained through a single cause and condition, namely, the making of a vow."
The precepts of good conduct (*śīla*) are not like this; they possess five skillful means, namely the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Therefore, they are difficult to attain;
because they are difficult to attain, they must be fully perfected.

"If there is someone who says, 'The Upāsaka precepts do not include abstaining from idle chatter, double-tongued speech, or harsh words; therefore, the Upāsaka precepts, the Eightfold Precept fast, and the Śrāmaṇera and Bhikṣu precepts cannot be fully attained,' this interpretation is incorrect."
Why is this? It is because I now uphold pure verbal karma.
If someone should say, "I have received the five precepts to purify my body, speech, and mind," yet their mind is not pure, you should know that such a person has not attained the complete precepts.
For example, suppose there is a person who has received the evil precepts; even though they do not kill living beings, this person constantly possesses the accomplishment of those evil precepts.
A bhikṣu who violates the prohibitions is just like this.
Why is this? Because once one has received and upheld the precepts, there are many karmas and many fruits associated with each individual precept.
Sentient beings are immeasurable, and thus the precepts are also immeasurable.
Because objects are immeasurable, the precepts are also immeasurable.
These virtuous and unvirtuous precepts each have three grades: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
If one does not formally undertake unvirtuous precepts, then even if one commits many transgressions, it is not termed "unvirtuous precepts."
If someone should raise the objection:
"For what reason are the five precepts received for as long as one lives, while the eightfold fast-day discipline (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) is observed for only one day and one night?
one should reply:
“The Tathāgata, having thoroughly understood the characteristics of dharmas and attained unimpeded penetration, speaks thus: ‘Good son,
there are generally two kinds of fields of merit in the world:’”
First, the field of merit; second, the field of gratitude.
To destroy these two fields is called the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*).
These five heinous crimes have three causes and conditions:
First, there is an extremely evil mind; second, a lack of recognition for merit; third, a failure to perceive the true fruit [of karma].
If a person kills an Arhat with such mistaken perceptions, they do not incur the crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma); the same applies to one's parents.

If one lacks shame and remorse, disregards the repayment of kindness, and has no heart of reverence, yet merely employs expedient means without establishing the fundamental basis, although this does not constitute a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya), one will still incur a great karmic retribution.

Because they provide excellent instruction, because they give rise to affectionate love, because they are capable of endurance, because they perform what is difficult to do, and because they undergo great suffering, parents are called the field of gratitude.
Furthermore, if there is a person who has killed their father and mother, even if they subsequently cultivate wholesome deeds, these virtues will yield no retribution.
For this reason, I say that one should be careful not to damage or break the branches, flowers, or leaves of the tree under whose shade one has taken shelter, even for a brief moment.

“Good son! After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who will speak thus: ‘If one kills one’s father or mother with a different intention or under a different name, one does not incur the crime of immediate retribution. This refers to the Dharmaguptaka school.”

Furthermore, some say: "Even if one kills one's father or mother with a mistaken perception, one still incurs the crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma)," which refers to the Mahīśāsaka school. Others say:
"If one kills one's father or mother with both a mistaken perception and a mistaken designation, one incurs the crime of immediate retribution," which refers to the Sarvāstivāda school.

Why is this? Because worldly reality is trustworthy; since the reality of one's parents is such that even one's perception of them does not change, to kill them with an evil mind constitutes the immediate transgression (ānantarya).

In reality, they are one's parents; yet if one lacks the perception of them as parents and does not give rise to an evil mind, even though the parents have died, one does not incur the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya). Why is this? One incurs the offense of immediate retribution only when four conditions are fulfilled: [1] the perception of them as parents;
[2] the intent to kill; [3] the performance of the act; and [4] the resulting death. Since these are not all present here, there is no offense.
First, they are actually one's parents and one perceives them as such; second, a malicious mind; third, a mind of indifference; fourth, perceiving them as ordinary sentient beings.
If these four conditions are fulfilled, the crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya) is established;
if they are not fulfilled, it is not established.

Whether out of compassion, out of reverence, for the sake of receiving the Dharma, out of fear, or for the sake of reputation, if one provides the means of death, even though one does not kill with one's own hand, one still incurs the crime of immediate retribution.
If one is compelled by another to kill one's father or mother and performs the act while weeping and grieving, the characteristics of such a transgression are light in the beginning, middle, and end.
If one intends to kill one's parents but mistakenly strikes another person, the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya) is not incurred;
likewise, if one intends to kill another person but mistakenly strikes one's parents, the same applies.

When intending to kill one's mother, if one mistakenly kills someone who resembles her, and after having killed, hides the knife only to strike the mother’s body again, one does not incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
If the mother has a different perception and the son has a different intent regarding the killing, one incurs only the ordinary offense of killing, but not the offense of immediate retribution.

Among these five heinous crimes, killing one's father is light, while killing one's mother is heavy; killing an Arhat is heavier than killing one's mother; shedding the blood of a Buddha is heavier than killing an Arhat; and causing a schism in the Sangha is heavier than shedding the blood of a Buddha.

"There are things that are substantial but the intention is light; there are things that are light but the intention is heavy; there are things that are substantial and the intention is heavy; and there are things that are light and the intention is light.
An example of a thing being substantial while the intention is light is killing one's parents without an evil mind.
An example of a thing being light while the intention is heavy is killing an animal with an evil mind."
When the object is grave and the intention is grave, it refers to killing one's own mother with an extremely evil mind;
when the object is light and the intention is light, it is like killing an animal with a light mind.
Regarding such evil karma, there are cases where the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is heavy while the fundamental act (*maula*) and its completion (*niṣṭhā*) are light;
cases where the preparatory effort and the fundamental act are light while the completion is heavy;
and cases where the preparatory effort and the fundamental act are heavy while the completion is light.
There are cases where the fundamental offense is light, while the preparatory effort and the consummation are heavy.
Although the object is of one kind, due to the power of the mind, one obtains either a light or a heavy result. "Good son!
If someone gives food to me with the desire to offer it, but before giving it to me, transfers it instead to a hungry dog, I likewise praise such a person as a great donor.
Whether it be a field of merit or not a field of merit, one who gives without making mental discriminations obtains immeasurable merit. Why is this?
Because the mind is well-purified, these karmas are of four kinds:
first, those with retribution in the present life; second, those with retribution in the next life; third, those with retribution in subsequent lives; and fourth, those that are without retribution.
There are four types of karma:

first, that which is fixed in time but indeterminate in its retribution; second, that which is fixed in retribution but not necessarily fixed in time; third, that which is fixed both in time and in its retribution; and fourth, that which is indeterminate in both time and retribution.
Regarding the determinacy of time: this refers to the present life, the next birth, or future lives.
If the timing is not fixed and the retribution is not fixed, such karma can be transformed.
If the retribution is fixed such that it must be experienced in the future, this karma can be transformed so that it is experienced in the present.
Why is this? Because through the power of the causes and conditions of a virtuous mind and wisdom, even a fixed evil result can be transformed into something light.
For what reasons is it called "certainty of retribution"?

Because one always acts without regret; because one acts with single-minded devotion; because one acts with joy and delight; because one establishes a vow; and because one feels gladness after having acted—for these reasons, this karma attains certainty of retribution.
Apart from these, all others are termed indeterminate.

The karmic actions of sentient beings are some light and some heavy, some distant and some near; according to their respective causes and conditions, they experience the results either earlier or later.

If one cultivates the body, cultivates morality, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, knowing with certainty that good and evil must have their retributive fruits, such a person can transform heavy karma into light and ensure that what is light is not experienced at all.

If one encounters a field of merit and meets a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), practicing the Way and cultivating goodness, such a person can transform heavy retribution in future lives into light suffering experienced in the present life.
If a person possesses various karmas of the desire realm and attains the fruit of Anāgāmin, they can transform those future karmas to be experienced in the present;
the same applies to the fruit of Arhatship.

“Good son! If a wise person can cultivate the body, cultivate morality, cultivate the mind, and cultivate wisdom, that person can destroy even the most grievous karma, just as the agada medicine, incantations, and poison-removing jewels destroy malignant poisons.”

If one commits a minor offense that is slight at the initial stage of preparation but becomes grave once completed, it is because that person has failed to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, thereby causing what was light to become heavy.
If sentient beings perform one kind, two kinds, or even various kinds of actions, some are performed incompletely and some are performed completely.
Performing an action after first forming the intention is called "complete performance";
performing an action directly without first generating the intention is called "incomplete performance."
Furthermore, there are those who have performed actions that are incomplete, meaning that after the action has been performed, the retribution is not fixed;
and there are those who have performed actions that are complete, meaning that after the action has been performed, the retribution is certain to be obtained.
Furthermore, there are those who have performed [an action] that is incomplete; although the retribution is fixed, the timing is not.
Moreover, there are those who have performed [an action] that is complete; for these, both the timing and the retribution are fixed.
Furthermore, there are those who have performed [actions] but not fulfilled them, such as those with moral discipline and right view;
and there are those who have performed [actions] and also fulfilled them, such as those with broken precepts and wrong views.
Furthermore, there are those who, having acted, do not fulfill [the karmic result], yet believe in cause and believe in effect;
there are also those who, having acted, do fulfill it, yet do not believe in cause and effect.
Furthermore, there are those who, having acted and not fulfilling [the result], were surrounded by goodness at the time they committed evil.
Furthermore, there are those who, having committed [an act], also fulfill it: while committing evil, evil comes to surround them.
Again, there are those who, having committed [an act], do not fulfill it: although they commit many evils, they receive retribution among human beings.
Again, there are those who, having committed [an act], also fulfill it: having committed evil among human beings, they receive retribution in hell.
Furthermore, there are those who, having acted, do not fulfill [the deed], yet possess a mind of right mindfulness;
there are also those who, having acted, do fulfill it, yet lack a mind of mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are those who, having acted and not fulfilled [the deed], give rise to regret at the three times [past, present, and future].
Furthermore, there are those who, having performed [an action], also fulfill it by not regretting it throughout the three periods of time.
As it is with evil, so it is with good.
Because of this fulfillment after performing, one may obtain a great result from a small deed, or obtain a small result from a great deed.
"When one first conceives the thought of forming a body, once that body is accomplished, there arise immeasurable thoughts. The initial thought that conceived the body is itself virtuous.
Once the body is accomplished, two kinds of fruits are obtained:
mixed virtue and non-virtue."
As it is with humans, so it is with devas.
When beings in the hells grasp at a body with an evil intention, once that body has been formed, it is exclusively unwholesome.
Hungry ghosts and animals also grasp at a body with an evil intention; once their bodies have been formed, they are a mixture of wholesome and unwholesome.

In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of good or evil, one is endowed with a body according to those qualities; once the body has been formed, one receives a mixed retribution of both good and evil.
From the stage of the *kalala* until old age, one likewise receives a mixed retribution of both good and evil.
Therefore, the Sūtra states that there are four kinds of karma:
black karma with black retribution, white karma with white retribution, mixed karma with mixed retribution, and karma that is neither black nor white, which is without retribution.
Black karma brings black retribution, namely the hells;
white karma brings white retribution, namely the heavens of form;
mixed karma brings mixed retribution, namely the heavens of desire, among humans, as animals, and as hungry ghosts.
Neither white nor black, it is without retribution; this is what is called the untainted (*anāsrava*). "Good son!
If a person does not understand such karmic conditions, they will wander through birth and death for immeasurable eons."

Why is this? Because those who do not understand such karmic causes and conditions, though they may be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas, will fall back into the three evil realms once their merit is exhausted.
“Good son! Of all forms of drawing, none surpasses the mind. The mind draws afflictions; afflictions draw karma; and karma then draws the body.”
Due to the causal conditions of greed, one's physical appearance and voice are exquisite and pleasing, and one's deportment is composed and orderly;
due to the causal conditions of anger, one's physical appearance and voice are coarse and harsh, and one's deportment is abrupt and violent;
as it is with anger, so it is with delusion.
In immeasurable worlds, there are one hundred and thirty-six locations of hells, immeasurable animals, and immeasurable hungry ghosts, all produced by karma;
the same is true for humans and devas.
Immeasurable sentient beings attain liberation, and this is also due to karma.
"Good son! These ten paths of wholesome action have three aspects:
First, it can obstruct afflictions; second, it can give rise to wholesome states of mind; third, it can increase ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It is like the removal of poisonous medicine, which generally involves three things:
first, *agada* medicine; second, divine mantras; and third, genuine jewels.

If a person skillfully cultivates heedfulness, possesses right mindfulness, and discriminates between good and evil, one should know that such a person is certain to be able to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action;
if they are largely heedless, lacking a sense of shame, dread of blame, and faith, one should know that such a person is certain to commit the ten paths of unwholesome action.
These ten paths of action further consist of three factors:
first, the preliminary application (*upāya*); second, the fundamental act (*maula*); and third, the completion (*pṛṣṭha*).

Furthermore, if there is a person who diligently pays homage and makes offerings to their parents, teachers, preceptors, and virtuous persons; who greets them with a welcoming disposition and speaks with gentle words—this is called the preliminary application.
If, having completed the action, one is able to cultivate mindfulness with joy and without regret, this is called "completion";
being single-mindedly absorbed while performing it is called the "root."
“Good son! These ten paths of action are further divided into three types: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
Or, the preparatory stage may be superior, the fundamental stage middling, and the stage of completion inferior;”
In some cases, the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is superior while the consummation (*maula*) and subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) are inferior;
in other cases, the preparatory stage is inferior while the consummation and subsequent stage are middling.
These ten paths of action (*karmapatha*) are surrounded by three factors: namely, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, as well as attachment, hatred, and delusion.
Regarding these ten paths of action, there are those that are shared with the practice of precepts and those that are not shared.

There are six occasions for the relinquishing of the precepts: first, at the time of severing the roots of goodness; second, at the time of attaining both sexual organs; third, at the time of relinquishing one's life; fourth, at the time of undertaking the unwholesome precepts; fifth, at the time of formally renouncing the precepts; and sixth, at the time of relinquishing the body of the desire realm.
Furthermore, as for the claim that "one loses the precepts when the Buddha-dharma perishes," this meaning is not correct.
Why is this? Because once received, they are not lost; and if not yet received, they cannot be obtained.
The severing of evil in body, speech, and mind is called the precept of morality (*śīla-śīla*);
the four fundamental dhyānas and the four preparatory dhyānas are called the precept of concentration (*samādhi-śīla*);
the four fundamental dhyānas and the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna are called the untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*).
To refrain from committing further evil after leaving this body and entering the next life is called the precept of non-action (*akaraṇa-śīla*).

To guard and restrain the sense faculties, to cultivate right mindfulness, and to ensure that no negligence arises regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, or known—namely, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—is called the precept of guarding the senses (*indriya-saṃvara-śīla*).
For what reason is it called "precept" (*śīla*)?
"Precept" is named "restraint" (*saṃvara*); because it can restrain all unwholesome dharmas, it is called restraint.
Furthermore, "precept" is called "constriction" (*saṃvṛti*); although there are evil dharmas, its nature cannot tolerate them, and thus it is called constriction.
Furthermore, "precept" (śīla) is called "coolness," for it wards off the heat of the afflictions and prevents them from entering; therefore, it is called cool.
Furthermore, "precept" is called "superior," for it enables one to ascend to heaven and reach the unsurpassed path; therefore, it is called superior.
Furthermore, "precepts" (śīla) are called "training" (śikṣā); because one trains in subduing the mind and the faculties through wisdom, they are called training. "Good son!
Sometimes there is a person who fulfills a single precept, namely, the Prātimokṣa precepts."
Or they may possess two precepts, adding the precept of meditative concentration;
or they may possess three precepts, adding the untainted precept;
or they may possess four precepts, adding the precept of guarding the sense faculties.
Or one may possess the five precepts augmented by the unmanifested precept (*avijñapti-śīla*). Good son!
The *prātimokṣa* precepts are obtained in the present, whereas the precepts concomitant with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samvara*) are obtained throughout the three periods of time.
"Good son!

If there is another person who, when wishing to receive the precepts, is able with a sincere mind to contemplate the faults of birth and death and the merits of liberation, and does so with faith and joy, this person will simultaneously attain both the manifest (kriyā) and unmanifest (avijñapti) precepts."
Such precepts, according to the length of one's life—whether long or short—are obtained for that duration.
These are the unmanifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*), which are relinquished through three causes and conditions:
first, because of minor adornment; second, because of the mind’s relinquishment; and third, because of the lack of firmness in their performance.
There are three further matters concerning not abandoning causes and conditions:
first, because of the existence of original vows; second, because the performance of deeds is steadfast; and third, because of a sincere mind that is free from negligence.

“Good son! Apart from the ten wholesome karmas and the ten unwholesome karmas, as well as wholesome and unwholesome precepts, there are further karmas and precepts not subsumed under these, namely, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.”

Thus, there are both manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) forms of wholesome and unwholesome action. There are persons who possess both manifest and unmanifest action: while one is currently performing a wholesome act and has not yet relinquished it, one possesses both manifest and unmanifest action;
in the second moment, one accomplishes past manifest and unmanifest action;
once the manifest action has passed, there is only unmanifest action, and no longer manifest action.
If a person has received the precepts, even though they commit unwholesome deeds, that person accomplishes two dharmas in the present life:
the active manifestation (*vijñapti*) of unwholesome dharmas and the non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) of wholesome dharmas.
These two—active manifestation and non-manifestation—are abandoned through two causes and conditions:
First, the exhaustion of the material objects given; second, the mental relinquishment of virtue.
These constitute accomplishment in two time periods—past and present—while non-action pertains to all three time periods.
The two causes and conditions for the relinquishing of the precepts of meditative concentration are:
first, at the time of regression; second, at the time of severing the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, there are three times:
First, at the time of relinquishing the body; second, at the time of regression; third, at the time of being born into a higher realm.
Untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are relinquished at three times:
first, at the time of regression; second, at the time of transforming dull faculties into sharp ones; third, at the time of attaining a higher fruit.
The wholesome karma of the mind is lost all at once, namely at the time of falling from a higher rebirth;
the wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind is lost simultaneously at the time of severing the roots of goodness. Good son!

If one attains the complete precepts, the precepts of concentration, the untainted precepts, and the precepts that restrain the sense faculties, such a person will thoroughly understand the ten paths of karma. "Good son!
Due to the ten paths of karma, the lifespans of sentient beings increase and decrease:
they decrease until a lifespan of ten years, and they increase up to immeasurable years.
In Uttarakuru to the north, the lifespan is fixed at one thousand years; here [in Jambudvīpa], it is one hundred years; in the two directions of the east and west, it is two hundred and fifty years;
and where this lifespan is immeasurable, there too it is immeasurable.
The lifespan of the people of the Four Heavenly Kings is nine million years, yet their life span is also indefinite, just as it is in the three continents.
The lifespan of the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens is eighteen million years, yet their life span is also indefinite.
In the Yāma Heaven, the lifespan is three hundred and sixty million years, yet life is not fixed.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, the lifespan is seven hundred and twenty million years; with the exception of Bodhisattvas in their final birth, the lifespans of all others are likewise not fixed.
The lifespan in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is fourteen million four hundred thousand years, yet their life span is also uncertain.
The lifespan in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is twenty-eight million eight hundred thousand years, yet their life span is also uncertain.
One year in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) is equivalent to one day and night in the Hot Hell (*Tapana-naraka*).
Thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year; the lifespan in that hell is twenty-eight million eight hundred thousand years, though even this duration is not fixed.
One year in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) is equivalent to one day and night in the Great Sound (*Mahāśabda*) Hell;
thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year. The lifespan in that hell is fourteen million four hundred thousand years, though it is not fixed.
One year in Tuṣita Heaven is equivalent to one day and night in the Lesser Sound Hell (Kṣudra-śabda-naraka).
Thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve months constitute a year; the lifespan in that hell is seventy-two million years, though it is not fixed.
One year in the Yama Heaven is equivalent to one day and night in the Saṃghāta Hell;
thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year. The lifespan in that hell is three hundred and sixty million years, though it is not fixed.
One year in the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods is equivalent to one day and night in the Black Rope Hell;
thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year. The lifespan in that hell is eighteen million years, though it is not fixed.
One year in the realm of the Four Great Kings is equivalent to one day and one night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell;
thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year. The lifespan in that hell is nine million years, though it is not fixed.
The lifespan in the Avīci Hell is one kalpa; the lifespan in the Great Heat (Mahātapana) Hell is half a kalpa. Only in these two places is the lifespan fixed.
Five hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for hungry ghosts;
thirty such days make a month, and twelve months make a year. The lifespan of those ghosts is fifteen thousand years, yet even this life span is not fixed.
Within the realm of animals, with the exception of Nanda and Upananda, the lifespans of all others are also indefinite.
One year in the Avīci Hell is equivalent to one day and night in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Calculating thirty such days as a month and twelve such months as a year, the lifespan of those gods is eighty thousand great kalpas.
In the sphere of nothingness there are sixty thousand kalpas; in the sphere of consciousness, forty thousand kalpas; and in the sphere of infinite space, twenty thousand kalpas.
"If one gives rise to even slight afflictions and becomes attached to the meditative absorption of emptiness, you should know that such a person will be reborn in the four formless realms."

From increasing from ten years up to eighty thousand years, and decreasing from eighty thousand years back down to ten years—such cycles of increase and decrease, completed eighteen times, are called intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*).
Three calamities of famine, three calamities of disease, and one calamity of warfare constitute a minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
When five periods of the two calamities of water and fire have passed, followed by one calamity of wind, and after five such calamities of wind have passed, it is called a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).

When weapons arise in Jambudvīpa, people in the eastern and western directions may momentarily give rise to anger; when this disease arises, they suffer only slight headaches and their strength becomes slightly diminished; when grain is expensive here, they merely think of food—such evil conditions do not exist in Uttarakuru.
Because of non-killing, one's lifespan increases;
because of stealing, one's lifespan decreases.
There are two kinds of kalpas:
First is the water kalpa, and second is the fire kalpa.

When the fire kalpa arises, those sentient beings in the hells whose karmic retribution is exhausted are all able to escape; those whose retribution is not yet exhausted are transferred to other great hells in other directions.
If these eight great hells in this world are empty and devoid of sentient beings, this is called sentient beings being liberated from hell.
As for all sentient beings within the four great oceans, if their karma is exhausted, they shall all attain liberation;
if it is not yet exhausted, they shall all be reborn in the oceans of other directions.
If there were not a single sentient being in the ocean, this would be called attaining liberation.
Five hundred yojanas directly beneath the land of Jambudvīpa lies the city of King Yama, which is seven thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference and extent.
Thus, within this city, those hungry ghosts whose karma was exhausted were all able to escape;
those whose karma was not yet exhausted were reborn elsewhere in the presence of King Yama.
If there were not even a single sentient being within that city, it would be called "attaining liberation.
At that time, due to internal causes and conditions, a person attained the first dhyāna; having attained it, he immediately rose and cried out in a loud voice:
"The first dhyāna is tranquil!"
"The first dhyāna is tranquil!

Upon hearing this, each person reflected within themselves, and they all together attained the first dhyāna; immediately casting off their human bodies, they were reborn in the realm of the first dhyāna.

At that time, within the first dhyāna, there was another person who, due to internal causes and conditions, cultivated and attained the second dhyāna; having attained it, he immediately rose and cried out in a loud voice:
"The second dhyāna is tranquil!"
"The second dhyāna is tranquil!
Having heard this, the sentient beings each reflected upon it and again attained the second dhyāna; they cast off their bodies from the first dhyāna and were reborn in the realm of the second dhyāna.
At that time, from the Avīci Hell up to the First Dhyāna Heaven, not a single sentient being remained. "Good son!

Outside the four continents, there is Mount Yugandhara, within which are seven suns; yet by the power of the causes and conditions of the merit of sentient beings, only one sun appears, depending upon which the hundred grains, grasses, and trees are ripened and brought to fruition."

When the kalpa-ending fire arises, seven suns appear simultaneously, incinerating all grains, grasses, and trees, as well as the mountains, rivers, the great earth, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and even the First Dhyāna Heaven.
When the sentient beings of the second dhyāna see this fire calamity, fear arises in their minds; among them are devas who were born there earlier, who say to those devas who arrive later:
"Do not be afraid!"
"In the past, I have seen such fire calamities; they cease at that point and do not reach here.

Thus, as the lifespan of sentient beings increases from ten years to eighty thousand years, and decreases from eighty thousand years back to ten years, during all that time, the heat of such fire calamities has still not subsided.

At that time, a great rain poured down from the intermediate dhyāna realm; this continued for the duration of one increase and one decrease of the lifespan. By the power of the karmic actions and causes and conditions of sentient beings, seven layers of wind and clouds emerged below to sustain this water.
At that time, the rain ceased, and a film formed upon the water like cream or curdled milk.
Within the four continents, Sumeru, the king of mountains, gradually emerged; within the waters, all manner of various seeds spontaneously appeared.

At that time, there was another person in the second dhyāna whose life was short and whose merit was exhausted; by the power of karma, he fell and was born into this world with a lifespan of immeasurable years, his own radiance illuminating him. Having dwelt alone for a long time, sorrow and affliction arose in his mind, and he thought to himself:
"Since I dwell here alone, if I possess merit, I pray that another person may come to be born in this place to be my companion."

Having formed this thought, at that time there were sentient beings in the second dhyāna whose merit was exhausted and whose lives had ended; due to the causes and conditions of their karma, they were reborn here.
Upon seeing them, the person felt joy in his heart and immediately thought to himself:
"These people have been produced by my transformation; they are my creation, and I possess sovereign power over them."
That person also thinks:
"I am born from him; he has created me; he possesses sovereign power over my body.
For this reason, all sentient beings give rise to the notion of a self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Good son! The aggregates, elements, and sense bases, as well as the world of sentient beings and the world of lands, all exist by reason of the ten karmic causes and conditions.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a renunciant bodhisattva to be able to contemplate these ten paths of karmic action is not difficult;
for a householder to do so is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are frequently entangled by many adverse conditions.
Chapter Twenty-Five: The Perfection of Patience (*Kṣāntipāramitā*) From the *Upāsakaśīla Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Five: The Perfection of Patience. Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
The Buddha has already previously taught the *dānapāramitā* and the *śīlapāramitā*; how, then, does a bodhisattva cultivate and accumulate the *kṣāntipāramitā*?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
There are two kinds of patience:
first, worldly patience; second, supramundane patience.
To be able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, and suffering and pleasure is called worldly patience.

To be able to endure and have faith in morality, generosity, learning, and wisdom; to possess right view without error; to be patient toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; and to be able to endure all such things as verbal abuse, physical assault, harsh speech, evil deeds, greed, hatred, and delusion—to be able to endure what is difficult to endure, what is difficult to give, and what is difficult to do—is called supramundane patience (*lokottara-kṣānti*).
Good son!
If a bodhisattva encounters others beating, reviling, despising, slandering, using harsh words, or abusing him, at that time he harbors no thought of retaliation within his mind.
Although a bodhisattva performs such acts of patience, they do not do so for the sake of the present, but only for the benefit of the future.
They respond with goodness to good, but do not retaliate with evil for evil. "Good son!
There is patience that is not a pāramitā; there is a pāramitā that is not patience; there is that which is both patience and a pāramitā; and there is that which is neither patience nor a pāramitā.
That which is patience but not a pāramitā refers to worldly patience, the patience practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That which is a pāramitā but not patience refers to the dhyāna-pāramitā.

That which is both patience (*kṣānti*) and a *pāramitā* refers to not giving rise to even a single thought of anger, even when one's head, eyes, hands, or feet are being severed; this includes the *dāna-pāramitā*, the *śīla-pāramitā*, and the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
That which is neither patience nor a *pāramitā* refers to the observance of precepts and the practice of giving by *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. "Good son!

If one wishes to cultivate patience, that person should first destroy arrogance, anger, and delusion; they should not contemplate the marks of 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' nor the marks of lineage or permanence."
If a person can practice contemplations such as these, one should know that this person is able to cultivate patience; having cultivated it thus, the mind attains joy.
When a wise person encounters harsh abuse, they should form this thought:

"These abusive words do not arise simultaneously. When the first word emerges, the subsequent words have not yet arisen; when the subsequent words arise, the first word has already ceased. Since they do not exist at the same time, how can there be such a thing as 'abuse'?"
This is merely the sound of the wind; why should I be angry?

This present body of mine is a composite of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Since four of these aggregates are invisible, they cannot be reviled; it is only the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) that exists through the combination of ten elements. Such a combination is in a state of constant flux, ceasing from moment to moment. If it does not persist, who is there to receive the abuse?
However, that which reviles is simply the wind-element.
Wind is also of two kinds:
internal and external.
I do not give rise to anger toward external winds at all; how then could I give rise to anger toward what is internal?
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those who revile one in the world:
first, those who speak the truth, and second, those who speak falsely.
If what is said is true, why be angry at the truth?
If what is said is false, the falsehood will simply receive the abuse itself; it has no concern with my affairs, so for what reason should I be angry?
If I were to give way to anger, I would be committing evil myself.
Why is this? Because it is due to hatred that one is reborn in the three evil realms.

If I were to undergo suffering and affliction within those three evil realms, it would be that I myself created it and I myself am receiving its retribution; therefore, it is said that all good and evil are caused by my own body.
“Good son! There are five matters that serve as the causes and conditions for patience toward sentient beings:

first, not retaliating when evil is done to one; second, contemplating the perception of impermanence; third, cultivating loving-kindness and compassion; fourth, maintaining a mind free from negligence; and fifth, severing and eliminating anger.”
Good son! If a person can accomplish these five things, you should know that this person is able to cultivate patience (*kṣānti*).

If a person speaks with gentle words, purifies their physical and verbal karma, maintains a harmonious and joyful countenance, takes the initiative to inquire after others' welfare, and is able to contemplate the causal conditions of all suffering and pleasure—you should know that this person is able to cultivate patience.
If one can cultivate the samādhi of emptiness and contemplate all sentient beings as being entirely impermanent and subject to suffering;
when they are reviled, if one can regard the reviler as being like a madman or a fool, immature and lacking wisdom—then it should be known that this person is able to cultivate patience.
A wise person should contemplate thus:
"When one who is superior to me reviles me, I should not become angry. Why is this? [Because...]"
If I were to become angry, they might even take my life.
If I am not their equal, anger should likewise not be requited. Why is this?
Because he is not my equal, if I were to retaliate against him, it would bring disgrace upon my body and speech.
It is like a person who gives poison to another and incurs no reproach, yet if that same person were to consume it themselves, they would be mocked by all;
I am just the same—if I were to harbor anger toward him, I would suffer great affliction in the future, and all the noble ones (āryas) would surely reproach me.

For this reason, even if my body were to be cut, hacked, and dismembered, I should not give rise to anger; rather, I should deeply contemplate the causal conditions of past karma and cultivate loving-kindness and compassion for all beings.
If I cannot endure even such a minor matter as this, how shall I be able to discipline sentient beings?
Forbearance is the direct cause of bodhi; Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is the fruit of forbearance. If I do not plant such a seed, how shall I obtain such a correct fruit?

“Good son! If there is a wise person who delights in practicing patience, that person will always have a serene and joyful countenance, take pleasure in amusements, and bring joy to those who see them; people will never tire of beholding them, and their minds will not harbor greedy attachment toward those they convert.”
When a wise person sees an enemy approaching with harm, they should make this virtuous aspiration:
"May that enemy, in future lives, become my parent, brother, or relative; may they never give rise to thoughts of hatred or resentment toward me."
Furthermore, one should reflect:

"If a person is physically deformed, has an ugly complexion, lacks their sense faculties, or is destitute of wealth, know that all these conditions arise from the causes and conditions of anger; how then can I not now cultivate patience?"
For these reasons, the wise should deeply cultivate the virtue of patience. "Good son!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates patience, he constantly delights in observing the faults and transgressions of birth and death; he delights in practicing the Dharma, is diligent in vigor, and reads, recites, and copies the true scriptures of the Tathāgata. He makes offerings to teachers and elders, and to those of virtuous character; he is able to attend to the suffering of the sick, cultivates loving-kindness and compassion, feels pity for all beings, and when he sees those who are afflicted by pain and distress, he is able to cause them to be free from it."

They always delight in leaving the household life, maintaining the precepts with diligence until the end of their lives, and restraining the six sense faculties so as not to allow the causes and conditions for afflictions to arise; they would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than ever violate the precepts.
If others have business, he delights in managing it for them; he is always possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, and delights in praising the virtue of patience.
To harmonize sentient beings, he endures all manner of suffering; if he can even endure evil deeds from enemies, how much more so those from his own kin?
One is able to endure two kinds of anger: first, anger toward sentient beings; second, anger toward non-sentient things.

One relinquishes one’s own sources of pleasure so that others may obtain happiness; one does not dwell on much evil nor forget even a small amount of goodness. One stays far away from divisive speech, remaining silent regarding both past and present, and refrains from speaking of another's shortcomings. One speaks of the faults of the afflictions to enable the multitude to be free from them; one does not speak of what others do not find pleasing. One purifies body, speech, and mind, and brings all karmic offenses to an end.
If one commits an offense due to the conditions of adventitious afflictions, and having committed it, feels shame and remorse, giving rise to regret in the mind, [it is as follows]:
"Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:..."
The first is the householder, and the second is the renunciant.
For a renunciant bodhisattva to cultivate pure patience is not difficult;
for a householder to cultivate patience is truly difficult.
"Why is this? Because those who live at home are entangled by many evil causes and conditions. Chapter 26:
The Perfection of Vigor (*Vīrya-pāramitā*) From the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Six: The Perfection of Vigor. Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to cultivate the six pāramitās, what constitutes the primary cause? “Good son!”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, desiring to eliminate unwholesome states that have already arisen, to prevent unwholesome states not yet arisen from arising, to cause wholesome states not yet arisen to arise quickly, and to cause wholesome states already arisen to increase and expand, diligently cultivates vigor—this is called vigor. Such vigor is the direct cause for practicing the six pāramitās!
This diligent exertion is able to liberate one from the realm of all afflictions. "Good son!

If one can undergo the sufferings of the three evil realms, you should know that this person is truly able to cultivate the *vīryapāramitā*, cultivating and accumulating it with equanimity—neither too hurried nor too lax."
There are two kinds of diligence:
first, the correct; second, the erroneous.
Having distanced himself from erroneous diligence, the bodhisattva practices correct diligence.
Cultivating faith, generosity, ethical discipline, wisdom derived from hearing, and compassion is called right diligence;

to practice these with a sincere heart at all times without regret, and never to become complacent regarding wholesome dharmas—whether they be mundane or supramundane—is entirely what is termed right diligence.

Although a bodhisattva does not begrudge his own body or life, he should nevertheless cherish them for the sake of protecting the Dharma; he should always practice the four modes of deportment in accordance with the Dharma, maintain a mind free from indolence while cultivating wholesome dharmas, and never abandon the Dharma even at the cost of losing his body and life.
If one can reach the further shore of the six perfections, all of these are the causes and conditions of diligence.
If one personally recites, copies, and contemplates the twelve divisions of the sutras, it is called diligent practice for the sake of the Dharma for oneself;
if one is able to transform and subdue sentient beings through these means, it is called diligent practice for the sake of the Dharma for others.

If, for the sake of Bodhi, one cultivates the path to Bodhi—practicing giving, observing precepts, extensive learning, and wisdom; studying worldly dharmas; making offerings to parents, teachers, elders, and those of virtue; cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; reciting and transcribing the twelve divisions of the scriptures; and furthermore, being able to remain far removed from greed, hatred, and delusion—this is called "diligent application of effort toward Bodhi.
All such practices are termed "right effort" (*samyag-vyāyāma*), and they constitute the true cause of the six *pāramitās*.

“Good son! A person who is indolent cannot at one time practice all forms of giving, nor can they maintain the precepts, exert diligent effort, concentrate the mind in meditative absorption, endure evil matters, or discriminate between good and evil. Therefore, I say that the six pāramitās depend upon diligence.”

“Good son! There is diligent exertion that is not a pāramitā; there is a pāramitā that is not diligent exertion; there is that which is both diligent exertion and a pāramitā; and there is that which is neither diligent exertion nor a pāramitā.”
Vigor that is not a pāramitā includes, for example, wrong vigor, vigor in mundane good deeds, and the vigor possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
There is also that which is a pāramitā but is not vigor, namely, the prajñāpāramitā.
There are those that are both diligence and perfections, namely the five perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditation.

There are things that are neither diligence nor perfections: namely, the giving, ethical discipline, patience, meditative concentration, wisdom, and other virtuous dharmas of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a renunciant bodhisattva to practice diligent vigor is not difficult;
for a householder to practice vigor is indeed difficult. Why is this?
“Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions. 27.
Chapter on the Perfection of Dhyāna. In the Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-seven, the Chapter on the Perfection of Dhyāna, Sujāta said:
“World-Honored One!”
“When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the dhyāna-pāramitā, what is meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi)?

“Good son! Meditative concentration is precisely precept, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; it is the distancing from all fetters and the cultivation and accumulation of wholesome dharmas—this is called meditative concentration.”
Good son! If one is separated from meditative concentration, one cannot even attain worldly affairs, let alone supramundane ones.
Therefore, you should cultivate and accumulate it with a sincere mind.

“If a bodhisattva wishes to attain the dhyāna-pāramitā, they should first draw near to true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and cultivate the path of skillful means for samādhi, namely: the precept of individual liberation, the precept of restraining the sense faculties, and the abandonment of wrong livelihood, abiding in accordance with the Dharma.”
Following the teacher’s instructions, one does not give rise to complacency regarding wholesome dharmas; when practicing the good, the mind never rests.

One always delights in tranquility, remains far removed from the five hindrances, and finds joy in contemplating the faults of birth and death. One constantly cultivates wholesome dharmas with a sincere heart without ceasing, maintains perfect mindfulness, and abandons all negligence.
One should be sparing with speech and likewise moderate in sleep and food; thus the mind becomes pure and the body pure.
One does not associate with evil friends, does not consort with the wicked, and takes no pleasure in worldly affairs.
Knowing the proper time and knowing the Dharma, one thoroughly understands one's own self.

Contemplating the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), if there are signs of joy, sorrow, anger, softness, or hardness, one knows them and is able to eliminate them; it is like a goldsmith who skillfully knows the cold and the heat, ensuring that [the metal] does not lose its proper state.
Delighting in the flavor of the nectar of immortality, though dwelling amidst worldly dharmas, his body and mind remain unmoved, just as Mount Sumeru cannot be shaken by the four winds.
His right mindfulness is firm and steadfast, and he perceives that conditioned phenomena abound in faults.

If a person delights in cultivating this samādhi without ceasing or resting, you should know that such a person will be able to attain it in its full perfection; it is like drilling for fire: because one does not stop, the fire is easily obtained.
“Good son! If one seeks worldly dharmas or supramundane bodhi apart from samādhi, such a thing is impossible.
Good son!”
All samādhis are the very root of all wholesome dharmas; for this reason, one should collect the mind!
Just as a person holding a mirror sees all matters of good and evil, samādhi is thus called the adornment of the path to bodhi.
Experiencing physical and mental bliss is called samādhi;
being neither increasing nor decreasing is called equal samādhi.
From the initial contemplation of the skeleton up until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all are termed samādhi.
This samādhi has four conditions:
first, from desire; second, from diligence; third, from the mind; and fourth, from wisdom.
For these four reasons, one attains immeasurable merit and increases all wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, that which arises from hearing; second, that which arises from reflection; and third, that which arises from cultivation.
From these three factors, they gradually arise.
Furthermore, there are three periods:
namely, the period of arising, the period of abiding, and the period of increase.
"Good son! Within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there is the seed of samādhi; by means of this seed as a causal condition, one attains perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
This samādhi has stages of decline, stability, and increase; if it is present within the four dhyānas, its nature is firm and stable."
From the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the higher stages are progressively superior to the lower ones in this sequence.
Within the fundamental dhyānas, there is joy and bliss, but not in the intermediate dhyāna.
The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are likewise so: they reside in the fundamental [dhyānas] and not elsewhere.

This samādhi is named "Adornment of Bodhi" (*bodhālaṃkāra*); by means of this samādhi, one can attain the path of training (*śaikṣamārga*) and the path beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*), the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), self-benefit and benefit for others, immeasurable bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the ability to discipline sentient beings, immeasurable wisdom, and the samādhis of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). It transforms the dull into the sharp, severs all birth, old age, sickness, and death, enables the accomplishment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and allows one to perceive the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) as if looking through thin silk.
“Good son! A wise person should practice contemplation in this way:
‘All afflictions are my great enemies.’”

Why is this? Because these afflictions are able to destroy both oneself and others; for this reason, I shall cultivate and accumulate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, desiring to benefit all sentient beings and to attain immeasurable, purely wholesome dharmas.
If anyone were to say that one can attain wholesome dharmas apart from loving-kindness and compassion, such a thing is impossible.
In this way, loving-kindness and compassion can sever unwholesomeness, enable sentient beings to leave suffering and receive happiness, and can destroy the desire realm.
If this loving-kindness can take the desire realm as its object, it is called "loving-kindness of the desire realm.
"Good son! If sentient beings can cultivate and accumulate this mind of loving-kindness, such persons shall attain immeasurable merit."
When practicing the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), if one is able to first bestow peace upon one's enemies, this is called the cultivation of loving-kindness.
Good son! All sentient beings consist of three categories:
First, enemies; second, friends; third, neutral persons.
These three groups are called the objects of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
One who cultivates loving-kindness first begins with friends, desiring that they may experience happiness.
Once this contemplation is accomplished, it extends universally to include even one's enemies. Good son!
When the mind of loving-kindness arises, it may arise because of the precepts, or it may arise because of giving;
If one can regard an enemy as a child, this is called attaining loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Good son! Loving-kindness is only able to take [the object] as its cognitive support; it cannot rescue one from suffering.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is not like that; it both takes [the object] as its condition and provides rescue. Good son!
If one can perceive even a hair’s breadth of goodness in an enemy and does not see their faults, you should know that such a person is said to be practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

If one goes to inquire after an enemy who has encountered the suffering of illness, tending to their ailment and providing whatever they require, it should be known that such a person is able to skillfully cultivate loving-kindness.
"Good son! If one can cultivate patience, you should know that this is precisely the causal condition for cultivating loving-kindness.
Such a mind of loving-kindness is itself the causal condition for all peace and happiness."

If one can cultivate loving-kindness, it should be known that such a person is able to destroy all causes and conditions for arrogance, and is able to practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, cultivating them in accordance with the Dharma.
If a person cultivates meditative concentration, you should know that this person cultivates Brahma-merit—because they attain the body of Brahma, it is called Brahma-merit.
If a person can contemplate the faults of birth and death and the virtues of nirvana, the dung and soil trodden under their feet should be borne upon one's head.

This person can endure what is difficult to endure, can give what is difficult to give, and can perform what is difficult to perform; this person is able to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the eight liberations.
Again, he forms this thought:
"Whatever evil karma of body, speech, and mind all sentient beings have committed, should they suffer the retribution for it in the future, may I receive it all;
and whatever wholesome fruits of retribution I possess, may all sentient beings share in receiving them with me."
In this way, compassion is extensive because its objects are extensive, and limited because its objects are limited.
There are three types of compassion:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, taking a relative as the object; second, taking an enemy as the object; third, taking a neutral person as the object.
Again, there are three kinds:
First, that which takes greed as its object; second, that which takes sentient beings as its object; third, that which takes non-sentient beings as its object.
Such objects of focus are all termed samādhi.
The same applies to the minds of compassion, joy, and equanimity.
"Good son! There is dhyāna that is not a pāramitā;
there is a pāramitā that is not dhyāna; there is that which is both dhyāna and a pāramitā; and there is that which is neither dhyāna nor a pāramitā."
That which is dhyāna but not pāramitā refers to mundane dhyāna and the meditative concentrations possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That which is pāramitā but not meditative concentration refers to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence.
That which is both dhyāna and pāramitā refers to the vajra-samādhi.
That which is neither dhyāna nor pāramitā refers to all wholesome dharmas arising from hearing and reflection produced by all sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a renunciant bodhisattva to cultivate pure dhyāna is not difficult;
for a householder to cultivate purity is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions. 28.
*Prajñāpāramitā-parivarta*. In the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, the twenty-eighth chapter, "The Chapter on Prajñāpāramitā," Sujāta said:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva cultivate the pure perfection of wisdom?

"Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who maintains the precepts with diligence, possesses extensive learning and a right livelihood, cultivates patience, has compassion for sentient beings, possesses a mind of great shame and remorse, stays far removed from envy and jealousy, and truly understands all skillful means; [then he cultivates the pure perfection of wisdom]."

Undergoing suffering for the sake of the multitude without giving rise to regret or retreat; delighting in the practice of giving; being able to discipline sentient beings; skillfully knowing the characteristics of the gravity or lightness of transgressions; diligently exhorting sentient beings to perform meritorious deeds; knowing both words and their meanings;
having a mind free from arrogance; drawing near to virtuous friends; being able to benefit oneself and others;

reverencing the Triple Gem, teachers, preceptors, elders, and those of virtue; not conceiving thoughts of contempt toward one's own body or toward Bodhi; and being able to contemplate the profound and wondrous merits of Bodhi.

One who knows the characteristics of good and evil, knows all worldly and world-transcending treatises on sound, knows causes and effects, and knows both initial expedients and their fundamental basis—such a person should be known as one capable of attaining wisdom.
Such wisdom is of three kinds:
first, that which arises from hearing; second, that which arises from reflection; and third, that which arises from cultivation.
Attaining the meaning through the words is called that which arises from hearing.
Attaining meaning through reflection is called "arising from reflection";
attaining meaning through cultivation is called "arising from cultivation.

Being able to read the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras, being able to eliminate the net of doubts, being able to read all worldly treatises and mundane affairs, and being able to skillfully distinguish between the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox—this is called wisdom.

To be able to skillfully discern the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the meanings of the terms for the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) along with their causes and effects, the characteristics of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and tranquility (*śamatha*), the superior, middling, and inferior characteristics, the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, as well as the four perversions, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
to be able to skillfully discern such matters as these is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
“Good son! A person of wisdom who seeks the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness should always draw near to the Buddha and his disciples.”

In a world where the Buddha-dharma does not exist, he takes pleasure in leaving home to study under non-Buddhist teachers; though situated within heterodox paths, he delights in seeking the essential right path, constantly cultivating the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the five supernormal powers.

Having attained the five supernormal powers, he contemplates the perception of impurity and the perception of impermanence, and is able to speak of the many faults and transgressions of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

For the sake of right speech, he teaches all sentient beings the science of phonology (*śabda-vidyā*), enabling them to be free from the diseases of body and mind. He delights in instructing others in worldly affairs, and there is nothing that surpasses his professional accomplishments, namely incantations, prescriptions, and various medicinal drugs.
He is able to skillfully seek wealth and, having acquired it, is able to protect it; he employs it according to principle and bestows it as gifts in accordance with the Dharma.

Although he knows all things, he does not give rise to arrogance; he attains great merit yet does not become complacent; and he is able to teach sentient beings to practice faith, generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom.

He knows the skillful means regarding the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate; he thoroughly understands the sequence of causes and conditions for training and practice; he knows the path to enlightenment and the adornments of that path; he knows the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings; he knows external treatises on sound without his mind becoming attached to them; he knows how to discipline sentient beings according to the appropriate time and circumstances; he knows the world of sentient beings and the world of lands; and he knows [the path] starting from the fulfillment of the six *pāramitās*.

“Good son! There is wisdom that is not a pāramitā; there is a pāramitā that is not wisdom; there is that which is both wisdom and a pāramitā; and there is that which is neither wisdom nor a pāramitā.”
That which is wisdom but not a *pāramitā* refers to all worldly wisdom and the wisdom practiced by *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
That which is a *pāramitā* but not wisdom—such a thing is impossible.
That which is both wisdom and a pāramitā refers to all six pāramitās.
That which is neither wisdom nor a pāramitā refers to the generosity, ethical discipline, and diligence of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

“Good son! If there are those who can diligently cultivate these six pāramitās, such persons are said to be making offerings to the six directions, and they are able to increase their wealth and lifespan.”
“Good son! There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.”
For a renunciant bodhisattva to cultivate pure wisdom is not difficult;
for a householder to cultivate purity is indeed difficult. Why is this?
"This is because those who live as householders are entangled by many evil causes and conditions.
When this Dharma was spoken, the elder’s son Suvikrāntavikrāmin and one thousand other upāsakas resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having thus resolved his mind, he immediately rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, withdrew, and took leave to return to his dwelling.
*Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
